title: N-Acetylgalactosamine-Conjugated Small Interfering RNA Targeting Hepatic Angiotensinogen in Hypertension: A Phase I Clinical Trial With Randomized Part A and Open-Label Part B.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Angiotensinogen (AGT) is the precursor of angiotensin peptides and a key determinant of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activity. ART101 is an investigational N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA (GalNAc-siRNA) designed to durably suppress hepatic AGT synthesis.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of single ascending doses of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA in healthy volunteers and to provide an initial exploratory assessment of blood pressure effects in patients with hypertension.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase I study was conducted from January 2025 to April 2026 with 24-week follow-up. Part A was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, single ascending-dose trial; part B was an open-label, single-dose study. The study took place at Beijing Friendship Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. Part A enrolled 40 healthy adults randomized 6:2 to receive the GalNAc-siRNA (25-600 mg) or placebo; 39 completed the study. Part B enrolled 8 patients with hypertension receiving the GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg; all completed the study.
INTERVENTIONS: A single subcutaneous injection of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA (25, 75, 150, 300, or 600 mg) or placebo in part A; a single open-label subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg, in part B.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was safety and tolerability; secondary outcomes included pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, exploratory blood pressure assessments, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system biomarkers.
RESULTS: Among 40 healthy volunteers (27 [67.5%] male; mean [SD] age, 40.4 [7.8] years) and 8 patients (6 [75.0%] male; mean [SD] age, 47.3 [10.3] years) with hypertension, the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA was well tolerated. In part A, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 23 of 30 active-treatment participants (76.7%) vs 7 of 10 placebo recipients (70.0%); in part B, 6 of 8 patients (75.0%) had TEAEs. No serious adverse events, injection site reactions, or hyperkalemia were observed; all TEAEs were mild to moderate. Plasma exposure (maximum plasma concentration [Cmax] and area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) increased with dose over the wide dose range from 25 mg to 600 mg. Mean maximum serum AGT reductions of 93% (at 600 mg) in healthy volunteers and 90% (at 600 mg) in patients with hypertension were observed. At 24 weeks after a single 600-mg dose, the placebo-corrected 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure decreased by 12.9 mm Hg in healthy participants.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this phase I study, no serious treatment-related safety signals were identified. Sustained, dose-dependent AGT reductions and exploratory blood pressure lowering were observed. These findings support further investigation of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA as a potential long-acting therapeutic for hypertension.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: China Drug Clinical Registry Identifiers: CTR20250041 (part A) and CTR20253973 (part B).

title: A role for eIF5A in translational control of stress-inducible proteins in multiple myeloma cell lines.
abstract: Impaired protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) causes ER stress and activates the unfolded protein response (UPR), which can induce apoptosis during prolonged ER stress. ER stress is therapeutically targeted in plasma cell malignancies, such as multiple myeloma (MM), but these treatments remain noncurative, and UPR signaling in B-cell malignancies is incompletely understood. A targeted CRISPR-Cas9 screen in RPMI-8226 cells exposed to thapsigargin identified known ER stress regulators (XBP1, IRE1, and calreticulin) and the translation factor eIF5A (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5A), whose role in ER stress remains unclear. Competition assays showed that eIF5A depletion is detrimental under basal conditions but confers a proliferation advantage during thapsigargin treatment. Inducible EIF5A knockouts confirmed reduced sensitivity specifically to thapsigargin, loss of eIF5A had no or sensitizing effects on cell death induced by other ER stress drugs. Polysome profiling revealed that not general translation, but the translation of specific mRNA transcripts coding for UPR components and apoptotic proteins was affected by eIF5A depletion. Correspondingly, EIF5A KO cells showed reduced thapsigargin-induced UPR activation. In conclusion, these findings indicate that loss of eIF5A alters the stress response in MM cells.

title: Reprogramming tumor cells with LCOR mRNA nanotherapy to enhance immunotherapy.
abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) are often considered undruggable due to their structural complexity. mRNA technologies can overcome this therapeutic limitation by enabling dynamic protein replacement therapies. Here, we explore the TF activity of LCOR (Ligand-dependent corepressor), which suppresses tumor growth, at least in part by inducing the antigen presentation machinery (APM) in tumor cells and constraining cellular plasticity. These effects facilitate tumor immune recognition and immune-mediated tumor eradication. We used poly β-(amino esters) (pBAE) nanoparticles (NPs) for local delivery of Lcor mRNA in multiple breast cancer models. pBAE-NPs efficiently encapsulate mRNA and facilitate cellular uptake, achieving optimal endosomal escape, resulting in high transfection efficiency in vitro and in vivo, restoring LCOR function in tumor cells and engaging their APM. In preclinical models, intratumoral delivery of Lcor mRNA reduced tumor growth. Importantly, the combination of Lcor mRNA-loaded RH-pBAE-NPs with anti-PDL1 or anti-CTLA4 immunotherapies eradicated most of the tumors in our preclinical TNBC model. Overall, our nanotherapeutic strategy emerges as an innovative TF-replacement therapy in a lock-in/wipe-out fashion, leveraging the immunogenic effects of LCOR to eradicate breast cancer tumors when combined with immunotherapy.

title: Prostate Cancer Patient-Derived Organoids (PDOs) as Functional Avatars for Antisense Oligonucleotide (ASO)-Based Personalized Therapy.
abstract: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDOs) closely preserve the cellular heterogeneity, histopathology, and molecular features of the original tumors, making them powerful preclinical models. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are an emerging class of precision medicines that modulate gene expression at the RNA level with high target specificity, yet their application in organoid systems remains underexplored. Here, we adapted previously described protocols to establish a biobank of prostate cancer (PC) PDOs, achieving a high initial growth success rate (>90%). Histological and molecular analyses confirmed the preservation of key tumor features. Using these models, we assessed several ASOs, with particular emphasis on OGX-427 (Apatorsen), an ASO targeting heat shock protein 27 (HSP27) that has been evaluated in phase I/II clinical trials. While OGX-427 effectively suppressed HSP27 expression and inhibited cell growth in 2D cultures, its efficacy was markedly limited in 3D organoids, likely due to extracellular matrix and structural barriers. Removing Matrigel and applying single-cell transfection overcame these barriers, achieving efficient ASO uptake, significant target protein downregulation, and robust, dose-dependent inhibition of organoid growth. These findings underscore the utility of PDOs for evaluating ASO-based therapies and their potential to accelerate precision oncology strategies for PC and other malignancies.

title: Inhibiting Lactylation-Mediated Metabolic-Epigenetic Reprogramming to Potentiate Tumor Photo-Immunotherapy.
abstract: Cancer immunotherapies face limitations in treating "cold" tumors due to immune suppression driven by metabolic dysregulation within the tumor microenvironment. Research has revealed that tumor cells produce excess lactate via hypoxia-induced glycolysis, promoting histone lactylation and establishing immunosuppression-associated metabolic-epigenetic reprogramming. Here, a near-infrared (NIR)-triggered nanoplatform (RgA-L-I/P/R) has been developed to fundamentally dismantle the immunosuppression via the metabolic-epigenetic axis. Upon NIR excitation, the platform released oxygen from perfluoropentane (PFP) ("oxygen unlocking chamber") in the tumor through dual targeting of AS1411 and Rg3 ("nano-warhead"), liberating the IR-1048 and the CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) ("NIR immune trigger" and "metabolic nanolock"). IR-1048 induced immunogenic cell death (ICD) to trigger dendritic cell maturation and cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration, while CRISPR/Cas9 RNP induced LDHA (lactate dehydrogenase A) gene knockdown that locked the lactate supply and reprogrammed metabolism and epigenetics. These changes reduced histone lactylation and IL-10 expression, promoting the conversion of tumor-associated macrophages to the M1 type and synergistically downregulating hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression upon oxygen release. This nanoplatform enables synergistic photothermal immunostimulation with CRISPR-mediated metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. Rather than merely countering mild downstream immune regulation by ICD, it seeks to fundamentally eliminate the immunosuppression, offering novel therapeutic strategies through the metabolic-epigenetic pathway for poorly immunoresponsive tumors.

title: Emerging Lipid Nanoparticle Targeting Strategies for Extrahepatic Delivery of RNA Therapeutics.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed RNA therapeutics through their high delivery efficiency, scalable manufacturing, and favorable safety profiles, as demonstrated by COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and clinically approved small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutics. However, extending RNA delivery beyond the liver to extrahepatic tissues, including the spleen, lungs, lymph nodes, brain, and tumors, remains challenging because of the intrinsic hepatotropism of conventional LNPs and their limited cell-type specificity. Recent advances in lipid chemistry, particle engineering, surface functionalization, protein corona modulation, and route-specific administration have enabled new strategies to redirect LNPs toward specific tissues and cell populations. This review systematically examines these approaches and highlights key determinants of LNP tropism, including formulation composition, surface properties, endogenous protein adsorption, and administration route. We further discuss the clinical translation of extrahepatic LNP delivery, covering clinically validated products, emerging therapeutic candidates, and gaps between preclinical models and human applications. Major challenges include cell-resolved biodistribution, long-term safety, repeated-dose immunogenicity, cross-study comparability, and standardized quantitative assessment. Finally, we explore how high-throughput screening, machine learning, and data-driven design can accelerate the rational optimization of next-generation LNPs. These advances may facilitate precise tissue- and cell-selective RNA delivery, expanding the therapeutic potential of RNA medicines beyond the liver.

title: CausalCellInfer: Prioritizing Cell-Type-Specific Disease Associations From Genetically Predicted Transcriptomes in Biobank Cohorts.
abstract: Integrating single-cell RNA sequencing(scRNA-seq) with the phenotypic depth of population-scale biobanks is essential for elucidating the cellular basis of complex diseases. However, this is hindered by limited scRNA-seq sample size and the lack of cellular resolution in biobanks. We present CausalCellInfer, a scalable computational framework bringing cellular resolution to bulk and genotype-imputed transcriptomes. CausalCellInfer employs an invariant causal prediction-inspired method(scRNA-seq-based invariant generalized covariance measure, scI-GCM) to select environment-stable marker genes, a parsimonious deep neural network for cell-fraction deconvolution, and regularized matrix completion to reconstruct cell-type-specific (CTS) expression profiles. This design is optimized for biobank-scale data with technical heterogeneity and limited gene overlap. Validated across simulated data, pseudo-bulk and real peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) datasets, CausalCellInfer demonstrated superior accuracy and efficiency over existing methods. Applied to ∼500 000 UK Biobank (UKBB) participants across 29 traits, it captured known pathological shifts, such as reduced pancreatic β-cell proportions in type 2 diabetes, and identified novel biological signals, including disrupted excitatory neuron-oligodendrocyte interactions in depression. Inferred CTS differential expression patterns showed significant concordance with independent single-cell studies and were enriched for Open Targets disease genes. Overall, CausalCellInfer bridges single-cell insights and population-scale genomics, enabling systematic discovery of putative disease mechanisms at cellular resolution.

title: CRISPR-Scan: Cas13a Mismatch Tolerance Enabled Ultra-Multiplexed Detection of Same-Site Indels in Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
abstract: Detection of gene mutations related to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is crucial for its early diagnosis, personalized treatment, and recurrence monitoring. However, accurate detection of diverse mutations occurring at the same locus remains technically challenging. The CRISPR/Cas system, with its unique programmable nucleic acid recognition capabilities, provides a promising solution. Here, we elucidated that CRISPR/LwaCas13a is tolerant to consecutive substitutions but highly sensitive to insertions or deletions (indels) at specific positions of the spacer sequence, enabling rational CRISPR RNA (crRNA) design for multiplex detection of same-site indels. Guided by these principles, we achieved effective detection of ultra-multiplex nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) c.863_864 4-bp insertions with a single crRNA, while maintaining specificity against the wild-type transcripts. We further established a one-pot CRISPR system, CRISPR-Scan, by integrating recombinase polymerase amplification with LwaCas13a cleavage. CRISPR-Scan enabled detection of mutations in backgrounds as low as 0.01%. In clinical validation, it identified NPM1 mutations in 43 of 120 AML patients, consistent with next-generation sequencing (NGS). Continuous monitoring of four AML patients indicated early recurrence with higher sensitivity than first-generation sequencing (FGS) and full concordance with NGS. A microfluidic chip and portable device further facilitate accurate AML mutation detection. This platform offers an efficient and convenient approach for early AML diagnosis and measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring.

title: A Dual-Delivery System Designed to Overcome EV-Mediated Ferroptosis Resistance for Efficient Solid Tumor Therapy.
abstract: Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) are emerging as critical mediators of metabolic adaptation, yet their role in orchestrating ferroptosis resistance within the tumor microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, we show that highly malignant osteosarcoma (OS) cells respond to ferroptotic stress by secreting EVs enriched with Alpha-enolase (ENO1). These EVs-ENO1 not only bolster the antioxidant capacity of tumor cells but also confer widespread ferroptosis resistance to macrophages and neutrophils, fostering an immunosuppressive niche. To disrupt this metabolic defense, we developed an OS-targeting lipid nanoparticle (LNP) system for the synergistic delivery of BAP1 mRNA and ENO1 siRNA. We demonstrate that this dual-delivery platform enhances ferroptosis through two complementary regulatory pathways, BAP1/SLC7A11 and ENO1/GPX4, leading to potent lipid peroxidation and tumor cell death. In syngeneic orthotopic and lung metastasis models, these targeted LNPs significantly suppress tumor progression and catalyze anti-tumor immunity by activating M1-type macrophages and cytotoxic T cells. Our findings identify the secretion of EVs-ENO1 as a key reactive mechanism against ferroptosis and provide a translatable nanomedicine strategy to overcome metabolic and epigenetic resistance in solid tumors.

title: Mitochondrial Quality Control in Degenerative Musculoskeletal Diseases: Signaling Networks and Therapeutic Landscapes.
abstract: Degenerative musculoskeletal disorders, including osteoarthritis (OA), intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD), and osteoporosis (OP), are increasingly viewed as disorders of mitochondrial quality control (MQC) rather than passive mechanical wear. The MQC network, comprising mitochondrial dynamics, mitophagy-biogenesis coupling, and inter-organelle communication, organizes the aging-inflammation-metabolism axis. Its collapse releases mtDNA fragments that act as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) activating innate immunity via cGAS-STING, and metabolic intermediates that remodel the epigenome through histone lactylation, potentially locking acute stress into a "metabolic memory", although the mtDNA-methylation component remains hypothesis-level. Multi-omics and cell-free mtDNA liquid biopsy underpin a proposed subtyping into bioenergetic failure, immuno-inflammatory activation, and senescent cell accumulation, still a within-OA hypothesis pending independent and cross-disease validation. Therapy is shifting from symptom management toward organelle medicine, including cardiolipin stabilizers, PROTAC-mediated protein degradation, mitochondrial base editing, and engineered mitochondrial transplantation. Metformin has randomized trial evidence in knee OA pending confirmation, NAD+ precursors are in early clinical testing, and SS-31 holds accelerated approval only for Barth syndrome; other strategies remain preclinical. Delivery barriers and disease heterogeneity require precision stratification, biomimetic models, and AI-driven decision-making. This review delineates the shared molecular logic of the three diseases and proposes a prototype subtyping-to-treatment roadmap pending validation.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Screen Identifies RPS19 as an Immunotherapy Target in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNPSS) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNPSS efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNPSS-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

title: Comparative Analysis of Poly(Ethylene Glycol) (PEG) and Poly(2-Ethyl-2-Oxazoline) (PEtOx) for Organic Solvent-Free Lipid Nanoparticle Formulations.
abstract: Efficient, biocompatible, and flexible application of CRISPR-Cas9 remains a major challenge in gene therapy. This study addresses a novel formulation method, focusing on organic solvent-free lipid nanoparticles for the efficient delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components. Therefore, novel stealth lipids comprising the lipid anchor cholesterol hemisuccinate conjugated to poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx) were synthesized and evaluated as a promising in vitro alternative to commercially available poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based lipids. Our study identified PEtOx-lipids as markedly more biocompatible compared to PEG-based analogues (12-fold reduction in cytotoxicity; 99% reduced hemolytic effect) with high efficiency for mRNA gene delivery. We demonstrate successful CRISPR-Cas9 activity ex vivo and efficient uptake of PEtOx nanoparticles by macrophages in vivo (66.5% pos. F4/80+ macrophages). Our data demonstrate that PEtOx-based stealth lipids are a promising alternative to PEG. The resulting LNPs, optimized for fully aqueous manufacturing, address key limitations of current LNP systems, including immunogenicity and the reliance on ethanol-based production processes.

title: Hybridization-Mediated Reversible sgRNA Caging Enables Tumor-Selective Gene Editing for Potentiating Antitumor Immunity via cGAS Demethylation.
abstract: Spatiotemporal precision remains a critical challenge against the gene editing technology used for disease treatment. We herein developed a tumor cell-selective CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system by introducing a complementary single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) containing apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) sites (AP-ssDNA) along the target region of single-guided RNA (sgRNA). The engineered hybrid (AP-ssDNA/sgRNA) could tracelessly release the native sgRNA in tumor cells due to cleavage of AP-ssDNA by the overexpressed apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1), thus enabling tumor-selective gene editing. Subsequently, a biodegradable lipid nanoparticle based on dynamic covalent bonding was developed to codeliver Cas9-encoding mRNA (mCas9) with AP-ssDNA/sgRNA targeting the SUV39H1 gene, which mediated silence of cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) methylation to activate stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and enhanced antitumor immunity. As thus, when coupled with radiotherapy, the gene editing platform provoked robust antitumor efficacy in B16F10 xenograft tumor-bearing mice. This study provides a versatile paradigm for conditionally controlled gene editing and highlights the therapeutic potential of cGAS demethylation in reactivating cGAS-STING pathway for antitumor immunotherapy.

title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design.
abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

title: Toward a Platform PBPK Model to Characterize the Plasma and Tissue Disposition of Unconjugated Antisense Oligonucleotides and GalNAc-Conjugated Small Interfering RNAs in Preclinical Species and Human.
abstract: Unconjugated antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as transformative therapeutic modalities, but their translation remains hindered by complex pharmacokinetics characterized by rapid plasma clearance, heterogeneous tissue uptake, and prolonged intracellular retention. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling offers a mechanistic framework to integrate these processes across species, yet applications to oligonucleotides remain limited, and existing efforts are typically restricted to specific chemistries or routes of administration. This study aimed to develop a cross-species PBPK platform to characterize the plasma and tissue disposition of unconjugated ASOs and GalNAc-siRNAs in preclinical species and humans, and to evaluate the consistency of estimated drug-specific parameters with pre-specified allometric scaling relationships within the domain of compounds and routes considered. Published datasets spanning mice, rats, non-human primates, and humans were integrated for representative unconjugated ASOs (Malat-1, GluR1, p-tau, tominersen) and GalNAc-siRNAs (ALN-AT3, givosiran, fitusiran). The PBPK model incorporated 11 tissue compartments, cerebrospinal fluid substructures, tissue substructures, endosomal trafficking, non-specific binding in kidney and liver, and ASGPR-mediated internalization for GalNAc-siRNAs. Parameters for endocytosis, exocytosis, and degradation were estimated, and estimated values were compared with pre-specified allometric exponents to assess physiological plausibility (i.e., as a consistency check rather than independent inference of scaling laws). The model captured plasma, liver, kidney, and CNS profiles across species, reproducing rapid systemic clearance with prolonged tissue half-lives. Estimated parameter values for endocytosis, exocytosis, and non-specific kidney binding were consistent with pre-specified allometric exponents (b = -0.25 and -0.2, respectively), supporting the physiological plausibility of the estimates. Sensitivity analyses identified endocytosis and rate of degradation as dominant determinants of systemic and tissue disposition. This work establishes a translational PBPK platform for unconjugated ASOs and GalNAc-conjugated siRNAs, enabling quantitative interspecies extrapolation within the domain of the compounds, routes, and species studied. The framework provides a mechanistic basis to support dose selection, safety assessment, and clinical translation for these subclasses; extrapolation to other oligonucleotide subclasses (e.g., GalNAc-ASOs, unconjugated siRNAs, LNP-formulated oligonucleotides) will require additional datasets and dedicated validation.

title: From delivery to integration: CRISPR-mediated large insert gene editing in primary human T cells.
abstract: Large insert gene editing in ex vivo, primary human T cells represents an important approach for engineering next-generation cellular immunotherapies. While CRISPR-based editing is well-established for small genetic modifications, large insert knock-in remains a technical bottleneck. This review examines current strategies for achieving efficient, precise and safe integration of large genetic elements. We compare delivery methods for CRISPR components, highlighting electroporation of Cas9 ribonucleoproteins as the most efficient but often cytotoxic approach; emerging alternatives such as cell-penetrating peptides and lipid nanoparticles offer improved cell viability at the expense of editing efficiency. The influence of genomic locus selection, guide RNA design and chromatin context on editing outcomes, as well as the role of homology-directed repair (HDR) template design is evaluated. Various template formats-including linear double- and single-stranded DNA, plasmids, circular single-stranded (css) DNA and recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV)-are assessed for their efficiency, toxicity and risk of off-target integration. Where possible, cross-study normalisation is used to enable meaningful comparisons. rAAV templates consistently achieve the highest insertion rates but come with concerns regarding cost, size limitations and insertional mutagenesis, whereas non-viral approaches such as cssDNA templates show promise. Additionally, we review the use of small-molecule modulators to enhance HDR efficiency, noting trade-offs between improved insertion rates and potential genomic instability. Overall, successful large insert editing requires balancing of editing efficiency, cell viability and genomic safety considerations. Continued optimisation of delivery systems, template design and repair pathway modulation will be critical for advancing scalable and clinically viable T-cell therapies.

title: Comprehensive Evaluation of Gastrointestinal Factors Influencing the Stability and Function of mRNA-Encapsulated Lipid Nanoparticles.
abstract: Owing to the intrinsic instability of mRNA, its routes of administration are limited, and to date, only injectable delivery has been clinically applied. In contrast, oral administration exposes mRNA to a variety of substances in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Despite these challenges, oral delivery remains the most familiar and convenient route for patients, making the development of orally administrable mRNA-encapsulated lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) highly desirable. However, no studies have directly examined how mRNA-LNPs are affected within the GI environment. In the present study, we investigated the effects of representative GI components on mRNA-LNPs. Among several digestive enzymes, pepsin markedly reduced the protein-expression efficiency of the particles, whereas amylase had no effect. Pepsin-treated particles exhibited increased size, suggesting that structural alterations contributed to the observed functional loss. Lipase at high concentrations impaired nanoparticle function. Because lipase hydrolyzes ester bonds in lipids, we examined LNPs incorporating C12-200, an ionizable lipid lacking ester bonds, instead of SM-102. The C12-200 formulation showed reduced susceptibility to lipase-induced functional loss, indicating that enzymatic lipid degradation underlay the observed effects. Simulated gastric fluid also significantly diminished particle functionality. A detailed analysis of the relationship between functionality and pH revealed that impairment primarily occurred at approximately pH 1 but not at pH ≥ 3. Collectively, these findings identify the key GI factors that compromise mRNA-LNP integrity and provide important insights into the rational design of orally administrable mRNA-LNP formulations.

title: Mitochondrial Genome Characteristics of Rhodobryum laxelimbatum and Comparative Analysis of RNA Editing and Codon Usage Bias With the Chloroplast Genome.
abstract: Rhodobryum laxelimbatum is a traditional medicinal plant belonging to the genus Rhodobryum. To date, studies on this genus have focused primarily on its geographical distribution, chemical constituents, and biological activities, whereas genomic data within the genus are limited. The mitochondrial genome of R. laxelimbatum was sequenced, assembled, and annotated. Genomic structural features and simple sequence repeats (SSRs) were comprehensively characterized. Comparative analyses of RNA editing patterns and codon usage bias were performed using the mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes of R. laxelimbatum. The results revealed that the complete mitochondrial genome of R. laxelimbatum was 103,071 bp in length. It comprises 40 protein-coding genes (Nad7 is a pseudogene), 24 transfer RNA genes, and 3 ribosomal RNA genes. In total, 76 SSRs were detected. The mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes contained 189 and 608 RNA editing sites, respectively, with the conversion of hydrophilic amino acids to hydrophobic amino acids being dominant. Both organellar genomes exhibited the highest GC content at the first codon position. GC12 was significantly associated with GC3 only in chloroplasts with steeper regression trends. Mitochondrial genes exhibited greater variation in the effective number of codons (ENC), and most genes in both genomes clustered near the expected ENC curve. Parity Rule 2 plot revealed a distinct base-composition imbalance at synonymous third codon positions-mitochondria exhibited T3s > A3s with comparable G3s and C3s, whereas chloroplasts exhibited T3s > A3s and G3s > C3s. Five optimal codons were identified in the mitochondrial genome, predominantly ending in G/A/C, whereas nine were identified in the chloroplast genome, ending in A/U. Correspondence analysis demonstrated that codon usage bias was shaped by multiple interacting factors rather than a single determinant. This study provides crucial evidence for clarifying the evolutionary patterns of organelle genomes in Rhodobryum, and for understanding its genetic characteristics and molecular basis.

title: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical neurons from monozygotic twins with the Gαo1 K278del mutation reveal disease mechanisms relevant to GNAO1-related encephalopathy.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Rare de novo variants in GNAO1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a heterogenous display of early onset epilepsy, movement abnormalities, and global developmental delay. More than 100 pathogenic variants in GNAO1 have been identified and categorized into four groups according to their protein features. Most pathogenic variants affect both GNAO1 isoforms, whereas approximately 20% of patients have a GNAO1A-specific variant. Response to therapy is notoriously variable, even among patients harboring the same variant. Here, we set out to model GNAO1A-related encephalopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from monozygotic twins carrying the Gαo1 K278del variant and uncovered-while taking advantage of the identical genomic setting-phenotypic features that further our understanding of the defects underlying the disorder.
METHODS: We generated hiPSCs expressing the c.832_834delAAG; p.K278del variant in GNAO1A obtained from monozygotic twins who both developed seizures 2 days after birth. For either twin, Gαo1 K278del and CRISPR-Cas9-repaired isogenic control hiPSC lines were differentiated into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and subsequently into cortical neurons. Variant-specific transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological characteristics were analyzed.
RESULTS: Gαo1 K278del mutated hiPSC-derived NPCs showed disorganized neural rosette structures and revealed an altered transcriptome. In cortical neurons, the Gαo1 K278del variant caused a reduction in the size and complexity of dendrites that was accompanied by an increase in pre- and postsynaptic puncta. Multielectrode array (MEA) recordings revealed an abnormal cortical neuron bursting activity pattern with fewer bursts and more spikes per burst. The antiepileptic drug levetiracetam reduced the spike frequency and the number of spikes per burst in cortical neurons from both patients.
SIGNIFICANCE: The developed GNAO1A hiPSC-derived in vitro model uncovered key structural and functional features of GNAO1-related encephalopathy. The comparable in vitro phenotypes in neurons from both twins underscore the utility of hiPSC-derived models to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying GNAO1-related encephalopathy as well as effects of therapeutic intervention.

title: SFRP2 Editing Enhances Dermal Papilla Cell Function via Activation of the PI3K-Akt Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Secreted frizzled-related protein 2 (SFRP2) is an important molecule that regulates cell growth and development and participates in hair follicle (HF) development and homeostasis. The present study seeks to determine whether SFRP2 directly targets dermal papilla cells (DPCs), the pivotal functional cell population within HF, and characterize the intracellular signaling regulatory network triggered downstream. In this study, a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SFRP2 gene editing DPC model was established in vitro. Multi-omics analyses, including transcriptomics and metabolomics, were performed alongside functional assays to investigate the regulatory mechanisms of SFRP2 in DPCs. Among three designed single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), sgRNA3 showed the highest editing efficiency (67.0%) without off-target effects. Genetic editing of SFRP2 markedly increased the transcript levels of pivotal hair follicle‑development‑related genes (LEF1, CCND1 and Wnt2). Meanwhile, it suppressed TGF‑β1 transcription, which resulted in elevated proliferation capacity and diminished apoptotic activity within DPCs. Transcriptomic profiling identified 2288 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in PI3K-Akt, MAPK and TNF signaling pathways, while metabolomic analysis identified 185 differential metabolites (DMs) associated with apoptosis, ABC transporters, and PI3K-Akt signaling. Integrated multi-omics analysis confirmed PI3K-Akt signaling as a central regulatory axis. Western blot analysis revealed increased phosphorylation of PI3K and Akt following SFRP2 editing, indicating pathway activation. Treatment of SFRP2-edited DPCs with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 reduced the elevated phosphorylation and reversed the functional phenotypes, confirming PI3K-Akt pathway involvement. Collectively, these findings indicate that SFRP2 mediates DPC biological activities by means of PI3K‑Akt‑driven transcriptional‑metabolic networks, yielding novel perspectives on the molecular regulatory machinery controlling HF physiology.

title: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in Rare Disease: From Precision Medicine to Programmable Platforms.
abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics (NATs), including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics and programmable editing technologies, are reshaping the therapeutic landscape for inherited metabolic and genetic disease. Unlike conventional small molecules or biologics, NATs enable sequence-directed modulation of target gene expression and therefore provide unprecedented flexibility for targeting pathogenic mechanisms previously considered undruggable. Recent clinical successes have established proof of concept for multiple NAT modalities across neurological, hepatic, muscular and metabolic disorders. However, broader implementation remains constrained by challenges in tissue-specific delivery, biomarker validation, natural-history infrastructure and evidence generation in ultra-rare populations. In parallel, increasing platform reproducibility is beginning to challenge traditional product-based regulatory paradigms. This review examines the principal classes of NATs and proposes a practical framework for modality selection based on disease biology, tissue accessibility, durability, reversibility and clinical context. We discuss key translational bottlenecks beyond delivery, including biomarker-outcome relationships, small-population trial design and the limitations of conventional evidentiary frameworks in rare disease. A central theme of this review is the growing transition from isolated precision medicines towards increasingly programmable therapeutic platforms. We explore how advances in extrahepatic delivery, computational oligonucleotide design, artificial intelligence-assisted optimisation and programmable editing technologies may progressively support more scalable and individualised therapeutic development. Finally, we discuss emerging regulatory frameworks that may better accommodate platform-level predictability while maintaining rigorous evaluation of sequence-specific and disease-specific risks.

title: Inhaled Nanomedicines for Lung Diseases and Injuries: Pharmacological Advances and Clinical Translation.
abstract: Respiratory diseases remain major causes of morbidity and mortality; however, inadequate pulmonary drug exposure and systemic toxicity continue to limit treatment efficacy. Inhaled nanomedicines offer opportunities for localized, sustained, and targeted therapy. This review examines how disease biology informs pulmonary delivery design across pulmonary fibrosis, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary infections, and acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome. It outlines anatomical and biological barriers and compares liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric and hybrid systems, biomimetic carriers, and stimuli-responsive formulations. Particular attention is given to matching therapeutic cargo and carrier properties to fibroblasts, macrophages, tumor cells, and alveolar type II cells. Emerging approaches include mRNA delivery, siRNA-mediated gene silencing, antisense oligonucleotides, and CRISPR-based editing, alongside alveolar regeneration and biomarker-guided treatment. These strategies are evaluated in relation to their delivery requirements and stage of development. The review also addresses aerosol-device compatibility, manufacturing, repeated-dose safety, regulatory considerations, and clinical outcomes. By connecting delivery mechanisms with disease-specific applications and clinical evidence, this review identifies both therapeutic opportunities and barriers to translation. This integrated perspective can guide the development of inhaled nanomedicines with more reproducible pulmonary delivery, improved treatment efficacy, and acceptable safety.

title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Advances.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative condition accompanied by widespread central nervous system damage and complex networked pathogenesis spanning molecular, cellular, and systemic dimensions. Existing studies tend to focus on individual pathological cascades or monotherapeutic approaches, while overlooking the intrinsic crosstalk among protein pathology, neuroinflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and gut-brain axis imbalance, with insufficient systematic integration of nonpharmacological strategies and multifunctional nanoplatforms. Driven by intertwined molecular aberrations, glial dysregulation and systemic metabolic disorders, AD presents profound pathological complexity. Correspondingly, multitarget pharmacotherapy integrated with hierarchical nonpharmacological and nanotherapeutic interventions has achieved substantial progress, exerting synergistic effects on alleviating AD pathological cascades and optimizing overall therapeutic regimens. We comprehensively review current evidence to delineate the mechanistic landscape of AD and update therapeutic advances, including pharmacological agents, multimodal nonpharmacological interventions, and brain-targeted nanosystems for blood-brain barrier penetration, protein modulation, microenvironment remodeling, and gene editing delivery. This study underscores major research limitations and translational obstacles in therapeutic efficacy, biosafety, and nanomedicine applications. This work emphasizes biomarker-based early stratification and staged combined interventions, providing novel integrated insights into AD pathogenesis and prospective targeted therapeutic development.

title: Adipose-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells: Isolation, Origin, Phenotype Applications, and Challenges.
abstract: Traditional adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (AD-MSCs) research has relied on unfractionated bulk populations, whose therapeutic efficacy is constrained by cellular heterogeneity, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and rapid postengraftment functional exhaustion, resulting in inconsistent outcomes and impeding clinical translation. This review systematically examines AD-MSC developmental origins, tissue niches, isolation and purification strategies, functional phenotypes, and biomanufacturing bottlenecks. It integrates preclinical and clinical evidence for AD-MSCs and their extracellular vesicles (EVs) in bone and cartilage regeneration, chronic cutaneous diseases, neurological disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and other conditions. These therapies remodel injured microenvironments through immunometabolic reprogramming, antifibrotic signaling, angiogenesis, mitochondrial transfer, and paracrine regulation rather than direct tissue replacement. Major translational barriers include cellular heterogeneity, safety concerns, the transdifferentiation controversy, nonstandardized preconditioning, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and low cell retention after transplantation. We propose that clinical translation should be based on prospective isolation of functional subpopulations, coupled with tailored preconditioning, precision gene editing, three-dimensional biomaterials, EV engineering, and automated closed-system biomanufacturing. This framework aims to preserve potency, phenotypic stability, and paracrine function, transforming AD-MSCs and their bioactive derivatives from variable, unfractionated preparations into well-characterized, standardized, highly potent precision biologics. More broadly, it offers a mechanism-driven, function-defined, engineering-enabled, and clinically accessible roadmap for next-generation regenerative medicine.

title: Assessment of Allometric Scaling Methods for the Prediction of Human Pharmacokinetic of LNA-i-miR-221.
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides are small synthetic DNA or RNA molecules that can be used to modulate gene expression, particularly to block the production of unwanted proteins. This makes them potentially powerful drugs to contrast cancer growth. Drug development is a long process that includes preclinical and clinical studies. Preclinical animal studies are designed to assess drug kinetics and safety before progressing to clinical trials, as they may predict the therapeutic dose to be used in the "first in human" (FIH) studies. This is usually achieved by applying allometric scaling methods that allow predicting the human pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters from those estimated in animals. Selecting the appropriate scaling formula reduces the risk of translational uncertainty and supports the design of FIH studies. The aim of this study is to compare the accuracy of different allometric scaling methods in predicting human PK of the antisense oligonucleotide LNA-i-miR-221, a powerful inhibitor of microRNA miR-221, which was found to be deregulated in several malignancies, favoring cancer progression. To do that, we exploited the availability of PK data of the drug in both Sprague Dawley rats and humans and we found that the best scaling method for both clearance and distribution volume is the simple allometry, with predictions laying within the 2-fold and 4-fold error interval, respectively. This study contributes to identifying the most accurate scaling methods among the evaluated single-species approaches to extrapolate human pharmacokinetic for LNA-i-miR-221, possibly offering a starting point for future studies involving antisense oligonucleotides.

title: Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy Aptasensors for Nucleic-Acid Detection: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-based nanodelivery systems for precision gene editing in neuroinflammation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuroinflammation is a characteristic feature of many neurological diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Uncontrolled activation of microglia and astrocytes results in the production of proinflammatory mediators that contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration.
PURPOSE: CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technology provides highly precise targeting of genes involved in these pathways, enabling the deletion, correction, or modulation of disease-associated genetic alterations. Nonetheless, effective delivery of CRISPR components to the central nervous system (CNS) remains a major challenge because of protective barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), as well as concerns regarding genomic instability and immunogenicity.
METHODS: Nanotechnology-guided delivery platforms, such as lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, dendrimers and polymeric carriers, have been developed as promising strategies to address these challenges. These nanosystems can improve biodistribution, pharmacokinetic behavior, and cellular uptake, while potentially reducing off-target effects and systemic toxicity.
RESULTS: The preclinical studies demonstrate successful modulation of key neuroinflammatory targets, including the NLRP3 inflammasome, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, and the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, with potential therapeutic relevance to neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, novel techniques, such as mitochondrial base editing, prime editing, and epigenetic modulation, expand the scope of CRISPR-mediated therapeutic strategies. Although outcomes from animal models are promising, translation to the clinical setting requires careful consideration of safety, ethical concerns, and long-term efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights the potential of integrating CRISPR/Cas9 with nanodelivery systems to advance precision medicine for neuroinflammatory disorders, while emphasizing their potential for therapeutic applications in complex CNS conditions. Ongoing studies aimed at optimizing delivery and reducing off-target effects will be essential for advancing these approaches toward clinical practice.

title: Microbial serotonin signalling axes in irritable bowel syndrome: integrative molecular crosstalk among enterochromaffin cells, gut microbiota, neuroimmune circuits, and precision therapeutic engineering.
abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common, often disabling disorder of gut-brain interaction whose molecular basis remains incompletely defined, leaving diagnosis largely symptom-based and treatment largely non-mechanistic. We argue that the serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; hereafter 5-HT, the primary term used throughout, with "serotonin" retained in less technical contexts) signalling axis-positioned at the interface of the gut microbiota, enterochromaffin (EC) cells, enteric neurons, and the mucosal immune system-is a central, unifying integrator of IBS pathophysiology, and that reframing IBS around this axis offers a route toward mechanism-based subtyping and therapy. We first synthesise how microbiota-driven tryptophan metabolism, short-chain fatty acid and secondary bile acid signalling, and epigenetic regulation of tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) shape EC-cell serotonin output, before examining the neuroimmune consequences of dysregulated serotonin secretion-mast cell activation, macrophage polarisation, neurogenic inflammation-and the microbiota-serotonin-gut-brain connectome linking vagal afferent signalling, blood-brain barrier permeability, and central neurotransmitter networks. We then discuss molecular stratification of IBS subtypes through serotonergic endotyping-incorporating SLC6A4 and TPH1 polymorphisms, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics-and critically evaluate next-generation therapeutic strategies, including engineered probiotic chassis, CRISPR-mediated microbial editing, and AI-guided nanomedicine, distinguishing proof-of-concept findings from clinically validated approaches. We conclude that reconceptualising IBS as a disorder of disrupted microbial serotonergic ecosystems, rather than a purely symptom-defined syndrome, offers a coherent and testable framework for biomarker discovery and precision, mechanism-directed therapy, while highlighting the causal-directionality and clinical-translation gaps that must be closed before this framework can be applied at the bedside.

title: Integrating RNA technologies with CAR-T cell therapy: strategies to overcome current limitations and expand clinical applications.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has emerged as a prominent cancer treatment modality, demonstrating significant clinical success. To date, several CAR-T products have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of hematological malignancies. Despite these advances, several challenges continue to limit the broader application of CAR-T therapy. These challenges include complex and costly manufacturing processes, safety concerns associated with integrating viral vectors, individualized production requirements, therapy-related adverse effects, and limited efficacy against solid tumors. Recent progress in ribonucleic acid (RNA)-based technologies has introduced promising strategies to improve the safety, adaptability, and therapeutic performance of CAR-T cells. This review provides a comprehensive translational perspective on the integration of RNA technologies with CAR-T therapy. Specifically, it categorizes current approaches into four key areas: RNA-driven non-viral CAR-T cell manufacturing, RNA vaccine-mediated enhancement of CAR-T activity, RNA interference (RNAi)-based modulation, and in vivo CAR-T cell generation. Among the reviewed approaches, ex vivo messenger RNA (mRNA)-based CAR-T engineering currently has the greatest clinical maturity, whereas RNA vaccine-mediated boosting shows particular promise for enhancing CAR-T expansion and persistence, especially in solid tumors. In vivo RNA-mediated CAR-T generation remains at an early stage of development, with evidence still predominantly derived from preclinical studies, but may ultimately represent the most transformative approach by simplifying manufacturing and improving accessibility.Trial registration number: Not applicable.

title: PROTACs in personalized and precision medicine: transforming targeted therapy with advances in selectivity and patient stratification.
abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) have emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy that extends beyond conventional occupancy-driven pharmacology by enabling the selective degradation of disease-causing proteins through the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS). Unlike traditional small-molecule inhibitors that transiently suppress protein function, PROTACs catalytically eliminate target proteins, thereby offering sustained pharmacological effects and the potential to bypass selected resistance mechanisms associated with conventional target inhibition, and expanding the druggable proteome to include previously undruggable targets. These unique properties position PROTACs as a promising platform for personalized and precision medicine. This review comprehensively examines recent advances in PROTAC technology with a particular emphasis on therapeutic selectivity, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and clinical translation. We discuss the structural design and mechanistic principles of PROTACs, including ternary complex formation, E3 ligase recruitment, ubiquitination, and proteasomal degradation. Recent innovations such as reversible covalent PROTACs, macrocyclic PROTACs, photo-switchable degraders (PHOTACs), conditional PROTACs, and the expanding repertoire of E3 ligases are highlighted for their potential to improve tissue specificity and therapeutic precision. Furthermore, the integration of computational modelling, artificial intelligence, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, multi-omics technologies, CRISPR-based functional screening, and patient-derived organoids is discussed as a framework for rational degrader design and individualized therapeutic decision-making. The review also explores emerging applications of PROTACs in oncology, neurodegenerative disorders, autoimmune diseases, and infectious diseases while addressing current challenges related to pharmacokinetics, drug delivery, resistance mechanisms, biomarker validation, and regulatory considerations. Finally, we discuss emerging nanotechnology-enabled delivery strategies, companion-diagnostic concepts, and patient-specific degrader development as potential approaches to address pharmacokinetic, delivery, and translational barriers, while emphasizing that most of these strategies remain preclinical or investigational. Collectively, this review highlights the growing role of PROTACs as next-generation therapeutics capable of bridging chemical biology with precision medicine, supporting the development of potentially selective, biomarker-informed, and individualized treatment strategies.

title: The CRISPR-dCas9 epigenetic toolbox: prospects for modulating gene expression in climate-resilient crops.
abstract: CRISPR-dCas9 epigenome editing represents a paradigm shift from static DNA sequence editing to dynamic reprogramming of gene expression, offering a powerful and precise toolbox with the potential to develop stable and climate-resilient crops without altering DNA sequences. The escalating challenges of global food security, driven by climate change and population growth, necessitate innovative crop improvement strategies that extend beyond conventional breeding. Although CRISPR-Cas9 has revolutionized plant biotechnology through direct genome editing, CRISPR-based epigenome editing has emerged as a new frontier. By repurposing nuclease-dead Cas9 as a programmable targeting platform fused to epigenetic effector domains, researchers can precisely modulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence. This approach has already yielded compelling successes, such as the engineering of durable resistance to cassava bacterial blight through targeted epigenetic silencing of a susceptibility gene. This review focuses primarily on the current state of CRISPR-based epigenome editing systems, including acetyltransferases, demethylases, DNA methyltransferases, and deacetylases, and their applications in crop improvement research. We critically evaluate their mechanisms in rewriting epigenetic regulatory information, their demonstrated efficacy in enhancing yield components, disease resistance, and abiotic stress tolerance, and their potential to create stable meiotically heritable epialleles, although most demonstrations remain at the proof-of-concept stage in model plants, with field validation in major crops still limited. This review provides a balanced analysis of key challenges, including editing specificity, context-dependency, delivery limitations, and regulatory considerations. Finally, we outline future directions focusing on technological refinement, multi-omics integration, and field validation. Epigenome editing shows promise as a conceptually distinct and transformative approach in crop biotechnology, through targeted modulation of a plant's epigenetic landscape. However, its full potential hinges on overcoming challenges related to stability, predictability, and field-scale validation.

title: CAR-NK cell immunotherapy: a comprehensive review of engineering platforms, clinical applications in hematological and solid tumors.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-β, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.

title: Research progress of gene correction for genetic diseases via in vivo prime editing.
abstract: Curative therapies for genetic diseases caused by pathogenic mutations demand precise and safe genome editing technologies. Prime editing (PE), a CRISPR-Cas9-derived technology that enables precise base conversions without double-strand breaks (DSBs), has emerged as a transformative tool with the ability to correct 89% of human pathogenic mutations. However, transitioning PE from preclinical models to clinical applications faces critical challenges, particularly in the development of in vivo delivery systems and scalable manufacturing. This review systematically summarizes advances of in vivo PE therapeutics, focusing on the therapeutic outcomes across some retinal, metabolic, and hematologic genetic diseases. We further dissect barriers to clinical translation, including in the immunogenicity of viral vectors, off-target risks in nondividing cells, and large-scale production bottlenecks. By highlighting the unique advantages of in vivo PE and proposing actionable solutions for scalable manufacturing, the work provides a roadmap for accelerating in vivo PE-based therapies toward clinical reality.

title: ATP1A3-related neurological disorders: updated insights into clinical heterogeneity, molecular mechanisms and precision therapeutics.
abstract: ATP1A3-related neurological disorders comprise a rapidly expanding spectrum of rare neurogenetic diseases characterized by remarkable clinical heterogeneity and complex genotype-phenotype relationships. Since the publication of previous comprehensive reviews, the identification of novel ATP1A3-associated phenotypes, refinement of genotype-phenotype correlations, and advances in molecular pathogenesis and precision therapeutic strategies have substantially expanded current understanding of these disorders, highlighting the need for an updated synthesis. This narrative review summarizes recent advances in the clinical spectrum of ATP1A3-related disorders and discusses current insights into genotype-phenotype correlations, molecular mechanisms, and disease pathogenesis. Particular emphasis is placed on the molecular consequences of ATP1A3 dysfunction, including impaired Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, disrupted neuronal excitability, altered ion homeostasis, and downstream cellular responses. We further review current symptomatic management and emerging disease-modifying therapeutic strategies, including antisense oligonucleotide therapy, viral vector-mediated gene delivery, genome editing technologies, and other precision medicine approaches. Current challenges and future research priorities are also discussed. By integrating recent clinical and experimental evidence, this review provides an updated perspective on ATP1A3-related disorders and aims to facilitate improved disease recognition, mechanistic understanding, and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Next-generation pharmacological strategies for Parkinson's disease: a systematic literature review of symptom management and disease modification.
abstract: Parkinson disease is an ongoing neurodegenerative disorder, and both motor and non-motor symptoms are involved with the existing therapies having minimal effects on the disease but only symptom alleviation. The goal of this systematic literature review was to generalize up-to-date evidence on the next-generation pharmacological strategies to manage the symptoms and the disease in a patient with Parkinson disease. The review was based on PRISMA 2020 and included the analysis of peer-reviewed studies of human research published in 2015-2026 and retrieved in the key databases, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library. This included 30 eligible studies consisting of randomized studies, observational studies, and early clinical trials. The results show that, although dopaminergic treatment continues to play a central role in managing motor symptoms, new methods such as gene therapy, gene editing, stem cell-based regeneration, nanomedicine delivery systems, repurposed drugs, artificial intelligence-based precision medicine approaches have a good neuroprotective and disease-modifying potential. Nonetheless, the majority of new interventions are still in preclinical or first line clinical phase, with a defined subset of emerging gene-, cell-, and nanotechnology-based approaches evaluated only in animal or in-vitro models rather than in PD patients and associated with small sample size, invasive delivery, limited follow-up and lack of long-term safety information. In general, the review concludes by stating that there has been significant advancement in diversification of therapeutic targets and mechanisms, but rigorous large-scale biomarker-directed clinical trials are needed to translate these advances to effective and sustainable treatment of the Parkinson disease.

title: A-to-I edited miRNA-99a-5p in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes promotes fracture healing by regulating GDF11.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Impaired fracture healing remains a significant clinical challenge. Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and the exosomes (BMSC-Exos) play a pivotal role in bone regeneration, partly by transferring functional microRNAs (miRNAs). A-to-I RNA editing can profoundly alter miRNA function, but its role in fracture healing, particularly for miRNA-99a-5p, is underexplored. We first profiled differentially edited miRNAs in serum from 50 fracture patients and healthy controls. A murine fracture model was established and treated with BMSC-Exos, where either the edited or wild-type form of miRNA-99a-5p was knocked down. In vitro studies involved transfecting BMSCs with ADAR expression vectors to investigate editing mechanisms, and overexpressing/inhibiting edited/wild-type miRNA-99a-5p in MC3T3-E1C osteoblasts to elucidate its direct functional impacts on osteogenic differentiation, apoptosis, proliferation, and migration. Validation of target genes were performed by dual-luciferase reporter assays, qPCR, and Western blot. Key readouts included alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining, flow cytometry, Transwell migration, CCK-8 proliferation assays and HE staining. Clinical analysis revealed significantly lower A-to-I edited miRNA-99a-5p levels in fracture patients, correlating with delayed union. In mice, BMSC-Exos promoted fracture healing, an effect attenuated by edited miRNA-99a-5p knockdown. In vitro, edited miRNA-99a-5p enhanced osteogenesis and inhibited apoptosis, while the wild-type form had opposing effects. ADAR2 mediated this editing. Edited miRNA-99a-5p directly targeted and suppressed Growth Differentiation Factor 11 (GDF11) expression. Importantly, GDF11 overexpression reversed the pro-osteogenic effects of edited miRNA-99a-5p, in both direct and exosome-mediated contexts. Reduced A-to-I editing of miRNA-99a-5p is associated with impaired fracture healing. BMSC-Exos facilitate bone repair by delivering ADAR2-edited miRNA-99a-5p, which promotes osteogenic differentiation and bone formation through the specific targeting and downregulation of GDF11. This study uncovers a novel exosome-mediated RNA editing pathway critical for fracture healing and highlights edited miRNA-99a-5p and GDF11 as potential therapeutic targets for bone repair.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10616-026-01080-x.

title: Engineering a Synthetic Fluorogenic RNA Switch for Oxidized Guanine.
abstract: Reactive oxygen species generate a family of oxidized guanine species that serve as important biomarkers of oxidative damage. Here, we report the development of a fluorogenic RNA switch that selectively recognizes oxidized guanine species. We first systematically characterized an oxidized guanine RNA aptamer, defining its minimum functional binding domain and molecular recognition profile. Structural minimization produced a compact aptamer with higher affinity than the full-length sequence that retained broad recognition of structurally diverse oxidized guanine species while discriminating against their unmodified counterparts. We subsequently incorporated the optimized aptamer into fluorogenic RNA switch architectures, revealing that fluorescence activation required iterative optimization of aptamer topology, scaffold architecture, and communication-linker design. The resulting fluorogenic RNA switch exhibited target-dependent fluorescence activation while retaining the aptamer's molecular recognition profile. This work establishes a fluorogenic RNA switch for oxidized guanine species and highlights the importance of systematic aptamer characterization and optimization in fluorogenic RNA switch development.

title: A comprehensive review of mixed-species biofilm infections and innovative therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Mixed-species biofilm infections are important causes of persistent and difficult-to-treat infections. Compared with monospecies biofilms, mixed-species communities contain microorganisms with different physiological and genetic characteristics that interact through metabolic cooperation, chemical signaling, competition, and modification of the local environment. These interactions, together with the EPS matrix, physiological heterogeneity, and HGT, can increase antimicrobial tolerance, contributing to treatment failure and infection recurrence. Polymicrobial biofilms are associated with chronic wounds, respiratory infections, catheter- and device-associated infections, and other persistent infections. However, treatment of polymicrobial biofilms remains challenging because their complex structure and interspecies interactions can reduce antimicrobial efficacy. This review summarizes the clinical significance, formation, and persistence of mixed-species biofilms and discusses recent therapeutic strategies for their control. We also discuss recent approaches for controlling polymicrobial biofilms, including natural compounds, QS inhibition, CRISPR-Cas-based approaches, biofilm matrix targeting, metabolic and nutrient disruption, nanotechnology, and phage therapy. Recent studies show that these approaches can inhibit biofilm formation, disrupt established biofilms, enhance antimicrobial activity, and selectively target specific microbial populations. However, their effectiveness varies with microbial composition, biofilm maturity, matrix characteristics, and treatment conditions. Overall, current evidence supports the development of targeted and combination-based strategies for mixed-species biofilms. Further studies using clinically relevant models are needed to exactly define treatment efficacy and support the translation of these approaches into clinical practice.

title: Recent trends and innovative strategies in the curative approach for β-thalassemia: a current prospect and future perspective.
abstract: β-Thalassemia, a major genetic disease affecting the global population, has seen new strategies being pursued in terms of curative attempts directed at the specific gene defect present. Iron chelation therapy and lifelong blood transfusions have historically been used to treat β-thalassemia, a severe hereditary hemoglobin condition marked by decreased or missing β-globin chain synthesis. These methods have significantly increased patient survival, but they do not offer a permanent solution and are linked to serious side effects and a high cost of care. With a focus on hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), lentiviral gene-addition treatment, and future genome-editing techniques, this study outlines new and creative methods to long-term disease correction in β-thalassemia. Although allogeneic HSCT is still a proven treatment option, its use is constrained by the availability of donors, graft-related issues, and transplant-related hazards. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell-based gene therapy has become a significant substitute, provided the possibility of long-term transfusion independence while prevented graft-versus-host disease. With the creation of exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel; Casgevy), which reactivates fetal hemoglobin expression through modification of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer and has shown significant rates of sustained transfusion independence in eligible patients with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia, CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has recently marked a significant clinical milestone. Notwithstanding these encouraging developments, myeloablative conditioning, long-term safety and durability, high treatment costs, complicated manufacturing requirements, and restricted accessibility continue to be major obstacles, especially in low- and middle-income nations. All things considered, the therapeutic landscape for β-thalassemia is changing from lifelong supportive management to potentially curative and transformative interventions; however, the wider application of these cutting-edge therapies depends on ongoing long-term evaluation and efforts to increase affordability and global accessibility.
