title: Efficacy and safety of exon skipping therapies for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and muscle wasting. Exon skipping therapies have been approved as part of the therapeutic arsenal for DMD, however, there is contrasting evidence regarding their clinical benefits. The aim of this study was to determine the efficacy and safety of exon skipping therapies for DMD.
METHOD: ology: A systematic review was conducted in three databases including PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Cochrane-Ovid, based on the following question using PICO strategy: What is the efficacy of exon skipping therapies for DMD? Search was limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and Open Label RCTs with reported results, published between January 2016 and December 2024, involving patients with DMD treated with any of the existing exon-skipping therapies, reporting efficacy measured by primary clinical and secondary molecular outcomes. Secondary safety outcomes were also registered. Eligible studies were assessed for risk of bias. A descriptive analysis was performed in subgroups according to variants amenable to exon 45, 51, or 53 skipping.
RESULTS: A total of nine studies were left after the final filters were applied. Studies were conducted across centers in seven different countries. Four studies used viltolarsen (exon 53), three eteplirsen (exon 51), and two golodirsen (exon 53). Trial length was heterogeneous with an average length of 119.6 weeks (±78.5). Overall, studies with exon skipping medications reported improvement in the clinical outcomes including the 6-minute walking test, time to stand and the North Star Ambulatory Assessment. Biological measurements showed an increase in dystrophin expression and exon skipping percentage. Long term follow up evidenced stabilization of both clinical and molecular outcomes in DMD patients, compared to age and treatment-matched controls.
CONCLUSION: Exon skipping therapies have evidenced improved clinical and molecular outcomes. Longer follow-up extension studies are needed to further elucidate their effect in comparison to age-matched controls.

title: Deletion of a rheumatoid arthritis risk enhancer in mouse disrupts Bim expression and immune homeostasis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to characterise the in vivo function of a murine regulatory region syntenic to the human rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-associated enhancer at the ACOXL locus and its role in immunity.
METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9, we generated the Bim-eΔ mouse model by excising a 15 kb genomic region syntenic to the human RA-associated locus tagged by rs13401811 from C57BL/6J zygotes. Bim expression was assessed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Thymocytes and splenocytes were profiled by flow cytometry, and whole-spleen RNA-seq was used to define transcriptional changes. Immune responses were tested using a Trichuris muris infection model and an antigen-induced arthritis (AIA) protocol.
RESULTS: Bim-eΔ mice show reduced Bim expression vs wild-type counterparts. This indicates that Bim is a transcriptional target of this region. Enhancer loss was correlated with differences in T cell proportions across age- and sex-stratified cohorts consistent with altered thymic selection. Splenic T and B cells were altered, and the transcriptome skewed toward inflammation. Bim-eΔ and wild-type mice mounted comparable responses to T. muris, whereas Bim-eΔ mice developed a severe adverse response during the sensitisation phase of the AIA protocol.
CONCLUSIONS: A murine noncoding regulatory region modulates Bim expression and immunity in vivo. Enhancer deletion altered the splenic transcriptional profile and lymphocyte composition while revealing a context-dependent phenotype upon inflammatory in vivo challenge. These findings support a role for RA-associated regulatory architecture in shaping immunity and point to BIM regulation as a potential therapeutic lever for restoring immune balance.

title: Gene Therapy for Inherited Platelet Disorders: From Proof of Concept to Clinical Translation.
abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.

title: Zein-based hybrid nanocarriers for non-viral gene delivery: A review.
abstract: Gene therapy and RNA-based therapeutics are increasingly limited by the challenge of delivering fragile, anionic nucleic acids to the correct intracellular compartment. Zein, the principal maize prolamin, has attracted interest as a biodegradable, self-assembling carrier that can protect cargo and be combined with polymeric, lipidic, targeted and biomimetic components. This review critically evaluates zein-based systems for plasmid DNA, siRNA, antisense oligonucleotides and related nucleic-acid cargos. Native zein is best regarded as a protective and sustained-release matrix rather than a stand-alone high-efficiency transfection vector. In contrast, hybrid systems can add nucleic-acid condensation, colloidal stabilization, targeting and intracellular-trafficking functions through components such as chitosan, polyethylenimine, dendritic poly(l-lysine), lipids and targeting ligands. Direct evidence of endosomal escape remains limited, with only one reviewed study providing imaging evidence consistent with improved lysosomal escape. Cargo-specific evidence is strongest for plasmid DNA, with functional proof-of-concept also reported for selected siRNA and antisense oligonucleotide systems, whereas robust mRNA translation and CRISPR genome editing have not yet been demonstrated with zein-based carriers. The translational rationale for zein lies not in superior intrinsic transfection efficiency, but in route-specific protection, sustained release, hydrophobic drug co-loading and use as a biodegradable scaffold within multifunctional hybrids. Zein-based gene delivery remains preclinical and requires stronger mechanistic, cargo-specific and route-specific validation.

title: A nuclease-associated short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis with dual DNA and RNA collateral activity.
abstract: Argonaute (Ago) proteins play pivotal roles in nucleic acid targeting across eukaryotes and prokaryotes. While eukaryotic Ago (eAgo) proteins utilize RNA guides to cleave complementary RNA, prokaryotic Ago (pAgo) proteins often employ DNA guides for DNA targeting. This study focuses on the short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis (Pko-SPARDA), which consists of a DUF4365-APAZ protein (PkoRE) and an Ago protein (PkoAgo). Upon RNA-guided target DNA recognition, Pko-SPARDA exhibits nonspecific cleavage activity toward ssDNA, dsDNA, and RNA, demonstrating potential for nucleic acid detection. Biochemical characterization revealed that Pko-SPARDA prefers Mn2+ or Mg2+ as cofactors, operates optimally at 40-45 °C, and is sensitive to mismatches in the central and 3'-supplementary regions of the guide RNA. Notably, the system accommodates a range of guide lengths (14-40 nt) and shows higher activity with 5'-phosphorylated guides. Additionally, guide RNA 5'-phosphorylation universally enhances Pko-SPARDA trans-cleavage activity, and this principle extends to microRNA-guided activation, advancing the understanding of short pAgos and highlighting Pko-SPARDA's utility in molecular diagnostics by bridging a gap left by CRISPR systems due to its lack of sequence constraints like PAM motifs.

title: One-pot dual RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a lateral flow biosensor for rapid detection of carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae.
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) poses a major public health threat due to high mortality and limited therapeutic options. Rapid and accurate detection of both species identity and resistance determinants is critical for clinical management. Here, we developed a dual-target recombinase polymerase amplification-CRISPR/Cas12a multiplex lateral flow assay (DRC-MLFA) for simultaneous detection of K. pneumoniae and blaKPC in a single reaction. This platform introduces a functionally differentiated dual-channel detection strategy, in which the K. pneumoniae signal is generated directly via RPA-lateral flow readout, while blaKPC detection is achieved through an additional CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated verification step. To enable one-pot integration, suboptimal protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequences were employed to delay Cas12a activation, thereby coordinating amplification and CRISPR detection within a single reaction system. Under optimized conditions, the assay achieved dual-target detection within 50 min at 37 °C, with a limit of detection of 101 CFU/μL and high specificity against non-target pathogens. Validation with 30 clinical samples showed strong concordance with quantitative PCR. This portable and low-cost biosensor provides a practical solution for point-of-care detection of CRKP and establishes a framework for integrating hierarchical specificity control into multiplex CRISPR diagnostics.

title: Non-viral delivery and genome editing for CAR-NK engineering in solid tumors: from ex vivo manufacturing to in vivo reprogramming.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered natural killer (NK) cell therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer treatment, offering advantages over CAR-T cells such as a lower risk of cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease and the potential for off-the-shelf manufacturing. Viral vectors have long served as effective tools for CAR-NK engineering, but their dependence on complex manufacturing procedures, considerable production costs, and the potential risks associated with genomic integration has encouraged increasing interest in non-viral alternatives. Recent advances in genetic engineering technologies have facilitated the development of CAR-NK platforms, particularly through non-viral delivery approaches including electroporation, transposon systems and lipid nanoparticles, while CRISPR-based tools enable targeted genome editing. Meanwhile, an increasing number of clinical trials have begun to evaluate the safety and therapeutic potential of CAR-NK cells in both hematological malignancies and solid tumors. However, challenges such as limited NK-cell persistence, antigen heterogeneity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remain. In this review, we summarize recent progress in non-viral CAR-NK engineering strategies, analyze the current landscape of preclinical and clinical trials, and discuss key challenges and future directions for advancing CAR-NK therapy. Collectively, these advances suggest that non-viral engineering technologies may serve as an important technological foundation for next-generation CAR-NK therapies, enabling more flexible ex vivo manufacturing and potentially supporting the future development of in vivo CAR-NK generation strategies for solid tumors.

title: Simple heat-assisted method for mRNA loading into empty lipid nanoparticles enables robust in vitro and in vivo delivery.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNP) have emerged as a versatile modality, enabling diverse applications by changing encoded mRNA sequences. However, the conventional mRNA-LNP preparation process poses significant barriers to non-specialists because it requires specialized equipment and technical expertise. In this study, we aimed to report a simple post-encapsulation approach where mRNA is mixed with preformed empty LNP in solution to form mRNA-LNP for effective in vitro and in vivo delivery. Process optimization revealed that heating mRNA and empty LNP at 75°C and pH 4.0 achieved approximately 90% mRNA encapsulation while maintaining an LNP size of approximately 100 nm. The resulting post-encapsulated LNP were comprehensively compared with conventional LNP prepared via microfluidic mixing. Both LNP formulations exhibited over 90% cellular uptake and comparable concentration-dependent expression in vitro. The intravenous administration of post-encapsulated LNP in mice resulted in robust luciferase expression in the liver and spleen at 0.01 mg/kg, with no notable changes in serum chemistry at 1 and 3 mg/kg. However, the activity of the post-encapsulated LNP was slightly reduced compared with that of the conventional LNP. Sucrose density gradient centrifugation indicated that post-encapsulated mRNA-LNP formed heterogeneous populations with varying mRNA/lipid ratios, in contrast to conventional mRNA-LNP. These findings support a working hypothesis that this heterogeneity could contribute to the reduced in vivo activity. Our simple post-encapsulation method potentially could lower entry barriers for non-specialists in this field and accelerate RNA-LNP research through its compatibility with 96-well-format preparation.

title: Machine learning-guided chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticles for intra-articular SOX9 mRNA therapy of osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) progression involves cartilage matrix loss and persistent inflammation. This study developed a machine learning-guided and chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticle carrying messenger RNA (CM-LNP@mRNA) platform for intra-articular SOX9 delivery. Random forest analysis identified the nitrogen-to-phosphorus and SM-102 ratios as primary determinants with feature importance values of 0.57 and 0.32 respectively. Following ML-guided formulation selection and experimental membrane-coating optimization, the final CM-LNP@mRNA formulation showed an encapsulation efficiency of 95.50% and a particle size of 133.70 nm. Compared with the conventional reference formulation prepared under the same final coating condition, encapsulation efficiency increased from 89.20% to 95.50% and particle size decreased from 145.40 nm to 133.70 nm. Membrane coating shifted the zeta potential from -25.57 mV to -35.07 mV. This transition provided biophysical evidence of successful surface modification. In interleukin-1β-stimulated chondrocytes, CM-LNP@mRNA increased the relative expression of Col2a1 and Acan from 0.20 to 0.33 and from 0.50 to 0.73, respectively, while reducing the relative expression of Mmp3 and Adamts5 from 10.50 to 7.80 and from 4.00 to 2.50, respectively. These alterations indicated a shift toward a matrix-preserving transcriptional state. Downstream matrix metalloproteinase 3 and prostaglandin E2 concentrations decreased from 37.10 ng/mL to 18.50 ng/mL and from 113.70 pg/mL to 76.50 pg/mL by day 7. This reduction demonstrated effective suppression of catabolic and inflammatory activity. In OA rats, CM-LNP@mRNA reduced the osteophyte volume from 4.00 mm3 to 2.00 mm3 and prolonged the thermal response latency from 7.50 s to 11.80 s. These improvements linked cellular metabolic regulation to functional joint recovery. These findings establish a strategy integrating formulation optimization with biomimetic membrane coating to modulate the OA microenvironment.

title: Enhancing mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine-induced T cell responses by simple supplementation with class B CpG oligodeoxynucleotides.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines can elicit robust T cell responses; however, these responses remain insufficient, particularly in the context of cancer vaccine therapy. Although several types of adjuvants reportedly enhance T cell responses induced by mRNA-LNP vaccines, few comprehensive side-by-side comparisons exist, and it remains unclear which adjuvants are most suitable. Herein, we screened 15 adjuvants. The addition of class B CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (ODNs) markedly augmented T cell induction in an interleukin-12-dependent manner and promoted the antitumor effects of mRNA-LNP vaccines in mice. Class B CpG ODN-adjuvanted mRNA-LNP vaccines induced more potent T cell responses than the mRNA-LNP vaccine administered at a 10-fold higher dose, while exhibiting a more favorable safety profile. However, this approach also reduced the cellular uptake of mRNA-LNPs and antigen expression. As a possible mechanism underlying this reduced delivery efficiency, we found that class B CpG ODNs adsorbed onto LNPs and altered their particle characteristics. These findings demonstrate that supplementation with class B CpG ODN is a simple, safe, and readily implementable approach for enhancing mRNA-LNP vaccine-induced T cell responses. This study also highlights that adding auxiliary components to mRNA-LNPs can potentially affect the performance of LNPs as delivery carriers.

title: Lactate dehydrogenase A-dependent redox control of selective mRNA translation directs monocyte fate commitment.
abstract: Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation is a central process that shapes immune responses across diverse contexts, yet how inflammatory cues engage metabolism to instruct monocyte fate commitment remains unclear. Here, using a CRISPR-based metabolic screen combined with monocyte-specific perturbations in bacterial lung infection, we identified lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) as a key metabolic regulator of monocyte commitment to the nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2)+ macrophage fate in vivo. LDHA-dependent cytosolic nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) regeneration enabled selective hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1α) translation through its 5' untranslated region (UTR) and is associated with structural remodeling of this region. HIF1α then functioned as a downstream effector that promoted the NOS2+ macrophage fate. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) further acted as an upstream metabolic priming signal that enhanced LDHA-dependent HIF1α regulation and supported this differentiation process. Together, these findings suggest that metabolic redox state regulates monocyte fate commitment through selective mRNA translation coupled to RNA structural remodeling.

title: Quadruple HLA-I/II gene homo/heterozygous knockout hESC line: generation, multi-omics profiling, pluripotency, and immunogenicity.
abstract: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) exhibit pluripotency, self-renewal, and broad therapeutic potential in diverse disease contexts. Meanwhile, allogeneic grafts derived from hESCs are confronted with the formidable challenge of immune rejection. Specific human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) are critically involved in mediating transplant rejection, thus establishing HLA-deficient stem cells can be an important step toward achieving immune evasion. However, there is currently no consensus on which gene editing strategy can reduce hESC immunogenicity to a level suitable for broad clinical applications. This study performed HLA-A/-B gene hetero/homozygous knockout in an HLA double-knockout hESC line using a CRISPR/Cas9 system, established HLA-DRA-/-/-DQA1-/-/-A+/-/-B-/- knockout monoclonal cell lines, and revealed the multi-omics profiles, along with preserved pluripotency and trends to reduced immunogenicity of the hESC lines, through multi-omics analyses, in vitro assessment of pluripotency-related gene expression, in vivo teratoma formation assays and xenotransplantation experiments in mouse models. This study presents two novel monoclonal HLA genes homo/heterozygous knockout hESC lines, along with their multi-omics landscapes, pluripotency and immunogenicity. The findings exhibit crucial application potential and reference value in the development of hypoimmunogenic hESCs for their universal clinical use.

title: TRIM2 facilitates macrophage mediated anti-tumor immunity in renal cell carcinoma through enhancing SIRPA ubiquitination and degradation.
abstract: SIRPA delivers an anti-phagocytic "don't-eat-me" signal through its expression on macrophage membrane surface and promotes tumor progression via membrane-independent mechanism. However, current CD47- and SIRPA-targeting agents only disrupt cell-surface inhibitory signaling, highlighting the therapeutic potential of degrading SIRPA. Here, we identified that E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM2 interacted with SIRPA in vitro. Clinically, elevated TRIM2 expression is associated with prolonged overall and progression-free survival in renal-cell carcinoma (RCC) patients. Mechanistically, TRIM2 catalyzes K48-linked poly-ubiquitination of SIRPA, promoting its proteasomal degradation and reducing SIRPA protein levels. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of TRIM2 in macrophages upregulated SIRPA, significantly impairing phagocytosis of tumor cells. TRIM2 deficiency also promoted tumor growth by increasing intratumoral infiltration of M2-type macrophage, reducing accumulation of anti-tumor M1-like and antigen-presenting macrophages, and impairing effector CD8+ T-cell recruitment. Importantly, combined TRIM2 overexpression and PD-L1 blockade synergistically enhance anti-tumor immunity. Together, these results suggest that targeting TRIM2 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy against RCC by degrading SIRPA in macrophage and provide a roadmap for clinical application.

title: Endogenous targets of Zuo1-mediated mRNA surveillance encode proteins with higher predicted disorder.
abstract: Zuo1 slows elongating ribosomes in response to nascent peptide misfolding, which in turn triggers co-translational decay of the transcript. The endogenous substrates of this pathway have remained undefined. Using RNA-sequencing and ribosome profiling of unstressed wild-type and zuo1Δ cells, we identified transcripts that accumulate in the absence of Zuo1, representing mRNAs normally downregulated by Zuo1-mediated surveillance. Proteins encoded by these transcripts displayed higher predicted disorder across multiple metrics, were enriched in basic residues, were depleted of proline residues, and were shorter in length. Ribosome profiling revealed that Zuo1 target transcripts exhibited higher ribosome occupancy in the presence of Zuo1, and the ratio of wild-type to zuo1Δ ribosome occupancy positively correlated with predicted disorder. These findings indicate that Zuo1 surveillance acts preferentially on transcripts encoding nascent chains that fail to acquire stable structure.

title: Integrative proximity labeling and multiomic profiling uncover domain-specific interactomes and molecular vulnerabilities of oncogenic PI3K.
abstract: Activating mutations in PIK3CA (encoding the p110α kinase) are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers in human tumors. The two major hotspot mutations, E545K (helical domain) and H1047R (kinase domain), both hyperactivate PI3K-AKT signaling, yet they exhibit distinct functional behaviors and differential drug sensitivities. The mutation-specific protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks underlying the differences, however, remain largely unexplored. In this study, we established experimental approaches to identify proteins in proximity to oncogenic PI3K using biotin ligase-based proximity labeling. Our data revealed that the PIK3CA H1047R and E545K mutants fused to BioID2 formed structurally distinct complexes, each associating with unique proximal proteins identified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Further integration of the PPI networks with CRISPR dependency screens and multiomic profiling mapped the divergent functional interactomes of p110α hotspot mutants. H1047R exhibited a synthetic lethal dependency on the adaptor protein TAB2, which is associated with aggressive clinical phenotypes in breast cancer. Distinctly, E545K interacted with core subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, corresponding to a globally repressive chromatin state at distal enhancers. This SWI/SNF association also revealed a mutation-specific epigenetic vulnerability, with E545K-mutant cells displaying increased sensitivity to EZH2 inhibitors. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the molecular network complexity of oncogenic PI3K can be interrogated through proximity labeling and that distinct PIK3CA point mutations rewire non-overlapping PPI networks, revealing domain-specific dependencies. Our study provides a framework for mapping mutation-specific interactomes and offers molecular insights and potential therapeutic strategies for PIK3CA-mutant tumors.

title: The Lysine Methyltransferase SETDB1 Alleviates Methionine- and Choline-Deficient Diet-Induced Steatohepatitis by Suppressing Ferroptosis.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent chronic liver disorder, with its progressive form, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), characterized by steatosis, inflammation, hepatocyte injury, and fibrosis. However, the underlying mechanism remains incompletely understood. Here, we performed an in vivo CRISPR screen in Cas9 mice fed a methionine- and choline-deficient (MCD) diet to identify epigenetic regulators of MASH. SETDB1 emerged as a key modulator: hepatocyte-specific loss of Setdb1 exacerbated steatosis, inflammation, ductular reaction, and fibrosis, whereas Setdb1 overexpression markedly alleviated these pathological features. Notably, human liver samples showed decreased SETDB1 expression with advancing MASLD. Furthermore, SETDB1 deficiency increased hepatic ferroptosis by upregulating ACSL4, aggravating MASH pathology, whereas ACSL4 knockout reduced liver injury in the absence of SETDB1. SETDB1 overexpression protected against liver damage by repressing ACSL4. Therefore, the SETDB1-ACSL4-ferroptosis axis regulates MASH progression and represents a potential therapeutic target.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated co-delivery of human RB1 mRNA and triptolide for localized genetic therapy of retinoblastoma.
abstract: Retinoblastoma is a rare pediatric intraocular malignancy for which intravitreal administration offers a clinically attractive route for localized therapy owing to its minimally invasive nature and direct access to intraocular tumors. However, efficient intravitreal delivery of nucleic acids remains challenging because the protein-poor vitreous microenvironment restricts nanoparticle transport and subsequent intracellular delivery. Conventional lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which have been primarily developed for systemic administration, are therefore not necessarily suited to this unique biological environment. Here, we developed a C12-200-containing lipid nanoparticle (CLNP) engineered for efficient intravitreal gene delivery through systematic optimization of lipid composition. The optimized CLNP exhibited favorable diffusion within the vitreous, efficient intracellular mRNA delivery, and reduced dependence on extracellular protein-assisted uptake under vitreous-mimetic conditions. To demonstrate the therapeutic versatility of the platform, human RB transcriptional corepressor 1 mRNA and triptolide were co-delivered as representative gene and small-molecule therapeutics. CLNP-mediated co-delivery of hRB1 mRNA and triptolide produced greater antiproliferative activity than either monotherapy in vitro and markedly suppressed tumor progression in an orthotopic retinoblastoma model following a single intravitreal administration, with no detectable abnormalities in retinal function, structure, or apoptosis during the evaluation period. Collectively, this study establishes a vitreous-oriented lipid engineering strategy that simultaneously improves extracellular transport through the vitreous and intracellular nucleic acid delivery, providing a broadly applicable platform for localized gene delivery and combination gene-drug therapy for ocular diseases.

title: Ionizable lipid impact on mRNA vaccine formulation properties and immunogenicity.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted global supply chains, causing shortages of critical lipid-based raw materials for mRNA vaccine production. To enhance formulation resilience, we systematically evaluated the impact of five ionizable lipids (ILs) on lipid nanoparticle (LNP) organization, mRNA delivery and immunogenicity. The physiochemical analysis revealed the potential coexistence of liquid crystalline lamellar (Lα) and inverse hexagonal (HII) phases, or a mixture of nucleotide-loaded and non-loaded HII phases within developed LNP formulations. Furthermore, ILs with saturated, multi-tail structures, such as Lipid-5 and SM-102, favored inverse hexagonal (HII) internal organization and fusion intermediates, correlating with enhanced endosomal fusion and higher in vivo protein expression. In contrast, ILs such as cKK-E12, which featured dual ionization headgroups and tended to form lamellar-like structures, showed reduced encapsulation efficiency and transfection potency. The preclinical experiments demonstrated that all developed formulations induced robust binding and neutralizing antibody responses; however, antibody responses were lower in mRNA Lipid 5 LNPs and mRNA SM-102 LNPs than in other formulations. Notably, within the limited panel of ILs in this study, protein expression levels did not show a clear correlation with antibody titers, highlighting that efficient antigen expression alone is not predictive of humoral immunity. These findings underscore how IL structural features influence LNP architecture and function, informing the rational design of next-generation mRNA vaccines.

title: Overcoming the cutaneous barrier: Topical delivery platforms for targeted gene-based therapeutics in psoriasis.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated skin disorder characterized by persistent inflammation, epidermal hyperproliferation, and complex interactions among immune cells, keratinocytes, cytokines, and genetic factors. Although conventional topical agents, systemic small molecules, and biologics have improved disease management, their clinical utility is often limited by insufficient efficacy, adverse effects, treatment resistance, and poor patient adherence. Recent advances in molecular biology have identified numerous pathogenic genes, signaling pathways, and regulatory RNAs involved in psoriasis, providing opportunities for the development of gene-based therapeutics, including antisense oligonucleotides, plasmid DNAs, small interfering RNAs, messenger RNAs, microRNAs, aptamers, and CRISPR/Cas9 systems. These therapeutics enable precise modulation of disease-associated targets at the genomic and transcriptional levels, offering advantages over conventional pharmacological approaches. However, their topical administration is hindered by the formidable cutaneous barrier, limited skin penetration, poor cellular uptake, and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation. This review summarizes the cellular, molecular, and genetic mechanisms underlying psoriasis pathogenesis and discusses the therapeutic potential of diverse gene-based approaches. Particular emphasis is placed on topical delivery platforms designed to overcome cutaneous barriers, including permeation enhancers, nanocarrier-based systems, and physical enhancement technologies. Recent advances in the integration of these delivery strategies with gene therapeutics for targeted psoriasis treatment are highlighted. Finally, current challenges related to delivery efficiency, long-term safety, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory approval are discussed, together with future perspectives for the clinical translation of topical gene-based therapeutics toward precision psoriasis management.

title: Uncovering the lymphatic uptake, pharmacokinetics, and biodistribution of mRNA-lipid nanoparticles after intravenous and subcutaneous injection.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations have enabled the in vivo delivery of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) vaccines and therapeutics yet the delivery of RNA remains relatively inefficient. In order to improve LNP design there is a need to better understand how current mRNA-LNP formulations are trafficked and expressed in vivo. Importantly, no prior work has quantified mRNA-LNP transport through lymphatics. In the current study we profile the thoracic lymph uptake, plasma pharmacokinetics (PK), and tissue protein expression after intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) administration in rats of three common LNP formulations (ALC-0315, SM-102 and MC3 ionizable lipids) containing muGFP-P2A-nLuc reporter mRNA. After IV administration, the SM-102 and MC3 LNP formulations provided the most effective protection of mRNA in plasma. Despite this, tissue NanoLuc® Luciferase (nLuc) expression at 32 h post-dosing was relatively similar across formulations with highest expression seen in the liver and spleen. After SC injection, all formulations supported relatively low bioavailability of mRNA (0.42-0.87% dose) and slightly higher bioavailability of ionizable and PEG lipid (<5% dose) with PK profiles of the ionizable lipid and PEG lipid not completely matching the mRNA PK profiles. There was also greater lymphatic recovery of all ionizable lipids (3.1-4.3% dose) compared to mRNA (0.62-1.4% dose) and PEG lipid (1.9-2.0% dose). Together this data suggests that mRNA is lost prior to or during lymphatic transport. Importantly, concentrations of all mRNA-LNP components were 10-1000 fold higher in thoracic lymph compared to plasma after SC injection. At 32 h after SC injection, highest nLuc expression was seen in lymph nodes and tissues near the dosing site and in the liver and spleen. These findings demonstrating that mRNA-LNPs predominantly traffic from tissue injection sites via lymphatics, mRNA-LNP components may traffic separately from each other in both lymph and blood, and tissue protein expression reflects the PK of mRNA-LNPs at early timepoints.

title: Overcoming technological and biological barriers to pulmonary mRNA delivery with lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles.
abstract: Delivering mRNA to the lungs promises treatment of genetic, infectious and non-communicable lung diseases. Yet, conventional lipid nanoparticle formulations lack the stability needed to endure the harsh mechanical stress during nebulization. Additionally, once deposited in the respiratory tract, gene delivery systems may first have to overcome the mucus barrier, before actually transfecting the target cells. To overcome these challenges, we utilize lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles (LPH), merging the stability of pharmaceutical polymers with the transfection efficiency of cationic and ionizable lipids. LPH are produced in a robust microfluidic process, accomplish near-complete encapsulation efficiency, even after nebulization, and confer high transfection efficiency in A549 cells. To provide colloidal stability after aerosolization, we developed a coating strategy with hyaluronic acid (HA) and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), ensuring ideal nebulization stability by steric shielding. This formulation showed good transfection efficiency of air-liquid interface grown Calu-3 cells, producing and covered by mucus. The potential of LPH to deliver mRNA to mammalian cells was first shown in primary human lung fibroblasts in vitro and could also be confirmed after intratracheal administration to mice in vivo. Together, these findings validate LPH as a versatile and aerosolizable mRNA delivery platform, overcoming the key technological and biological barriers in pulmonary gene delivery.

title: mRNA folding facilitates efficient and spleen-targeted delivery by highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics hold great promise in preventing and treating various diseases. However, the instability and high immunogenicity of raw mRNA molecules, along with the inefficient delivery vectors, strictly limited the proteins translation and therapeutic applications. In this work, we successfully engineered a folded structural mRNA for enhancing its stability by leveraging a magnesium ion (Mg2+)-mediated charge neutralization and structural compression strategy. Further, a functionalized highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s (HPAEs) was utilized to efficiently deliver the folded mRNA, achieving specifically targeting to the spleen. Notably, compared with polyplexes containing non-folded mRNA, the optimal folded mRNA-based polyplexes exhibited stronger mRNA encapsulation, smaller size, and a more homogeneous morphology; ultimately, demonstrated higher mRNA transfection efficiency up to 85.4% across five different cell types, maintaining high cell viability. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that Mg2+-mediated mRNA folding strategy dramatically enhanced the folded mRNA-formulated polyplexes cellular uptake and endosomal escape. Encouragingly, when administered systemically, the representative folded mRNA-based polyplexes demonstrated robust protein expression, yielding 3-fold enhancement in spleen, compared to the unfolded mRNA-based nanoparticles, showing superior biosafety in vivo. Collectively, the work establishes a new class of the folded structure mRNA polymer delivery system, and provides a foundation for the next generation of RNA-based therapeutic drugs for spleen-related diseases.

title: Exploring lipid nanoparticle design spaces using self-regulating microfluidic machines and multiplexed in vivo biodistribution.
abstract: Delivering therapeutic mRNA relies on lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Finding optimal process parameters for new lipid combinations in LNP formulations remains a challenge. We used an automated, self-regulating microfluidic formulation platform developed for PEG-containing LNPs that actively changes process parameters to meet preset LNP diameters, and now explore how this automated production setup can be expanded to LNPs decorated with poly(2-oxazoline) (POx)-lipids. We also examine how the choice of lipopolymer affects the resulting physicochemical properties and in vivo biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. For that, we tested new LNPs by swapping poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipopolymers for alternatives based on poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) (PMeOx) and poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx). For both POx-lipid variants, the platform independently identified optimal production conditions in four or fewer iterative cycles, yielding particles of the preset size and high mRNA encapsulation. Small-angle X-ray scattering revealed that smaller LNPs modified with PEtOx had greater structural surface variety and higher mRNA loading efficiency. When multiplexing these formulations in mice, the PEtOx-containing LNPs accumulated more in bone marrow and liver (and less in spleen and pancreas), compared to those with PEG, indicating trends that the chemistry of the lipopolymer affects the biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. By combining automated formulation and in vivo multiplexed testing, our approach provides a practical way to rapidly plan, formulate, and evaluate large pharmaceutical design spaces to select excipients and process parameters yielding optimal biological performance of LNPs.

title: Macrophage-targeted GAS6 siRNA delivery by a multifunctional mannan-peptide nanocarrier attenuates pulmonary fibrosis progression.
abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal interstitial lung disease with limited treatment options. Here, we investigated MR3, a macrophage-targeted polysaccharide-peptide delivery system, for the pulmonary delivery of siRNA against growth arrest-specific protein 6 (GAS6). MR3 facilitated effective siRNA endosomal escape, while intratracheal administration ensured sustained lung retention with targeted uptake by macrophages. Functionally, siGAS6@MR3 selectively downregulated macrophage GAS6 expression to inhibit profibrotic M2 polarization, thereby improving survival, restoring lung function, and reversing histological and molecular indices of fibrosis in IPF models. Furthermore, MR3 conferred intrinsic antioxidant protection that enhanced macrophage survival under oxidative stress. siGAS6@MR3 was well tolerated in long-term repeat-dose studies, with no evidence of systemic toxicity. These findings identify GAS6 as a promising antifibrotic target and establish MR3 as a versatile, macrophage-selective siRNA platform for fibrotic and other macrophage-driven diseases.

title: Nucleic acid technologies in crustacean disease management: Diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance.
abstract: Crustacean aquaculture, particularly shrimp, crab, and lobster production, contributes around US$10 billion annually to the global food supply but remains highly vulnerable to viral and bacterial diseases. Pathogens such as White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV), Yellow Head Virus (YHV), Taura Syndrome Virus (TSV), and Vibrio species continue to cause substantial economic losses, and conventional management based on visual inspection, histopathology, and antimicrobial treatment is often slow and insensitive. This review examines how nucleic acid technologies are reshaping diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance in crustacean health management. Molecular diagnostic platforms including PCR, quantitative PCR, reverse transcription PCR, loop mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, and multiplex assays allow rapid, sensitive, and specific detection of pathogens, often before clinical signs appear. RNA interference shows strong therapeutic promise against viral pathogens, with experimental studies reporting 40 to 80% reductions in cumulative mortality, although stability, dosing, delivery, and production cost continue to limit commercial use. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) and Cas (CRISPR-associated) has emerged as a powerful platform for functional genomics, immune gene characterisation, and the future development of disease resistant strains, though application in crustaceans remains largely proof of concept. Environmental DNA and molecular biosurveillance enable early pathogen detection through water and sediment sampling, supporting proactive biosecurity and precision aquaculture. Persistent barriers include scalability, infrastructure gaps in producing regions, regulatory uncertainty, and public acceptance. Future progress will rely on improved delivery systems, expanded crustacean genomic resources, and integration of molecular tools with digital farm management to deliver sustainable disease control.

title: Biomaterials for environmental control of AMR dissemination.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens human, animal, agricultural, and environmental health, driven by horizontal and vertical gene transfer. Conventional wastewater treatment removes 63-94% of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) but fails to eliminate ARGs and antibiotic-resistant bacteria, while generating toxic sludge. This review evaluates advanced biomaterials, including silver and gold nanoparticles, reactive oxygen species, magnetic nanocomposites, targeted disruption of metabolic pathways, carbon-based sorbents, biopolymers, metal-organic frameworks, functionalized enzymes/peptides, and engineered biofilms, for reducing ARG and resistant-bacteria loads, inhibiting horizontal gene transfer, and reducing the selective pressure exerted by residual antibiotics. These approaches offer enhanced performance across wastewater/agriculture/air/food supply chain systems. Challenges in scalability, ecological safety, and regulation remain, requiring integration with AI monitoring, CRISPR tools, and One Health strategies. This review aims to summarize and discuss the literature on the development and use of innovative biomaterial-based intervention strategies that address the environmental aspects of AMR in order to provide a comprehensive overview of what has been learned and developed to date.

title: Frailty as a determinant of mRNA vaccine efficacy.
abstract: Frailty, an age-related state of increased vulnerability, is associated with greater susceptibility to infection and impaired vaccine response. In this Review, we examine how frailty-associated immunosenescence, including altered haematopoiesis, chronic inflammation, and dysfunction of innate and adaptive immune responses, can affect the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines. Evidence from COVID-19 lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines and other vaccines suggests that people living with frailty can mount weaker or less durable responses than non-frail peers, although findings remain heterogeneous and frailty-specific evidence is scarce. The high customisability of lipid nanoparticle mRNA platforms creates opportunities for frailty-tailored vaccination. We discuss optimisation of lipid nanoparticle composition, targeting and dosing, mRNA cargo and combination-vaccine approaches, alongside host-directed measures addressing comorbidities, nutrition, and immune dysfunction. Integrating frailty into vaccine design, evaluation, and deployment could support safer, more effective, and more individualised vaccination strategies for older adults.

title: Genome editing for hereditary angioedema: A landmark trial and important unanswered questions.
abstract: Hereditary angioedema is a bradykinin-mediated genetic disorder increasingly controlled with effective long-term prophylaxis. In a phase 3 trial, a single dose of lonvoguran ziclumeran, an in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 therapy targeting KLKB1, significantly reduced attack rates. This approach represents a highly promising therapeutic strategy for HAE. However, it also raises important questions that require further investigation.

title: An overview of current technologies in the development of drugs and vaccines against dengue virus.
abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is a mosquito-borne flavivirus with four distinct serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. It can cause a range of illnesses, from self-resolving dengue fever to severe dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Dengue fever is a major public health hazard in tropical and subtropical areas. Advances in treatment and prevention have mainly focused on developing vaccines and antiviral medications. Currently, no treatment for dengue fever works for everyone. While some antiviral candidates are in clinical trials, most remain in preclinical or early research stages. Regarding vaccinations, the WHO has approved or prequalified two live-attenuated options: TAK-003 (Qdenga®) and Dengvaxia® (CYD-TDV). However, both vaccines have drawbacks, including limited effectiveness across serotypes and safety issues in seronegative individuals. Current research aims to elucidate the complex host immune responses that underlie dengue pathogenesis and vaccine-induced protection, to develop more effective treatments and preventive measures. Critically, most approaches remain at the experimental or preclinical stage and require further clinical evaluation.

title: Recent Progresses in Immune Cell Therapy for Tuberculosis.
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of global mortality. Its prevention and control face major challenges, including a large latent infection reservoir, high transmissibility, complex treatment protocols, rising drug-resistant TB (notably multidrug-resistant TB, MDR-TB), and comorbidities. MDR-TB has severely undermined conventional pharmacotherapy, with suboptimal global treatment success rates. Thus, novel strategies are urgently needed to accelerate elimination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and shorten treatment duration. Immune cell-based therapies, acting through multiple targeted mechanisms, align well with the complex demands of TB treatment. When integrated with advanced technologies such as genetic engineering and nanotechnology, immunotherapy holds substantial promise for developing novel regimens. This review systematically delineates major immune cell types involved and their mechanisms of action, critically assesses current technical bottlenecks, and explores future innovative directions. It also critically evaluates recent encouraging clinical trials in TB immunotherapy. Collectively, these efforts aim to establish a robust theoretical and practical translational framework, overcome existing limitations, accelerate clinical translation of immune cell-based therapies, provide new options for patients, and advance the field toward personalized and precision medicine.

title: Molecular insights into the long terminal repeat regions of therapeutic staphylococcal Twortvirinae phages.
abstract: Staphylococcal bacteriophages with proven therapeutic efficacy in anti-staphylococcal therapy have large (~140 kb) genomes and belong to subfamily Twortvirinae. Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.

title: Integrated engineering of antibiotic-marker-free cyanobacterial chassis for enhanced recombinant protein accumulation and intestinal localization.
abstract: Engineered cyanobacteria are promising microbial chassis for recombinant protein production and oral delivery, but low intracellular accumulation, expression-associated physiological burden, and residual antibiotic-resistance markers limit their application. Here, we developed an integrated protein-production and marker-removal strategy in Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and evaluated chromosomal reporter expression in Arthrospira platensis NIES-39. The CpcB-based expression configuration at the native phycocyanin locus resulted in markedly higher mVenus accumulation than free expression at the NSC1 neutral site, accompanied by reduced culture growth and altered photosynthetic characteristics. Incorporation of a tobacco etch virus protease recognition site, together with chromosomal TEV protease expression, enabled partial intracellular cleavage of the fusion protein. Sequential CRISPR-Cpf1 editing and SacB counterselection enabled the removal of targeted antibiotic-resistance cassettes in Synechocystis, as supported by locus-specific PCR and Sanger sequencing. Chromosomal mVenus expression was also established in A. platensis, although the complete marker-removal strategy was not successfully transferred to this host. Under zebrafish-oriented in vitro intestinal conditions, engineered Synechocystis exhibited pronounced structural disruption, whereas A. platensis filaments fragmented more gradually, accompanied by the release of intracellular components. Following zebrafish feeding, reporter-associated fluorescence was detected in the examined intestinal sections at 6 h after administration. Together, these results establish a Synechocystis engineering framework integrating enhanced recombinant protein accumulation, protease-mediated intracellular processing, and targeted antibiotic-marker removal, with complementary assessment of intestinal mVenus-associated fluorescence following oral administration.

title: Beyond prediction: The evolving role of artificial intelligence in genome editing.
abstract: Since the discovery of the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)-associated (Cas) system, genome-editing technologies have advanced rapidly, and the field has expanded substantially. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) has progressed at an unprecedented pace and is transforming genetic engineering. Early AI applications primarily addressed predictive tasks, including guide RNA (gRNA) activity, off-target effects, and editing outcomes for CRISPR-Cas nucleases, base editors, and prime editors. Recently, transformer-based protein language models (PLMs) and generative AI have expanded the role of AI beyond prediction to direct molecular design. Thus, AI-driven frameworks can now evolve genome-editing proteins, design molecular architectures, and generate de novo genome-editing enzymes. This review discusses how AI is reshaping genome engineering, from gRNA activity prediction to the design of next-generation editors.

title: Small genomes, big lessons: What viruses teach us about structure-based riboregulation.
abstract: RNA viruses encode multiple layers of information within a single molecule, which functions simultaneously as a template for protein synthesis and as a structured regulatory RNA. These structures control key aspects of viral gene expression, govern host interactions, and mediate immune evasion. Although the prevalence of RNA structure in viral genomes is now well established, only recently have functional and mechanistic studies begun to uncover how these elements act as regulatory modules that shape infection outcomes. With their compact genomes and experimentally tractable life cycles, RNA viruses represent powerful model systems for uncovering the fundamental building blocks of riboregulation and illuminating principles of gene control conserved across eukaryotes. Here, we review current mechanistic understanding of RNA structure-based regulation across diverse viral families and draw parallels to structure-mediated gene control in eukaryotic transcriptomes, highlighting RNA structure as a central regulatory layer in gene expression with broad therapeutic and synthetic biology potential.

title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation.
abstract: We have previously proposed a combined therapy for spinal muscular atrophy based on the upregulation of exon 7 (E7) inclusion into SMN2 mRNA by the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen (ASO1) together with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Using a CRISPR-deadCas-based strategy in a human cell line, we show here that targeting histone acetylation at the SMN2 E7 region duplicates the HDACi effect, which overcomes pleiotropic effects. Most noticeably, targeted acetylation at the E7 region causes acetylation and activation of the 30-kbp-distant promoter. Since the nusinersen target site maps near the SMN2 gene 3' end, this crosstalk between the two ends of the gene prompted us to use chromosome conformation analysis (3C) to find that ASO1 promotes gene looping. This unpredicted property of ASOs in modulating chromatin 3D configuration depends on cohesin, CTCF, cleavage/polyadenylation factors, and a canonical poly(A) signal and causes promoter activation at a long distance, which expands the therapeutic potential of splicing-correcting ASOs.

title: Rethinking nonsense suppression therapies in inherited retinal diseases.
abstract: Nonsense mutations account for approximately 20% of pathogenic variants in inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). With advances in gene therapy, nucleic acid-based nonsense suppression strategies, including suppressor tRNAs, RNA pseudouridylation, and adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing, have demonstrated therapeutic potential in preclinical studies. These next-generation approaches offer substantial opportunities for engineering and optimization, with the potential to enable precise and efficient restoration of full-length functional proteins. In this review, we propose that IRDs represent an attractive group of diseases for the clinical translation of these next-generation therapies owing to their high burden of nonsense mutations and the unique advantages of ocular gene therapy. We further outline key strategies to accelerate clinical translation, spanning therapeutic engineering, preclinical validation, and mutation-guided clinical trial design.

title: pH/ROS dual-responsive SmartGel-Cas9/TRPV4 for autophagy regulation in intervertebral disc degeneration.
abstract: This study developed a pH/ROS dual-responsive SmartGel platform for local CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery and TRPV4 inhibition in intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). The GelMA/PBA-based SmartGel responded to acidic and oxidative microenvironmental cues and released Cas9/sgRNA under disease-mimicking conditions. In nucleus pulposus (NP) cells, SmartGel-Cas9/TRPV4 lowered ROS accumulation, restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and coordinated apoptosis, senescence, Ca2+ homeostasis, CaMKKβ-dependent AMPK-mTOR signaling, and autophagic flux. CaMKKβ knockdown weakened AMPK activation and mTOR inhibition and autophagic-flux restoration, supporting CaMKKβ as a required link in this mechanism. In the rat IVDD model, the system preserved disc architecture, improved hydration status, reinforced extracellular matrix (ECM) homeostasis, and restrained downstream pathological signaling. Exploratory scRNA-seq and proteomic analyses further indicated treatment-associated shifts in Ca2+/autophagy/MAPK/Wnt-related programs. Overall, SmartGel-Cas9/TRPV4 may attenuate IVDD by restoring CaMKKβ-associated autophagic degradation and ECM balance while limiting aberrant signaling activation.

title: Distinct regulation of influenza HA head- versus stem-specific B cell responses in HA mRNA-LNP vaccinated and naïve infant African green monkeys.
abstract: The generation of memory B cells following influenza virus vaccination and their rapid recruitment into the virus-specific immune response following infection is an essential component of vaccine-induced protection. We have previously reported the capacity of an influenza hemagglutinin (HA) expressing mRNA-LNP vaccine administered to newborn African green monkeys (AGM) to elicit both HA head- and stem-specific antibodies that exhibit a wide array of effector functions. Vaccine-induced responses culminated in enhanced protection compared to non-vaccinated newborn AGM. These results were noteworthy given the lack of an approved influenza vaccine for this age group. Here, we evaluated early antibody and cellular responses following respiratory infection of vaccinated versus naïve animals to gain insights into the events that may be associated with the improved protection in vaccinated newborns. Seven days following challenge, we find an increase in the number of class-switched, affinity matured antibody secreting cells in the lung draining lymph nodes of vaccinated newborns, consistent with recall of memory B cells and rapid differentiation into antibody secreting cells (ASCs). Our data are consistent with a vaccine-mediated affinity advantage in the ASC population. While this benefit extended to HA head-specific germinal center B cells, it was not the case for cells binding HA stem. This was the result of unexpectedly higher apparent affinity of these cells in naïve animals. These data extend our understanding of how vaccination and infection shape activation and differentiation of the head- and stem-specific responses in infants following influenza virus infection.

title: Loss of APOBEC1 disrupts RNA editing homeostasis and accelerates prion disease progression.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: RNA editing is an epitranscriptomic mechanism that shapes transcriptome diversity and fine-tunes neuronal function. While adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative disorders, the role of cytidine-to-uridine (C-to-U) editing catalyzed by APOBEC1 remains largely unexplored.
METHODS: We investigated the impact of APOBEC1 on RNA editing homeostasis and prion disease progression using complementary in vitro and in vivo models. Global RNA editing and gene expression profiles were established in non-infected N2A and prion-infected sc-N2A murine neuroblastoma cells, under control conditions or following APOBEC1 depletion. APOBEC1 was silenced by shRNA-mediated knockdown to assess its regulatory contribution. In vivo disease progression was assessed in Apobec1 knockout mice subjected to RML prion infection to evaluate survival outcomes.
RESULTS: Prion infection was associated with a global increase in RNA editing and an expanded repertoire of edited transcripts in sc-N2A cells. APOBEC1 depletion markedly reduced the overall editing levels, affecting both A-to-I and C-to-U editing events, reshaping editing patterns in transcripts associated with RNA and protein transport, cellular stress responses, synaptic signaling, and neuroimmune interactions. Consistently, Apobec1 KO mice exhibited accelerated body weight loss and significantly shortened survival following RML prion challenge.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support APOBEC1 as a contributor to RNA editing homeostasis and suggest that APOBEC1 loss reduces resilience to prion-induced neurodegenerative stress. APOBEC1 deficiency was associated with altered editome profiles in prion-infected cells and accelerated disease progression in the RML prion model.

title: From iPSC Disease Modeling to Epigenome Editing: Toward Therapeutic Reversal of Genomic Imprinting Disorders.
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and organoids are increasingly important components of new approach methodologies because they provide experimentally accessible human systems that preserve patient-specific genetic backgrounds and can be differentiated into disease-relevant cell types. Genomic imprinting disorders are particularly attractive targets for this approach because their pathogenesis depends not only on DNA sequence but also on parent-of-origin-specific epigenetic regulation. Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) and Angelman syndrome (AS), which arise from distinct disruptions within the same imprinted domain on chromosome 15q11.2-q13, illustrate both the opportunities and the complexity of therapeutic epigenetic manipulation. Recent studies using PWS patient-derived iPSCs have shown that disease-associated imprinting states are largely retained after reprogramming and can be experimentally reversed by locus-specific epigenome editing. Targeted demethylation of the PWS imprinting control region restored multiple paternally expressed genes, and the corrected state persisted after differentiation into hypothalamic organoids, partially normalizing disease-associated transcriptomic and functional phenotypes. Here, we discuss how iPSC-based disease modeling is evolving from a platform for mechanism discovery toward a test bed for therapeutic epigenome engineering and outline the major challenges that must be addressed before epigenome editing can be translated to patients with imprinting disorders.

title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.

title: A cross-species AAV platform for precise microglial interrogation.
abstract: Targeting microglia with adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) remains challenging because of inefficient transduction, off-target expression, and inconsistent payload performance. Here, we develop an integrated, Cre-independent AAV platform that combines a compact 446-bp microglia-specific regulatory element (MSRE), a high-yield AAV2/9.m capsid, microRNA-mediated neuronal de-targeting, and a microglia-tailored codon-optimization strategy. Following direct intracranial delivery, the optimized vector achieves robust, long-lasting transgene expression with greater than 90% microglial specificity across multiple mouse brain regions, including in an Alzheimer's disease model. With doxorubicin-assisted delivery, the platform also enables efficient and selective microglial targeting in rats, rhesus macaques, and human ex vivo brain slices. Codon optimization supports the expression of otherwise challenging functional payloads, enabling calcium imaging, chemogenetic manipulation, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. This cross-species toolkit provides a versatile resource for investigating microglial biology and developing microglia-directed therapeutic strategies.

title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.
abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

title: Silencing hepatic complement factor B inhibits alternative pathway activation and attenuates arthritis in CAIA model.
abstract: The complement system comprises tightly regulated enzymatic cascades that are essential for innate immune defense and tissue homeostasis. Although protective under physiological conditions, complement dysregulation can drive inflammation and tissue injury and contributes to the pathogenesis of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, prompting the development of complement-targeted therapies. Here, we describe the development and nonclinical evaluation of AZD6912, a GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNA (siRNA) designed to silence hepatic complement factor B (CFB) as a potential treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. AZD6912 produced potent on-target knockdown of CFB in a hepatocyte cell line and a primary human hepatocyte spheroid model, with no evidence of off-target effects. In mice, a surrogate siRNA targeting hepatic Cfb achieved >90% reduction in liver Cfb mRNA and >95% reduction in circulating CFB protein. This target-specific silencing reduced local complement production, attenuated joint inflammation, and provided therapeutic benefit in the collagen antibody-induced arthritis (CAIA) model. In non-human primates, AZD6912 showed high hepatic exposure, >80% suppression of hepatic CFB mRNA, sustained reductions in serum CFB, and >95% inhibition of complement activity. Safety assessments were unremarkable. Collectively, these findings demonstrate durable siRNA-mediated silencing of CFB with downstream pharmacologic and therapeutic effects, support the clinical development of AZD6912, and highlight the potential of GalNAc-siRNA therapeutics in immune-mediated diseases.

title: AI-Enhanced CRISPR-Cas9 Therapeutics: Advances in Precision, Safety, and Delivery.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has transformed biomedical research and is advancing toward clinical translation. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) offers improved precision in guide RNA design, off-target prediction, and delivery optimization. This review synthesizes recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 for medical applications, covering core mechanisms, engineered variants, base and prime editors, and therapeutic applications including CAR T-cell and CAR-NK engineering, genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and regenerative medicine. Delivery strategies are evaluated with emphasis on AI-driven optimization. AI applications are highlighted across deep learning architectures for guide RNA design, AI-designed nucleases such as OpenCRISPR-1, structure-guided and AI-assisted design of compact high-fidelity SaCas9 variants, reinforcement learning for pipeline optimization, and roles in CAR T-cell therapy and safety assessment. Safety challenges are examined, including off-target effects, chromosomal rearrangements, immunogenicity, and regulatory concerns. Future directions emphasize multi-scale modeling, explainable AI, clinical validation, and integration with synthetic biology, single-cell sequencing, organoids, and nanomaterials. The convergence of AI and CRISPR-Cas9 holds substantial potential for personalized medicine.

title: Mechanisms of Lipid Droplet-Mitochondria Interactions and Their Roles in Diseases.
abstract: Lipid droplets (LDs) coordinate cellular lipid utilization, energy homeostasis, redox balance, and autophagy through dynamic inter-organelle communication with mitochondria. This review summarized recent advances in the molecular mechanisms regulating LD-mitochondria interactions and discusses how their dysregulation contributes to disease progression. Accumulating evidence has indicated that the contacts between LD and mitochondria are dynamically regulated through specialized membrane contact sites and protein complexes, such as Perilipin (PLIN) family of proteins, Mitofusin2 (Mfn2), and Rab GTPases. Rather than being a passive structural association, this interaction serves as a regulatory hub that integrates fatty acid (FA) transport, metabolic adaptation, and stress responses. It enables bidirectional regulation of lipid metabolism, allowing cells to flexibly and efficiently switch between lipid storage and FA oxidation in response to metabolic signals. Disruption of this inter-organelle communication impairs intracellular lipid utilization, compromises mitochondrial function, and exacerbates oxidative stress and ferroptosis. Such dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a core mechanism underlying metabolic disorders, cardiovascular diseases and neurodegenerative diseases. In the future, integration of protein regulation, gene editing technologies, and precision therapeutic approaches may enable specific targeting of LD-mitochondria communication, thereby offering new avenues for the treatment of relevant diseases.

title: Dysregulated Metal Homeostasis in Alzheimer's Disease: From Pathological Modulators to Therapeutic Targets.
abstract: The "metal ion hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained widespread acceptance, but translating this understanding into effective therapies remains elusive. This likely stems from a simplistic understanding of metal homeostasis as merely a matter of "excess and deficiency." This article reviews the context-dependent roles of iron, copper, zinc, aluminum, and manganese in the pathogenesis of AD, with a particular focus on their bidirectional interactions with classic AD pathology (the ferroptosis hypothesis is relatively mature, while emerging hypotheses such as cuproptosis have not been fully elucidated). Metal homeostasis dysregulation can directly promote β-amyloid aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Conversely, these pathological processes can also alter the binding, storage, transport, and subcellular distribution of metal ions. Dysregulated metal ions function as "context-dependent" modulators of pathological processes. Their functional effects depend on metal species, concentration, binding state, subcellular compartment, and disease stage. Metal homeostasis dysregulation associated with AD may essentially reflect a redistribution between physiological and pathological pools. Ideal interventions should selectively neutralize pathological metal pools while preserving or restoring essential metal-dependent neuronal functions. By integrating the latest advances in the field of metal-targeted therapies (chelators, metabolic modulators, biomarkers, metal imaging, and gene editing), we emphasize that future treatments should shift from nonspecific metal clearance toward precise metal regulation and precision medicine.

title: Omics-driven improvement of safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.) for climate resilience, oil quality, and high-value metabolites under changing environments.
abstract: Safflower is an Asteraceae oilseed crop valued for its high-quality unsaturated fatty acids (≈90% oleic and linoleic acids), natural floral pigments, and diverse bioactive compounds. These attributes underpin its applications in functional foods, nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals, and various industrial sectors. Safflower inherent tolerance to drought, heat, cold, and salinity positions it as a climate-resilient alternative to more temperature-sensitive oilseeds; however, omics-based research in this crop remains comparatively fragmented. This review consolidates recent advances across major omics domains. Genomics covers chromosome-scale assemblies, GWAS panels, QTL mapping, and diagnostic candidate genes for molecular breeding. Transcriptomics summarizes regulatory networks for flavonoid and oil biosynthesis, stress-responsive transcription factors (NAC, WRKY, bZIP, AP2/ERF), and seed developmental programs. The proteomics section addresses stress-inducible, therapeutic, and storage/lipid metabolic proteins linked to quality and stress adaptation. Metabolomics outlines quinochalcone and flavonoid pathway architecture, color-specific metabolic profiles, and emerging clinical and nutraceutical applications. Phenomics highlights UAV-based high-throughput phenotyping, RGB and multispectral imaging for salt and drought screening, and machine-learning-assisted germplasm authentication. Epigenomics focuses on DNA methylation and miRNA-mediated regulation. Finally, lipidomics and metagenomics consider oil authentication biomarkers, refining optimization, and microbiome-driven nutrient cycling shaping medicinally important compounds. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in multi-omics integration, CRISPR-based functional validation, genomic selection pipelines, and detailed characterization of root-shoot architecture under combined stresses. Addressing these gaps will advance mechanistic understanding of climate resilience and enable the development of stress-tolerant, high-yielding safflower cultivars with improved oil quality and bioactive profiles, thereby supporting climate-resilient production systems and high-value safflower-based products at scale.
