title: Beyond diagnostic categories: A narrative review of transdiagnostic mechanisms in neurodevelopmental disorders.
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) represent a heterogeneous class of early-onset conditions marked by impairments in cognition, reduced social function, hyperactivity and repetitive-stereotyped behaviour. Traditionally classified as discrete clinical entities, NDDs such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability (ID) are now increasingly understood as overlapping, multifactorial conditions shaped by converging genetic, epigenetic, immune, and environmental influences. This review synthesizes current evidence challenging categorical diagnostic boundaries and instead proposes a transdiagnostic and mechanistic framework that integrates shared disruptions in neural circuits, excitatory/inhibitory balance, synaptic architecture, and immune-metabolic signalling. We explore how genes and environment interact during early development, how epigenetics influences long-term outcomes, and how these insights are driving a shift toward precision medicine guided by biomarkers and patient-derived models. Emerging therapies include neuromodulation, immune and microbiota-based interventions, and gene editing, supported by insights from animal and iPSC models. A time-sensitive and biologically grounded approach is needed, moving beyond symptom-based classifications to allow for earlier diagnosis, personalized treatment, and the development of innovative interventions. This paradigm shift aligns with precision approaches already transforming other biomedical domains and holds the potential to more effectively address the complex and lifelong challenges posed by NDDs.

title: Formulation optimisation of an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle platform sustains in vivo production of the SARS-CoV-2-neutralizing nanobody VHH 72.
abstract: Neutralizing antibodies act rapidly against SARS-CoV-2, but monoclonal antibodies are costly to manufacture and single-domain antibodies are cleared rapidly. Here we evaluated an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platform encoding the neutralizing nanobody VHH 72 and optimized the carrier by raising DSPC from 10 to 40 mol% and the citrate buffer from 25 to 300 mM. Relative to 10%PC-25mM, 40%PC-300mM produced larger particles (approximately 193 versus 75 nm), lower polydispersity, high encapsulation efficiency and better mRNA preservation in 50% serum (approximately 80% versus 43% at 24 h). Molecular dynamics simulations of the two lipid compositions gave structural descriptors consistent with tighter packing at 40 mol% DSPC, but did not address free energy or the citrate effect. In HEK293T cells, 40%PC-300mM increased VHH 72-eGFP-positive cells at 24, 48 and 72 h and cell-associated fusion protein at 72 h. In CD-1 mice, DiD-associated fluorescence declined more slowly in blood and was higher in liver through 72 h and spleen through 48 h; a luciferase reporter showed higher organ expression and a whole-body advantage through day 5. Serum VHH 72 peaked later and higher with 40%PC-300mM, and neutralizing activity persisted through day 7. In K18-hACE2 mice challenged intraperitoneally or intratracheally 1, 3 or 7 days after treatment, 40%PC-300mM gave the lowest blood and lung pseudovirus reporter signals at day 3 and was the only treatment significantly below PBS at day 7. These data support formulation optimization as a way to improve mRNA protection, reporter expression and the duration of functional VHH 72 exposure. Because the study used reporter constructs, a lipophilic dye, pseudovirus and mice, it does not establish intact-LNP biodistribution or protection against authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection.

title: Fiber-2 induces autolysosome dysfunction and impairs autophagic flux to promote FAdV-4 replication.
abstract: Fowl adenovirus serotype 4 (FAdV-4) causes hepatitis-hydropericardium syndrome in poultry, yet viral subversion of host autophagy remains unclear. Here, we investigated the role of the viral structural protein Fiber-2 in modulating the host autophagy-lysosome pathway. Transcriptomic profiling of LMH cells expressing Fiber-2 revealed coordinated upregulation of autophagy-related genes, validated by quantitative PCR. Functional assays demonstrated that Fiber-2 expression leads to autophagosome accumulation and impaired autophagic flux, as shown by LC3-II/p62 analysis, tandem fluorescent LC3 reporter imaging, Bafilomycin A1 treatment, and transmission electron microscopy. Fiber-2 predominantly localizes to late endosomes and lysosomes, and GFP-Galectin-3 reporter assays indicate that it disrupts lysosomal membrane integrity rather than blocking autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) and enrichment analyses identified BECN1, a key autophagy regulator, as a Fiber-2-interacting protein, and associated host proteins were enriched in autophagy-related pathways. Finally, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Fiber-2 significantly reduced FAdV-4 replication at later stages of infection, consistent with a proviral role for Fiber-2. These findings indicate that Fiber-2 disrupts autophagic flux by inducing lysosomal dysfunction and membrane damage, thereby promoting FAdV-4 replication and uncovering a previously unrecognized mechanism of viral subversion of host degradative pathways.

title: CTRP3 disruption promotes a tendon-like matrix signature in tenogenically induced canine adipose-derived stem cells.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tendon injuries heal through disorganized extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition rather than the restoration of native collagen architecture, thus resulting in suboptimal functional recovery. Although adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) are attractive for tendon regeneration because of their accessibility and expandability, their tenogenic differentiation efficiency is lower than that of tendon-derived stem cells (TDSCs). C1q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3) is an adipokine implicated in ECM remodeling and fibrosis; however, its role in tendon lineage regulation is unknown.
OBJECTIVE: CTRP3 (C1q/TNF-related protein 3) contributes to extracellular-matrix remodeling and, in tendon, is associated with a pathological fibrotic matrix signature; we therefore reasoned that reducing CTRP3 would favor a more mature tendon-like matrix. Using a loss-of-function approach based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), we investigated whether CTRP3 disruption alters tenogenic marker expression, at both the transcript and protein levels, and the tendon-associated ECM marker profile of canine ADSCs relative to wild-type ADSCs and native TDSCs.
METHODS: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs were generated and validated using sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting. Wild-type ADSCs, CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs, and TDSCs were subjected to tenogenic induction for 0-3 weeks. Tenogenic transcriptional and ECM markers were analyzed at mRNA and protein levels.
RESULTS: CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs showed increased collagen type I and tenomodulin (TNMD) expression during tenogenic induction compared with wild-type ADSCs. COL III expression showed a transient increase followed by a decline, with lower expression in CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs than in WT cADSCs at week 2. CTRP3 disruption increased early Mkx and Scx expression at the earliest time points but did not consistently alter the early transcriptional program, which rose comparably across all groups. CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs showed partial, marker- and time-point-dependent overlap with native cTDSCs, mainly for selected late ECM markers rather than across the overall transcript and protein profiles.
CONCLUSION: CTRP3 disruption shifted the tendon-associated ECM marker profile during the tenogenic differentiation of ADSCs, with reduced COL III accumulation, rather than uniformly enhancing tenogenic differentiation. Although early transcriptional changes were observed, the more consistent differences were found in late tendon-associated ECM markers. The modulation of CTRP3 may represent a candidate strategy worth further investigation for stem cell-based tendon regeneration in veterinary medicine.

title: Oxidized phospholipids: evolution, signaling, cell death, and human diseases.
abstract: Oxidized phospholipids (OxPLs) represent a class of molecules generated during evolution that shift from fundamental membrane building-blocks to key signaling mediators, linking lipid metabolism, cellular redox homeostasis and multi-faceted cell-fate control. Generated by both enzymatic and non-enzymatic peroxidation events, OxPLs engage in extensive signaling crosstalk with lyso-phospholipids and oxylipins. The FerroLipid framework describes iron-lipid peroxidation crosstalk to contextualize iron-dependent lipid signaling. OxPLs govern diverse regulated cell-death programs: they act as lipid death signals in apoptosis and ferroptosis, tune ferroptotic outputs through intrinsic antioxidant systems, and exert context-specific modulatory effects on pyroptosis and other cell-death modalities. Beyond cell-death execution, OxPLs signal through pattern-recognition, scavenger and nuclear receptors to orchestrate inflammation, membrane remodeling, phagocytic clearance, autophagy, mitophagy and protein homeostasis. Threshold-dependent accumulation of OxPLs drives pathological processes across neurodegenerative, metabolic, cardiovascular, neoplastic and infectious diseases; their disease-specific molecular signatures confer potential as both diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Redox phospholipidomics coupled with mass-spectrometry imaging enables accurate, species-resolved profiling of distinct OxPL species. Multiple pharmacological approaches and gene-editing interventions have demonstrated tangible translational prospects for OxPL-oriented therapy. This review synthesizes existing knowledge of OxPL biology from evolutionary origins and signaling mechanisms to disease relevance, analytical tools and therapeutic opportunities. It highlights major unresolved research bottlenecks and provides a solid conceptual foundation for advancing lipid-targeted treatments for complex human disorders.

title: Generation of a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic control iPSC line (NIMHi001-A-1) from a Parkinson's disease Patient-Derived iPSC line carrying the LRRK2 I1371V mutation.
abstract: We report NIMHi001-A-1, a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic iPSC line derived from a patient line carrying a heterozygous LRRK2 missense mutation GRCh38 chr12:g.40308618A > G [(MANE transcript NM_198578.4:c.4111A > G); p.Ile1371Val] associated with familial Parkinson's disease. Sanger sequencing confirmed successful correction. The line retained iPSC morphology and expressed pluripotency markers (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2, TRA-1-60, SSEA4) by immunofluorescence, gene expression analysis, and flow cytometry. Normal karyotype (46, XY) and complete genetic identity with the parental line were established by STR profiling. No off-target modifications were detected. The line demonstrated trilineage differentiation potential and tested negative for mycoplasma, providing an isogenic platform to investigate LRRK2 I1371V-specific pathomechanisms and evaluate therapeutic strategies.

title: Generation of Spinocerebellar Ataxia 27B iPSC Lines and Isogenic Controls.
abstract: Spinocerebellar Ataxia 27B (SCA27B) is a late-onset neurodegenerative disorder caused by a heterozygous pathogenic GAA•TTC repeat expansion in intron 1 of FGF14. Despite being a common genetic cause of adult-onset cerebellar ataxia, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we performed simultaneous reprogramming and CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate four induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines and their respective isogenic gene-corrected controls. All lines exhibited normal karyotypes, pluripotency, and trilineage differentiation capacity. These paired iPSC lines provide a valuable platform for investigating the pathomechanism(s) of SCA27B and can be used for screening of potential therapeutic treatments.

title: When prevention constrains cure: Institutional lock-in and gene therapy access for beta-thalassemia.
abstract: On 16 November 2023, the United Kingdom Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first CRISPR-based gene therapy for a genetic disease, offering patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) freedom from lifelong monthly transfusions. Yet in China, which carries the world's largest TDT patient population, no patient has received the therapy through the public health system, and the access gap is not explained by price or manufacturing economics alone. This paper argues that prevention-era institutional architecture constrains cure-era access through three lock-in mechanisms: cognitive (the direction of genetic information flow), infrastructural (the spatial distribution of treatment capacity), and fiscal (the structure of payment responsibility). Drawing on a structured comparison of four countries selected to represent distinct institutional pathway types (Cyprus, ecclesiastical-public certification; China, administrative filing; Thailand, public health universal coverage; India, federal fragmentation), the analysis proposes a typology of barrier configurations and illustrates them through four exploratory cases. The administrative-filing pathway is associated with high barriers across information, geographic, and economic dimensions; trust-intention is not assessable on current evidence. The ecclesiastical-public pathway is associated with medium information and low geographic barriers with medium fiscal and low-confidence trust barriers; the universal-coverage pathway provides a balanced platform that remains under-activated for gene therapy; and the federal-fragmented pathway fails the precondition of patient identification. No pathway simultaneously optimizes all four readiness dimensions. Presented as a hypothesis-generating typology rather than a tested diagnostic model, the framework relates pathway type to barrier configuration and offers testable hypotheses for pathway-specific intervention design and for extension to sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and other genetic conditions entering the curative era.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen reveals that Wnt signaling regulates lipid accumulation in APOE4 oligodendrocytes.
abstract: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, yet the cellular mechanisms linking APOE variants to disease risk remain unclear. We previously found that APOE4 expression causes lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes, reducing myelination, but the underlying mechanisms were unknown. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) sequencing in human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived oligodendrocytes, we identified decreased Wnt signaling and overactive glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B) as key regulators of lipid-droplet accumulation. Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of GSK3B reduced lipid droplets in APOE4 oligodendrocytes and increased myelination in three-dimensional iPSC-derived brain organoids. Pharmacological GSK3B inhibition also reduced lipid droplets and improved myelination in APOE4;PS19 tau transgenic mice. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework linking Wnt/GSK3B signaling to APOE4-driven disruptions in oligodendrocyte lipid metabolism and myelination, pointing to GSK3B as a potential therapeutic target for APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease.

title: Evaluation of the minipig as an alternative model based on cross-study comparisons with rabbit in mRNA vaccine safety assessment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Robust non-clinical safety models are crucial to the development and evaluation of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA)-based drugs and vaccines. In this study, we leveraged cross-study data to explore whether the Göttingen minipig could serve as an alternative to the rabbit, a commonly used species in vaccine safety assessment.
METHODS: Results from two independent toxicity studies of lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding the hemagglutinin H3 antigen, administered at equivalent dose levels, were qualitatively compared. Clinical observations, local reactions, body weight, food consumption, body temperature, clinical pathology, immunogenicity, inflammatory biomarkers, and anatomical pathology endpoints were evaluated.
RESULTS: Both species exhibited expected vaccine responses, with minor differences in local reactogenicity and body temperature. The vaccine candidate was well tolerated at the injection site in both species. However, mild and transient vaccine-related effects (i.e., injection site induration and increased body temperature) were observed only in minipigs. Transient increases in neutrophil, fibrinogen, and C-reactive protein levels were observed in both species following vaccination, consistent with an inflammatory response. Microscopic findings (i.e., inflammation at the injection site and increased germinal center cellularity in the draining lymph nodes) were comparable between species and aligned with expected immune activation following vaccination.
CONCLUSIONS: This qualitative comparison provides preliminary, supportive evidence for the potential use of the minipig as an alternative to the rabbit in non-clinical safety evaluation of mRNA vaccines, with the added benefit of larger blood volume for sampling and availability of validated key inflammatory markers.

title: Seminal extracellular vesicles improve cryosurvival and fertility potential of kundhi buffalo sperm.
abstract: Buffaloes are important contributors to agricultural production in many developing countries, yet poor semen cryosurvival remains a major challenge for efficient artificial insemination and genetic improvement. In recent years, small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication and reproductive function; however, their potential as supplements for improving buffalo semen cryosurvival remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study evaluated the influence of adding a seminal plasma-derived small extracellular vesicle-enriched preparation to a Tris extender using post-thaw sperm traits, oxidative status, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and fertility of Kundhi buffalo bull semen. Seminal plasma-derived particles were isolated and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, showing a mean diameter of 117.8 ± 2.47 nm, modal diameter of 89.4 ± 1.41 nm, and concentration of (3.21 ± 0.05) × 1011 particles/mL. Thirty-two ejaculates from four Kundhi buffalo bulls were pooled and extended with a Tris extender supplemented with 0, 25, 50, 100, or 200 μg/mL sEV-enriched preparation before cryopreservation. Post-thaw sperm quality, early apoptosis, DNA fragmentation, lipid peroxidation, antioxidant enzymes, and relative mRNA abundance of HSP70 and PRM1 were assessed. All evaluated post-thaw variables differed (P < 0.05) after supplementation, whereas 50 μg/mL revealed the strongest response. The EV-50 group showed higher total motility, progressive motility, viability, and HOST-positive spermatozoa, however reduced early apoptotic sperm, DNA fragmentation, and MDA concentration than the control group. EV-50 also enhanced SOD, catalase, total glutathione, HSP70 and PRM1 expression (1.91 ± 0.07-fold and 1.69 ± 0.05-fold, respectively). In fertility validation, pregnancy rate increased from 41.7% in the control group to 56.7% in the EV-50-treated semen group, with higher odds of pregnancy (OR = 1.83; P = 0.028). In conclusion, supplementation with 50 μg/mL of the sEV-enriched preparation improved post-thaw sperm quality, redox homeostasis, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and field fertility, supporting its potential as a cryopreservation supplement for enhancing the reproductive performance of Kundhi buffalo semen.

title: PEAK: a phenotype-based classification of genetic variants.
abstract: Current variant classifications do not capture clinical severity relative to other pathogenic variants in the same gene. We propose phenotype-exceeding-(mono)allelic-knockout (PEAK) as a term for variants associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than that of heterozygous null alleles. This mechanism-independent designation may facilitate genotype-phenotype interpretation and identify candidates for allele-selective therapeutic development.

title: MANF promotes cell fitness and attenuates bortezomib sensitivity in multiple myeloma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy in which disease relapse and treatment resistance remain major clinical challenges. Identifying molecular dependencies that support myeloma cell fitness may reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond recurrent genomic alterations. Mesencephalic astrocyte-derived neurotrophic factor (MANF) is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, stress-responsive protein, but its clinical and biological significance in MM remains poorly defined.
METHODS: Publicly available DepMap CRISPR dependency data were analyzed to identify candidate MM-preferential dependencies. MANF expression and prognostic associations were examined in the MMRF CoMMpass cohort. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in silico perturbation analyses characterized its cellular distribution and predicted functional associations. MANF knockdown and genetic rescue using an siRNA-resistant MANF construct were performed in RPMI-8226 and OPM-2 cells to assess proliferation, cell-cycle distribution, and bortezomib sensitivity. Transcriptomic profiling characterized gene expression changes following MANF knockdown, while measurements at multiple time points assessed the temporal patterns of IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts.
RESULTS: MANF was identified as a candidate MM-preferential dependency. Higher MANF expression was associated with advanced ISS stage and inferior overall survival, with the survival association retained after adjustment for established clinical and cytogenetic risk factors. Single-cell analysis localized MANF expression predominantly to plasma cells, while virtual knockout predicted changes involving ER protein processing, proteasome function, and metabolism. MANF knockdown inhibited proliferation, increased G0/G1 accumulation, and reduced MYC/E2F-associated transcriptional programs and cell-cycle regulatory proteins. Time-course analyses revealed early enhancement followed by later attenuation in selected IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts. MANF knockdown also increased bortezomib-induced apoptosis and reduced its IC₅₀. MANF re-expression partially reversed proliferation and cell-cycle phenotypes, restored IRE1α-XBP1s-associated protein abundance, and attenuated bortezomib sensitization.
CONCLUSION: These findings identify MANF as a previously underexplored candidate myeloma-associated dependency that supports proliferative fitness and modulates bortezomib sensitivity in the tested MM models. MANF depletion is associated with dynamic changes in IRE1α-XBP1s-related readouts. These results support further investigation of MANF as a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in MM.

title: Emerging stem cell strategies for neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Degenerative diseases continue to impose a substantial global health burden with limited curative options. Neurodegenerative diseases, the principal focus of this review, are among the largest contributors to this burden. Stem cell therapies have emerged as a promising approach, offering the potential to replace lost cells, modulate pathological microenvironments, and restore tissue function through both direct cell replacement and paracrine mechanisms. However, conventional stem cell strategies encounter persistent obstacles including immune rejection, tumorigenicity, poor engraftment, and limited long-term efficacy in chronic disease settings. This narrative review synthesizes recent and emerging innovations in stem cell therapy for neurodegenerative diseases across four major domains: (i) emerging mechanisms of stem cell action, including activation of dormant neural stem cells (NSCs), exosome-based cell-free therapies, and rejuvenation of aged stem cells; (ii) emerging cell types such as pre-morula stem cells (PMSCs), perinatal stem cells, SSEA-4+ human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUC-MSCs), and iPSC-derived mesenchymal progenitor cells (MiMPCs); (iii) advanced delivery platforms including three-dimensional (3D) biomaterial scaffolds, injectable hydrogels, and stem cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CMNPs); and (iv) gene-editing strategies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9-mediated generation of hypoimmunogenic induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines for allogeneic, off-the-shelf cell therapies. Key translational gaps, including standardization of exosome isolation and scaffold fabrication protocols, long-term safety and immunogenicity assessment, and ethical and regulatory frameworks, are critically evaluated, and future research directions are proposed. In addition, the review states the level of evidence (in vitro, animal, or human) supporting each approach and summarizes their clinical status in a single table. Addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to realizing the full potential of stem cell-based regenerative medicine for degenerative diseases.

title: mRNA encoding norovirus VP1 produces antigenically functional virus-like particles in vitro.
abstract: Human norovirus is a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide across all age groups, yet no licensed vaccine is available. The major capsid protein, VP1, self-assembles into highly immunogenic virus-like particles (VLPs) that have shown promise in clinical studies. Recently, mRNA has emerged as a compelling platform for norovirus vaccination. However, whether VP1-encoding mRNA can drive authentic VLP formation in human cells relevant to the vaccination environment has remained unknown. In this study, we used multiple human cell lines, including THP-1-derived macrophage-like cells, to model the post-vaccination environment. Transfection with norovirus GII.4 VP1 mRNA or lipid nanoparticle-formulated VP1 mRNA induced both intracellular and extracellular VP1 expression. Sucrose gradient purification and electron microscopy confirmed VLP assembly. These particles retained key antigenic and functional properties, including recognition by norovirus-specific antibodies in human serum and binding to histo-blood group antigens. Collectively, our findings provide direct evidence that VP1-encoding mRNA can generate structurally and functionally relevant norovirus VLPs in physiologically relevant human cell systems. These results strengthen the mechanistic rationale for mRNA-based norovirus vaccines and support their continued development.

title: Particle occupancy in mRNA lipid nanoparticles: Measurement, manufacturing determinants, and relevance to product quality.
abstract: Encapsulation efficiency (EE) estimates the encapsulated fraction of measured RNA in an mRNA lipid nanoparticle (LNP) preparation, whereas particle occupancy measures the fraction of particles containing detectable RNA. Neither metric describes the full distribution of RNA among particles. Particle-resolved studies show that high bulk EE can coexist with RNA-negative particles and broad copy-number distributions, but reported empty-particle fractions vary with composition, preparation, and analytical method. This Minireview examines fluorescence spectroscopy, particle-resolved microscopy and RNA counting, mass spectrometry, and population-separation approaches, distinguishing direct RNA-sensitive measurements from inferred loading. It considers manufacturing determinants and evidence linking payload distributions to product performance. Process changes can alter loading without parallel changes in mean particle size. mRNA-expression, multi-cargo gene-editing, and adjacent siRNA-knockdown studies suggest possible functional consequences, although the independent effect of binary occupancy on potency remains unresolved. Historical lipid-mediated delivery experiments caution against assuming that eliminating RNA-negative particles always improves activity. Occupancy is therefore best considered a context-dependent extended-characterization metric for development and comparability. Product-specific evidence is needed to determine whether occupancy is a critical quality attribute. Its use in routine testing would also require a fit-for-purpose validated analytical procedure and an appropriate control strategy.

title: Protocol for engineering primary human and mouse T cells using peptide-assisted genome editing.
abstract: Efficient engineering of human and murine primary T cells without perturbation of cellular function is crucial for immunotherapy and immunology research. Here, we present a protocol for genome editing of primary T cells with minimal toxicity using peptide-assisted genome editing. We describe key steps required for primary T cell isolation and activation, CRISPR ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly and delivery mediated by peptide, and assessment of editing efficiency. This protocol maintains T cell proliferative capacity and functional potency. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Zhang et al.1.

title: A DNA-free CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein electroporation protocol for efficient knockout generation in cardiac and skeletal muscle cell lines.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Efficient, reproducible gene knockout in cardiomyocyte-related cell models is critical for cardiovascular research but remains challenging because of cell-type-specific sensitivity to genome-editing workflows.
METHODS: We developed an optimized CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing protocol using electroporation of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes to generate knockout lines in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. We also provide practical guidance for gRNA design, genotyping, and clonal line generation. Using human AC16 cardiomyocyte-like cells and rodent muscle-derived cell lines (C2C12, L6, and H9C2), we optimized electroporation conditions to maximize editing efficiency while maintaining viability.
RESULTS: SpCas9-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) RNPs targeting the lipid-trafficking regulator SAR1B/Sar1b produced high-frequency frameshift indels and marked loss of target protein expression in all models. A composite knockout score that combines editing efficiency and cell survival identified optimal electroporation settings of 1400 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for AC16 cells, and 1500 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for C2C12, L6, and H9C2 cells.
CONCLUSIONS: This protocol combines rational sgRNA design, chemically modified sgRNAs for efficient RNP assembly, and standardized genotyping to improve reproducibility. The framework is transferable to other cardiomyocyte and muscle-derived cell types and supports both pthe olyclonal and monoclonal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout approaches.

title: A Combinatorial mRNA Therapy for Treating Rheumatoid Arthritis and Osteoarthritis by Inhibiting Inflammation and Preventing Cartilage Degeneration.
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA) are debilitating joint disorders with distinct etiologies but share common pathological features of chronic inflammation and progressive cartilage damage. Current therapeutic options are largely palliative and yet fail to achieve desired effect. In this study, we developed a combinatorial mRNA therapy using a rationally engineered lipid nanoparticle (LNP) containing a novel ionizable lipid for enhanced cartilage penetration upon intra-articular administration. This LNP co-delivers mRNAs encoding two complementary therapeutic proteins: interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) for inflammation attenuation and a C-terminal truncated derivative of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANL3) for cartilage degeneration prevention. In pre-clinical models including collagen-induced arthritis mice, TNF-transgenic mice with spontaneous RA and destabilization of medial meniscus (DMM) surgical OA model, this dual therapy significantly ameliorated disease severity, reduced synovitis and bone erosion, and potently repaired cartilage damage. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling of joint specimens revealed that the combinatorial therapy concurrently suppressed inflammatory pathways and extracellular matrix degradation pathways, meanwhile upregulating anabolic genes facilitating chondrogenesis. Collectively, our study establishes a versatile and synergistic mRNA therapy that offers a potent disease-modifying immunomodulatory strategy capable of addressing the long-standing unmet needs in arthritis treatment.

title: De novo structural mining and engineering of TadA deaminases for high efficiency adenine base editors.
abstract: Conventional enzyme discovery relies primarily on sequence homology and phylogenetic relationships, limiting the identification of functionally related but sequence-divergent proteins. Here, we developed a structure-guided mining framework integrating AlphaFold2-predicted structures with Foldseek-based three-dimensional alignment to identify previously uncharacterized TadA scaffolds with conserved folds and divergent sequences. Two candidates, eMaTadA and eErTadA, were engineered into functional adenine base editors (ABEs) by fusion to Cas9 nickase. The resulting editors mediated robust A-to-G editing with high product purity and restricted bystander editing. Under expression-stratified and activity-matched conditions, eMa-ABE and eEr-ABE showed reduced guide-dependent DNA off-target editing relative to ABE8e, while orthogonal R-loop assays revealed lower SpCas9-independent deamination of exposed single-stranded DNA (ssDNA). In human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, eMa-ABE achieved up to approximately 80% editing at established HBG1/2 promoter targets and induced fetal hemoglobin expression following erythroid differentiation. Lipid nanoparticle delivery corrected approximately 50% of ATP7B P992L alleles in mouse liver, with no detectable increase in editing at the examined computationally predicted off-target loci. Furthermore, embedding eMaTadA within Cas9 expanded the editing window from A3-A9 to A3-A14 and enabled efficient start-codon-mediated gene inactivation. Collectively, this study establishes a structure-guided strategy for discovering and engineering sequence-divergent deaminases and expands the molecular diversity and therapeutic potential of the ABE toolkit.

title: A Scalable, Antibody-Free Lipid Nanoparticle Achieves Preferential mRNA Delivery to Human HSPCs In Vivo Without Conditioning.
abstract: Systemic nucleic acid delivery to hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) remains a major barrier to in vivo gene therapy due to hepatic sequestration of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Here, we report a scalable, ligand-free HSPC-tropic LNP enabling efficient mRNA delivery to human HSPCs in vivo without conditioning. In humanized NBSGW mice, the LNP preferentially delivered mRNA to human HSPCs and early myeloid progenitors, with limited delivery to lymphoid and non-hematopoietic cells. Single-cell transcriptomic and multiomic analyses revealed no broad transcriptional perturbation associated with delivery. Compared with the SM-102 LNP, the HSPC-tropic LNP achieved greater mRNA delivery to human HSPCs, while exhibiting substantially reduced hepatic delivery. The LNP also enabled functional delivery of Cas9 mRNA and β2M-targeting sgRNA to human CD34+ HSPCs, resulting in efficient gene editing and reduced β2M expression. These findings establish a ligand-free platform for functional RNA delivery and genome engineering in human HSPCs.

title: A Tocopherol-Related Methyltransferase SlVTE3(2) Regulates Tomato Fruit Ripening and Tocopherol Accumulation.
abstract: Tomato fruit ripening is a critical developmental process that determines the fruit quality. However, the regulatory mechanisms underlying the ripening initiation remain incompletely understood. Here, we characterized SlVTE3(2), a tocopherol-biosynthesis-related methyltransferase, and investigated its role in tomato fruit ripening. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutation of SlVTE3(2) accelerated ripening initiation, resulting in earlier ethylene production, faster softening, and an earlier color transition, whereas overexpression delayed these processes. Transcriptome analysis showed that SlVTE3(2) affected multiple ripening-related pathways, including ethylene biosynthesis and signaling, carotenoid metabolism, and cell wall modification. Although SlVTE3(2) significantly altered the tocopherol composition in tomato fruits, exogenous tocopherol treatment did not affect ripening initiation. These findings provide new insights into the regulation of tomato fruit ripening by the metabolic enzymes.

title: RNA-Lipid Interactions Control Structure and Dynamics of Lipid Nanoparticles.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the leading platform for RNA delivery, enabling applications ranging from mRNA vaccines to CRISPR therapeutics. Ionizable lipids, such as DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3), play a central role in nucleic acid encapsulation and intracellular delivery, yet the molecular mechanisms governing LNP structure and function remain incompletely understood. The internal organization of LNP cores is highly sensitive to pH and has been described by inverse hexagonal, cubic, and lamellar phases that influence delivery performance. Here, we investigate the pH-dependent structure and dynamics of MC3-containing LNPs using two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Both experiments and simulations reveal pronounced pH-dependent changes in the local environment surrounding the lipid ester linkage. At pH 4, strong electrostatic interactions between RNA and protonated MC3 produce broader spectral features consistent with increased interfacial heterogeneity and hydration. In addition, the frequency fluctuation dynamics exhibit a 46% slowdown in RNA-loaded LNPs relative to empty LNPs. In contrast, increasing the pH from 4 to 8 narrows the ester carbonyl band by ∼10 cm-1 and yields nearly identical dynamics for loaded and empty LNPs, indicating a more homogeneous and less hydrated lipid interface. MD simulations further demonstrate that MC3 protonation modulates RNA binding, interfacial hydration, and lipid packing. Together, these results highlight RNA-lipid electrostatic interactions as an important factor influencing the local environment within LNPs and potentially their pH-dependent behavior, providing molecular-level insights into the rational design of next-generation RNA delivery systems.

title: Enhanced Sampling of Ligand Binding Coupled to RNA Base-Flipping Dynamics.
abstract: Noncoding RNAs have recently emerged as promising targets for therapeutic drugs. However, their high conformational flexibility presents significant challenges in structure-based rational drug discovery. Therefore, it is essential to gain detailed mechanistic insights into the millisecond-time scale ligand recognition process coupled to RNA conformational dynamics. Enhanced sampling simulations can help investigate these intricate dynamical processes by effectively exploring the rugged conformational landscapes of RNA-ligand complexes. In this study, we applied the on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling algorithm and its flooding variant to compute the free energy surface, kinetics, and binding mechanism for three different natural and synthetic ligands to a prototypical RNA aptamer. Our simulations revealed the dynamic coupling between ligand recognition and the base-flipping transition. In addition to reproducing the relative trends of binding affinities and residence times, our results uncovered a competing effect between the conformational selection and the induced fit mechanisms. The preference for one mechanism over the other is influenced by the binding affinity. By integrating these mechanistic insights with the binding affinity and kinetics derived from our simulations, we provide an atomistically detailed understanding of the RNA-ligand recognition process.

title: RNA-Adjusted TUFM Protein State Captures Mitochondrial Proteome Organization in Lung Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Matched transcriptome-proteome measurements can reveal protein-state information not represented by RNA abundance. We integrated four lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) proteogenomic cohorts, two longitudinal osimertinib transcriptomic systems, and DepMap CRISPR screens to test whether the TUFM protein captures coordinated mitochondrial proteome organization beyond TUFM RNA. In discovery LUAD, the RNA-adjusted TUFM protein state (TUFM_PT) added substantial explanatory information beyond its transcript for mitochondrial-translation and oxidative-phosphorylation (OXPHOS) protein programs. Across three independent cohorts (n = 292), TUFM_PT replicated with pooled Spearman rho values of 0.564 and 0.620 for mitochondrial translation and OXPHOS, respectively, and ranked 40th and 23rd among 5,242 externally benchmarked RNA-adjusted protein states. Associations persisted after copy-number, clinical, tumor-purity, and background-proteome adjustment. Highest-ranked human TUFM_PT proteomic partners were enriched in an independent CRISPR codependency network, including after the exclusion of prespecified mitochondrial genes, demonstrating cross-modal convergence at the network tail. Longitudinal osimertinib data provided complementary temporal context: early drug tolerance suppressed mitochondrial translation and OXPHOS transcripts, followed by later recovery without universal TUFM mRNA recovery. Together, these findings identify TUFM_PT as a reproducible, network-embedded proteomic readout of mitochondrial organization beyond TUFM RNA, while the longitudinal transcriptomes define the treatment-stage context rather than treatment-linked TUFM protein dynamics.

title: Dual Antifibrotic Modulation via CTGF Silencing and Peptide Amphiphile Nanofibers for Topical Treatment of Skin Fibrosis.
abstract: Skin fibrosis is driven in part by transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling and the matricellular protein connective tissue growth factor (CTGF). Elevated CTGF expression is a hallmark of fibrotic skin lesions and contributes to pathological extracellular matrix remodeling. In this project, an antisense oligonucleotide (AON) delivery system was developed for the treatment of skin fibrosis. In this respect, two antifibrotic agents, i) AON against CTGF and ii) antifibrotic polypeptide amphiphile, were self-assembled into nanofibers to enhance antifibrotic efficacy. The nanofibers were encapsulated in chitosan nanoparticles (CNPs) for protection and sustained release. Loaded CNPs were characterized by morphology, size, endosomal escape, and skin penetration using a transwell-based 3D skin model. The nanoparticles exhibited an average size of 220 nm. The encapsulation efficiency of CNPs was 52%, providing sustained nanofiber release over 7 days. With the use of nanoparticles, clear reduction trends were observed in CTGF, α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA), and collagen expression. CNPs penetrated the skin model gradually, revealing no cytotoxicity to skin cells. Overall, these results reveal the potential of the designed nanofibers as a therapeutic agent and the CNPs as the carrier of the nanofibers. The developed delivery system can be used as an alternative approach for the treatment of lesions in fibrotic skin.

title: GCLC Deficiency Enhances Cellular Uptake of BNCT Agents via Oxidative Stress-Induced Macropinocytosis.
abstract: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a promising targeted radiotherapy for osteosarcoma, offering selective tumor cytotoxicity and localized energy deposition, but its efficacy is limited by heterogeneous intratumoral boron distribution. Using a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in U2OS osteosarcoma cells, we identified genetic regulators of boron uptake. GCLC deficiency markedly enhanced internalization of boron-containing agents. Mechanistically, GCLC loss depleted glutathione, triggered oxidative stress, and potentiated macropinocytosis, thereby boosting boron compound uptake. This effect was preferentially observed in tumor cells, as GCLC deficiency profoundly enhanced the uptake of boron delivery agents in tumor cells (such as U2OS and MDA-MB-231), far exceeding its impact on normal osteoblasts (HOB-SV40). In U2OS xenografts, GCLC silencing significantly enhanced preferential boron accumulation in tumors without altering normal tissue biodistribution. Our findings nominate GCLC as a druggable target to overcome boron delivery barriers in BNCT, providing a translatable strategy to improve efficacy for osteosarcoma, especially refractory cases.

title: Nanotechnology-Driven Precision Diagnostics and Therapeutics for Preeclampsia.
abstract: Preeclampsia originates in placental dysfunction yet it is detected only after maternal hypertension and proteinuria or other organ damage emerge, by which point disease-modifying interventions are not available, and delivery of the baby and placenta remains the only cure. Nanotechnology offers a route to reduce this diagnostic-therapeutic latency. Nanostructured biosensors and liquid biopsy platforms detect placental proteins, cell-free RNA/DNA, and extracellular vesicles at femtomolar concentrations and in a multiplex manner, enabling earlier risk stratification when integrated with machine-learning models. In parallel, placenta-targeted lipid-, peptide-, polymeric-, dendrimeric-, and small extracellular vesicle-based nanocarriers deliver angiogenic mRNA, antiangiogenic siRNA, antioxidants, and immunomodulators selectively to the trophoblast cells while limiting fetal exposure. Placenta-on-a-chip platforms and ex vivo placental perfusion models provide human-relevant test beds for these systems. We critically appraise these advances, examine the safety-by-design, manufacturing bottlenecks, and regulatory constraints unique to obstetric nanomedicine, and outline the convergence of theranostics and digital health that could move preeclampsia care from reactive symptom management toward proactive, placenta-targeted monitoring and therapy.

title: An Easy Oligonucleotide Platform for Rapid, Post-Isolation EV Modification: Dual-Function Uptake Control and Enhanced Targeting.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold immense therapeutic potential, yet their clinical translation is hindered by nonspecific cellular uptake and the complexity and cost of surface engineering. Here, we present the EZON (Easy OligoNucleotide) EV modification platform, a cost-effective, post-isolation modification system that addresses both limitations simultaneously. The EZON platform employs unmodified DNA aptamers that bind directly to tetraspanin proteins on EV surfaces, eliminating the need for cholesterol conjugation, covalent chemistry, or genetic engineering of producer cells. EVs are thus easily and rapidly functionalized in a single incubation step at substantially reduced oligonucleotide cost. The EZON platform enables dual functionality: (1) the oligonucleotide anchor (ONA) sequence inhibits nonspecific cellular uptake, while (2) the display strand enables targeted delivery through ligand-mediated internalization. We demonstrate that our optimized ONA construct efficiently functionalizes EVs from multiple mammalian cell types. Cancer cells selectively internalized EZON-modified EVs functionalized with AS1411, an aptamer that targets nucleolin, whereas off-target internalization was suppressed. The platform's versatility extends to protein display via histidine-tag aptamers and therapeutic cargo delivery, as demonstrated by targeted doxorubicin delivery to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells. This rapid, modular approach transforms unmodified EVs into precision delivery vehicles within hours, offering a scalable solution for targeted therapeutics.

title: Advances in Odontogenic Regeneration: From Fundamental Research to Clinical Application.
abstract: Dentin is the primary mineralized tissue of the tooth, essential for pulp protection and enamel support. Its regenerative capacity is critical for dental health. This review summarizes recent progress in odontogenic regeneration, covering fundamental biological mechanisms and translational applications. A literature search of peer-reviewed studies on odontogenic regeneration, dental tissue engineering, and biomaterial-based strategies was conducted. Key advances include signaling pathway-guided stem cell differentiation into functional odontoblasts, which promotes reparative dentin matrix formation, and biomaterial innovations that provide optimized cellular microenvironments. Emerging clinical strategies, including 3D printing, growth factor delivery systems, and gene-editing approaches, are also discussed. Despite substantial progress, challenges remain in the precise control of stem cell fate specification, long-term biocompatibility of biomaterials, and high clinical costs. Future interdisciplinary integration holds promise for overcoming these hurdles, advancing personalized therapies, and expanding dental restoration and regenerative medicine. The evolving strategies offer meaningful potential for dentin-pulp complex regeneration, improved pulp preservation, personalized scaffold fabrication via 3D printing, and the eventual development of cost-effective, biocompatible clinical therapies.

title: High-Throughput Screening of a Lipid Nanoparticle (LNP) Library Identifies Lead Formulations for CRISPR-Cas9 Ribonucleoprotein Delivery and Gene Editing.
abstract: Delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) using synthetic materials can bypass the host translational machinery and limit the duration of genomic exposure, minimizing the risk of off-target mutations. Despite their advantages, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platforms for CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery that achieve highly efficient editing at low doses remain limited. In the present study, we developed a library of ionizable lipids (ILs) and corresponding LNPs to enhance the delivery and editing efficiencies of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP complexes. Following comprehensive in vitro screening and formulation optimization, an optimal LNP candidate containing the C12A9 IL (denoted as LNPC12A9) was identified that achieved ∼90% EGFP disruption in HEK293T-EGFP cells at an RNP concentration of 30 nM and ∼60% at 15 nM. The editing performance was consistently observed at an RNP concentration of 15 nM when editing the Gcgr and HPRT1 genes across multiple hepatic cell lines. Moreover, coencapsulation of RNP and a single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) template for homology-directed repair (HDR) within LNPC12A9 induced an HDR rate of 37.8%. Systemic administration of LNPC12A9 into C57BL/6J mice led to liver tropism and a total hepatic Pcsk9 gene disruption rate of 1.39%. In conclusion, this study provides insights into the construction of an LNP platform to improve the delivery efficiency of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP, thereby facilitating the development of LNPs for safe, precise, and tissue-specific Cas9 RNP-based genome editing therapies.

title: Sequentially Self-Assembled Supramolecular Nanocomplexes Enable Systemic Cas9 RNP Delivery and In Vivo Tumor Genome Editing.
abstract: In vivo genome editing utilizing Cas9/sgRNA ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) holds substantial therapeutic promise, yet rapid bloodstream clearance and degradation of RNPs have hindered its accumulation within the target site and effective gene editing. Herein, we report a supramolecular ternary complex platform where RNPs are co-assembled with tannic acid (TA) and phenylboronic acid (PBA)-conjugated polymers through sequential self-assembly. This ∼30 nm core-shell structure protects RNPs from enzymatic degradation and dissociates selectively at endosomal pH. Upon intravenous administration in subcutaneous tumor-bearing mice, the ternary complex exhibits prolonged blood circulation and preferential tumor accumulation, achieving 37.2% gene editing at tumor sites compared with only 1.5% for free RNPs. The platform successfully disrupts PLK1 in subcutaneous tumors, accompanied by significant tumor growth suppression. This is further applied to a KRASG13D-mutant tumor model, in which treatment delayed tumor growth. By integrating sequential supramolecular self-assembly with stimuli-responsive cargo release, this strategy presents a promising approach for systemic RNP delivery and tumor genome editing.

title: Pooled Screening of Cancer Cell Lines Identifies Vulnerability to Polyunsaturated Fatty-Acid-Induced Ferroptosis.
abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are essential nutrients supporting numerous cellular processes in normal and neoplastic cells, yet PUFA-containing phospholipids predispose cells to ferroptosis. How cancer cells from various lineages or genetic backgrounds proliferate in the presence of PUFA remains poorly understood. Here, by systematically profiling various fatty acids using a barcoded and pooled cancer cell line library, we show that a subset of cell lines is sensitive to PUFA treatment at concentrations comparable to physiological levels. We demonstrate that PUFA treatment alone is sufficient to induce ferroptosis in these cell lines that are also vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition. By correlating patterns of PUFA sensitivity with cancer cell line features including basal mRNA transcript levels, we show that PUFA sensitivity is positively associated with fatty acid binding protein 1 (FABP1) expression. Additionally, by profiling a diverse collection of fatty acids and analogs, we find that ferroptosis in cancer cells can be effectively induced by conjugated linolenic acids, in addition to PUFAs containing 1,4-pentadiene groups. Genome-wide CRISPR modifier screens in the PUFA-sensitive ES2 cells reveal a pro-ferroptosis pathway defined by enzymes that convert PUFAs to membrane-associated phospholipids, and an anti-ferroptosis pathway that segregates PUFAs by delivering them to lipid droplets. Together, we present the first comprehensive data set of PUFA-induced ferroptosis sensitivity in a collection of 554 cell lines from 19 primary lineages and suggest a potential therapeutic avenue to induce tumor cell ferroptosis using dietary metabolites.

title: In Vivo Blood Kinetics and Transcript Integrity of Three mRNA-Lipid Nanoparticle Vaccines in Humans.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines are detectable in human blood after vaccination, but platform-specific differences in systemic persistence and transcript integrity remain poorly defined. We analyzed serial blood samples from 73 participants receiving Moderna mRNA-1273 (three formulations), Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2, or an investigational receptor-binding domain (RBD) mRNA vaccine (three different doses). Using droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) assays, we quantified total and long-range linked ("intact") vaccine mRNA, and we measured vaccine-specific ionizable lipids by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Across platforms, mRNA decay was fastest for mRNA-1273, intermediate for BNT162b2, and slowest for the RBD vaccine, with ionizable lipid decay following the same rank order. Notably, intact spike mRNA declined 2-fold faster after mRNA-1273 than BNT162b2 vaccination. Kinetics modeling revealed platform-dependent coupling of mRNA and lipid kinetics: intact mRNA tracked closely with SM-102 for mRNA-1273, whereas ALC-0315 persisted longer than intact mRNA for BNT162b2. A ten-fragment linkage ddPCR panel spanning the spike transcript showed lower linkage toward 3'-proximal regions that mirrored the administered mRNA-1273 formulation. Together, these data provide a quantitative framework for benchmarking mRNA-LNP platform kinetics and transcript integrity in humans.

title: Poly(acrylamido) PEG-Alternative Lipids Rescue mRNA Efficacy during Repeated Dosing and Enhance Immune Cell Delivery.
abstract: Following the successes of the messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against COVID-19, mRNA-LNPs are being explored for varied multidose applications including cancer immunotherapies and protein replacement therapies. LNPs rely on poly(ethylene glycol)-lipid (PEG-lipid) coatings for stability, but increasing anti-PEG antibody prevalence threatens repeat-dose efficacy and increases pseudoallergic risk, creating an urgent need for alternatives. Here, we introduce poly(acrylamido) lipids (PAM-lipids), a family of polymer lipids that effectively replace PEG-lipids in mRNA-LNP formulations. Systematic variation of monomer chemistry, molar mass, and end group reveals critical structure-activity relationships determining LNP size, polydispersity, and transfection efficiency. Varying PAM monomer chemistry allows minimization of antipolymer antibody cross-reactivity, with multiple PAM-lipids demonstrating no anti-PEG antibody binding. Several PAM-LNPs exhibit superior mRNA transfection efficacy to PEGylated clinical benchmarks in vitro and in vivo across multiple cell types, organs, routes of administration, and mRNA cargos. In particular, lead PAM-LNPs enhance mRNA delivery to dendritic cells (up to 120-fold in vitro and 3-fold in vivo) and macrophages (4-fold in vivo), with 2.5-fold superior lymph node expression, driven in part by increased cellular association and lymphoid targeting. Crucially, PAM-LNPs evade circulating anti-PEG antibodies to rescue lost mRNA efficacy after repeated dosing, resulting in 300% mRNA expression relative to that of PEG-LNPs. These findings demonstrate PAM-lipids as a chemically varied, immunologically compatible family of PEG alternatives for mRNA-LNP therapeutics.

title: Nano Delivery Systems for In Vivo CRISPR/Cas-Based Gene Therapy: From Vectors to Clinical Outcomes.
abstract: As a powerful gene-editing tool, the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas) system features simple construction, precise targeting, and higher editing efficiency, bringing prospects of radical cures for numerous critical illnesses at the genomic level. To date, ex vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies represented by Casgevy have achieved significant clinical advances. Nevertheless, cumbersome operational workflows and prohibitive treatment costs severely hinder their widespread clinical accessibility. In contrast, in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies stand out with convenient administration procedures and reduced overall costs, endowing them with enormous translational potential. Although it holds great promise, the clinical translation of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies remains hampered by a number of factors. Among those multiple obstacles restricting the clinical translation of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies, delivery systems constitute the core bottleneck dominating in vivo editing efficiency and therapeutic potency. Centered on delivery platforms for in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies, this review systematically summarizes prevailing in vivo CRISPR/Cas nano delivery systems, recapitulates relevant preclinical and clinical outcomes, discusses translational hurdles, and prospects the evolution of next-generation delivery systems, aiming to facilitate further development of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies.

title: Nanoimaging, Spectroscopy, and Biosensor Assays for Alternatively Spliced RNA Isoforms in Disease Diagnostics.
abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) generates distinct mRNA isoforms, and frequently distinct proteins, from single genes; its dysregulation is established in cancer, neurodegeneration, and immune disease. Sequencing now nominates candidate splice events at scale, but a nominated event does not become a usable measurement until an isoform-discriminating sequence has been converted into a physical signal. Existing AS reviews concentrate on sequencing workflows, computational event calling, or disease catalogs; the assay-engineering step that follows target nomination remains comparatively underserved, and it is where most translational failures occur. This review addresses that gap. We group postsequencing detection into five classes defined by the physical origin of the signal: (i) fixed-tissue in situ localization, (ii) live-cell RNA imaging, (iii) plasmonic and spectroscopic readouts, (iv) label-free nanophotonic biosensing combined with site-specific RNA processing, and (v) protein-level proteogenomic confirmation. These classes are compared on target definition, reported analytical performance, multiplexing, matrix compatibility, perturbation risk, and clinical readiness. The reported performance spans single-copy imaging of splice variants in living cells to label-free detection at 580 fM in under 30 min without cDNA synthesis or PCR. Three conclusions follow. First, assay selection should be governed by the class of claim being made rather than by platform novelty. Second, analytical sensitivity measured on synthetic targets systematically overstates readiness in clinical matrices; therefore, matrix-matched validation is not optional. Third, cross-laboratory comparison is currently obstructed by inconsistent reporting, which we address by proposing a minimum performance-reporting set and explicit platform-selection criteria. We close with emerging directions, including CRISPR-based isoform detection, biosensor integration with nanopore sequencing, AI-assisted probe design, and digital and microfluidic formats.

title: Repurposing Type III CRISPR-Cas as Modular Cellular RNA Biosensors.
abstract: Over the past decade, CRISPR-Cas based biosensors have emerged as sensitive, specific and programmable platforms for nucleic acid detection, with applications ranging from diagnostic tools, environmental monitoring and various applications in fundamental research. The vast majority of these biosensors are currently limited to in vitro applications, highlighting the need for cellular platforms. Here, we provide a perspective on the potential of type III CRISPR-Cas systems as a platform for real-time RNA biosensing in living cells. We discuss the unique properties that distinguish type III from other CRISPR-Cas types, including their intrinsic cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signal amplification cascade, PAM-free RNA targeting and the extensive biochemical diversity of their downstream CARF and SAVED effector proteins. We outline the fundamental design principles of a genetically encoded type III cellular biosensor, comprising a programmable guide RNA, a multi-subunit sensing complex and a cOA-sensing effector protein capable of generating optical or electrochemical readout signals. A remaining challenge for type III cellular biosensors is the inherent cytotoxicity of canonical cOA-activated effectors. We propose several strategies to re-engineer these outputs towards non-cytotoxic reporter systems. While cellular biosensors present a natural route toward in vivo sensing, they face many challenges beyond the choice of the output signal and hardware strategy. We conclude that type III CRISPR-Cas is a promising platform for programmable real-time RNA sensing in living cells, utilizing its diverse modular effector outputs, representing a significant expansion of the CRISPR biosensor toolkit, while emphasizing appropriate deployment scenarios that enables full potential of these biosensors.

title: Probing the Conformational Dynamics of VeCas9 Using High-Resolution Single-Molecule Junctions.
abstract: Gene editing enables precise genetic modifications, revolutionizing disease treatment, crop improvement, and biotechnological innovation. VeCas9, a recently identified CRISPR endonuclease from the Veillonella genus, exhibits a broader protospacer adjacent motif recognition range in comparison with the widely used SpCas9 nuclease. However, its working mechanism and potential applications in gene editing still need to be fully characterized. In this work, by integrating VeCas9 into a graphene-molecule-graphene single-molecule junction platform, we carried out label-free, in situ mechanistic studies of VeCas9 function at the single-molecule level with high temporal resolution. Using this setup, we monitored the dynamic interactions between VeCas9, single-guide RNA, and double-stranded DNA in real time, in both stable and transient binding modes. Through temperature-dependent measurements, we determined the kinetic parameters of key steps in the interaction process. Moreover, a series of double-stranded DNA substrates was employed to examine how various sequence mismatches affect the VeCas9 activity, revealing that its sensitivity depends on the position of the mismatch. More importantly, we directly observed VeCas9-mediated R-loop formation and quantified the time scale of single-base expansion events. These single-molecule observations provide mechanistic insights into the Cas9 function and demonstrate the strong potential of high temporal-resolution single-molecule techniques for studying dynamic biological processes.

title: Cancer cell-specific FOXP3 licenses MMP19-dependent matrix remodeling and metastatic dissemination in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a dense desmoplastic stroma and early metastatic dissemination, both of which contribute to its poor prognosis. While forkhead box protein 3 (FOXP3) is best known as a lineage-defining transcription factor in regulatory T cells (Tregs), its aberrant expression in cancer cell-specific FOXP3 (c-FOXP3) may also support tumor-cell-intrinsic progression. Our findings suggest that high c-FOXP3 expression is closely linked to aggressive disease behavior and metastatic progression in PDAC. c-FOXP3 enhanced migration, invasion within three-dimensional collagen-rich matrices, and dissemination in orthotopic models. Integrated transcriptomic analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and wild-type versus binding-site-mutant promoter assays identified matrix metalloproteinase 19 (MMP19) as a direct transcriptional target of c-FOXP3. MMP19 silencing significantly attenuated c-FOXP3-driven migration, matrix invasion, and metastasis. Single-cell sequencing further showed that MMP19 is abundant in cancer-associated fibroblasts but also defines a distinct epithelial pool that is reduced after epithelial Foxp3 deletion. Pharmacological profiling did not identify a validated MMP19-selective inhibitor, whereas the FOXP3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide AZD8701 reduced FOXP3 together with MMP19 mRNA and was accompanied by lower PDAC-cell migration and invasion in vitro. Together, these findings extend the known functions of FOXP3 beyond its classical role in immune tolerance and define a tumor-cell-intrinsic c-FOXP3-MMP19 program that supports matrix-invasive behavior in PDAC and provide preliminary evidence that c-FOXP3 is pharmacologically accessible.

title: Arrhythmic events and genetic variants as drivers for Takotsubo Syndrome: a patient-specific atrial stem-cell model.
abstract: Takotsubo Syndrome (TTS) is an acute, potentially life-threatening condition often complicated by ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmias. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is common in TTS patients and associated with increased mortality. However, the arrhythmic mechanisms, genetic variability underlying TTS, and personalised therapy remain unclear. We generated induced pluripotent stem cell-derived atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from TTS patients and provoked TTS-like events by isoprenaline (Iso) stimulation. Compared with controls, atrial TTS iPSC-CMs exhibited enhanced diastolic sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca²⁺ leak and increased arrhythmogenic potential following Iso exposure. Iso-induced stress further increased systolic Ca²⁺ transient amplitude and reduced phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) activity in TTS iPSC-CMs. Under baseline conditions, atrial TTS iPSC-CMs demonstrated unchanged Ca2+ transient amplitude, reduced diastolic Ca2+, elevated SERCA2 activity with faster Ca²⁺ decay compared to controls, which could be explained by increased phosphorylation of PKA-specific phospholamban S16. In contrast, ventricular TTS-iPSC-CM showed increased L-Type Ca2+ current density, but reduced Ca2+ transient amplitude with increased resting Ca2+ leak and reduced PDE4 activity post-Iso-exposure. In atrial TTS iPSC-CMs, the PDE4 activator MR-L2 restored PDE4 activity, normalised several defects in Ca²⁺ handling and prevented arrhythmias more efficiently than the β-blocker metoprolol. Genetic analyses identified variants in the Ca²⁺ handling genes AHNAK and CASQ2 in TTS. Using CRISPR/Cas9, we generated isogenic rescue and mutation-insertion lines, confirming a causal role of p.P5390T in catecholamine-induced arrhythmogenic phenotypes in atrial TTS iPSC-CMs. Our findings support a mechanistic link between genetic predisposition to an excessive catecholaminergic stress response, dysregulated PDE/cAMP signalling, and atrial arrhythmogenesis in TTS-CMs, identifying PDE4 as a potential therapeutic target in this critical condition.

title: DCST1 drives cisplatin resistance via non-canonical ubiquitination and stabilization of NFAT5 to suppress PANoptosis in bladder cancer.
abstract: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy constitutes the cornerstone of first-line treatment for muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (BCa); however, the frequent emergence of chemoresistance presents a formidable clinical obstacle. In the present study, by combining a systematic CRISPR-Cas9 E3 ligase library screen with drug sensitivity data from the GDSC database, DCST1 (DC-STAMP Domain Containing 1) was identified as a pivotal driver of cisplatin resistance. DCST1 expression was found to be markedly upregulated in chemoresistant BCa tissues, and its elevated expression served as an independent predictor of poor patient prognosis. Functionally, DCST1 deficiency sensitizes BCa cells to cisplatin in vitro and in vivo by triggering PANoptosis (simultaneous apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis). Mechanistically, DCST1 functions as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase to catalyze the K11/K27-linked polyubiquitination of NFAT5 at residue K450. This non-canonical ubiquitination stabilizes NFAT5 by preventing its lysosomal degradation and promotes its nuclear accumulation. Nuclear NFAT5 then transcriptionally activates SOD2, orchestrating an anti-PANoptotic program that ensures BCa cell survival under chemotherapeutic stress. Furthermore, through molecular docking and CETSA validation, digoxin was identified as a potent pharmacological inhibitor of NFAT5 that overcomes DCST1-mediated chemoresistance and synergistically restores cisplatin sensitivity. Collectively, these findings unveil a previously unrecognized ubiquitination-dependent mechanism of chemoresistance and establish the DCST1-NFAT5 signaling axis as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming drug resistance in BCa.

title: A 5' tRNA-derived fragment tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal ischemia/reperfusion injury via ADAR1/autophagy/ROS/necroptosis signaling axis.
abstract: Transfer RNA-derived small RNAs (tDRs) are a class of functional small non-coding RNAs, many of which are induced by stress conditions and have been implicated in tissue injury and disease pathogenesis. However, their role in intestinal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains unclear. Using tDR sequencing, we identified that tDR-Glu-TTC was significantly upregulated in intestinal tissues, plasma, epithelial cells, and human clinical samples; and its levels positively correlated with the severity of intestinal injury. Functionally, tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal mucosal damage by activating TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis in intestinal epithelial cells. Mechanistically, tDR-Glu-TTC directly binds to and suppresses the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR1, impairing adenosine-to-inosine editing of autophagy-related transcripts (ATG18 and Lamp2). This inhibits autophagy, leading to the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, and the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS). The elevated ROS subsequently promotes TNF-α secretion, triggering TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis. Furthermore, increased ROS downregulates TRMT6/61A-dependent m¹A methylation of tRNA-Glu-TTC, increasing tDR-Glu-TTC biogenesis and forming a pathogenic positive feedback loop. Thus, therapeutic dual-target intervention using N-acetylcysteine combined with tDR-Glu-TTC-antagomir synergistically mitigated I/R-induced intestinal injury in vivo. In summary, our study unveiled a previously unrecognized mechanism by which tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal I/R injury via the ADAR1/autophagy/ROS/necroptosis signaling axis, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for combating intestinal I/R injury.

title: Deciphering the regulatory code of RNA inosine through enzymatic precision mapping and an explainable deep learning model.
abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is one of the most abundant RNA modifications and is involved in multiple critical biological processes; however, the precise localization of inosine and the mechanisms governing their selective editing remain incompletely understood. Integrating high-accuracy detection technologies with deep learning models can accelerate our understanding of the selective positioning and functional implications of A-to-I editing. To address these challenges, this study simultaneously developed RNA inosine sequencing by endonuclease V (EndoV) and XRN-1 (REX-seq), a highly sensitive and accurate detection method for inosine sites, and Inosine Deep Residual Enhanced Attention Model (InoDREAM), a predictive deep learning framework. REX-seq combines EndoV cleavage specificity with XRN-1 exonuclease activity to enable comprehensive A-to-I editome profiling while maintaining accurate gene expression quantification. Using this method, we identified 590,249 high-confidence inosine sites in HEK293T cells, including 84,645 novel sites. Leveraging the high-confidence A-to-I editing sites identified by REX-seq, we developed InoDREAM, which successfully predicted multiple regulatory proteins that exhibit specific binding affinity to A-to-I edited transcripts while simultaneously identifying disease-associated mutation sites and relevant cis-regulatory elements that are functionally linked to RNA editing events. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights into both the molecular regulation of RNA editing and its pathophysiological implications in disease development.

title: CRISPRa screen unveils noncanonical NF-κB to boost the antitumor activity of TCR-based CAR-T cells.
abstract: Engineering autologous T cells for adoptive therapies has revolutionized cancer treatment, yet limited persistence remains a major barrier to robust clinical responses and durable disease control. Although costimulation with 4-1BB markedly improves CAR-T-cell persistence, no comparably effective approach has been identified to enhance persistence in T-cell therapies that rely on native TCR signaling, including conventional TCR-T cells and synthetic T-cell receptor and antigen receptor (STAR) T cells. To identify intrinsic persistence regulators in a TCR-based context, we performed an in vivo CRISPR activation screen in STAR-T cells and identified the noncanonical NF-κB axis, with RELB as the top hit. Direct RELB overexpression, however, exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, motivating a translational alternative: overexpression of p52, the ncNF-κB transcription partner of RELB. Under prolonged antigen exposure, p52 overexpression sustained proliferation, preserved effector functions, and increased the intratumoral trafficking potential, particularly in CD8⁺ T cells, thereby yielding superior tumor control. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling revealed coordinated upregulation of cell cycle programs and chemokine receptors, along with downregulation of apoptosis and exhaustion-associated modules. Moreover, p52 overexpression restored RELB nuclear translocation in the context of PD-1/PD-L1 engagement, indicating partial resistance to checkpoint-mediated suppression and sustained ncNF-κB activity in PD-L1hi immunosuppressive environments. Collectively, our findings identify p52 as an antigen-dependent enhancer of ncNF-κB, conferring durable persistence and checkpoint resilience on TCR-based T cells and providing a feasible strategy to improve therapeutic effects in solid tumors.

title: Genotoxic safety and long-term engraftment dynamics of efficient translational CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-haemoglobinopathies from bench to clinical trials.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing targeting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer has transformed therapeutic approaches for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (β-thal) and sickle cell disease (SCD). Even though clinical efficacy is well demonstrated, translating these therapies to global patient populations requires a strong evidence-based framework to address critical concerns regarding long-term genotoxic safety and long-lasting engraftment dynamics.
METHODS: Following the 2020 PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review of 21 key clinical and preclinical studies (published during 2014-2026) to evaluate CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in β-thal and SCD. The inclusion criteria focused on studies reporting foetal haemoglobin (HbF) induction, transfusion independence (TI) and safety outcomes.
RESULTS: Clinical data indicate high efficacy, with exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) achieving TI in 91% of β-thal patients and a vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)-free status in 97% of SCD patients. Safety profiling confirmed that severe adverse events, including febrile neutropenia and stomatitis, are primarily associated with busulfan-based myeloablation rather than gene editing. Gene-editing safety and conditioning toxicity are interlinked because conditioning is part of the process, and edited clones might interact with stress pathways during long-term repopulation. Preclinical benchmarks substantiate molecular reliability, with negligible off-target activity reported in most validated platforms. However, rare instances of complex structural rearrangements and intergenic off-target indels highlight the necessity for in-depth, unbiased long-term genomic surveillance.
CONCLUSION: CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-thal and SCD treatment constitute a treatment option within current clinical frameworks. These therapies need continuous surveillance. Rather than establishing a perfect plan, this systematic review highlights that while current platforms are thought to have short-term molecular precision, the use of Multilayer Safety Risks Screening and Surveillance for pretransplant conditioning is critical. This approach helps address long-term genotoxic concerns and ensures the safety and scalability of gene-editing therapies for global β-thal and SCD patient care.
