title: The evolving landscape of fungal keratitis: from emerging pathogens to precision diagnostics and novel therapeutics.
abstract: Fungal keratitis (FK) remains a major cause of vision-threatening corneal infection, especially in tropical and subtropical regions, with an expanding epidemiological spectrum driven by environmental, climatic, occupational and host-related factors. Fusarium and Aspergillus were the most common pathogens reported. Greater etiological diversity is reflected by increasing recognition of dematiaceous fungi, uncommon molds, and cryptic species. The literature search was performed by searching bibliographic databases (PubMed and Google Scholar), covering publications from January 2000 to August 2026. Additional relevant studies were identified by screening the reference lists of key publications. This review provides an overview of the current state of FK including changing epidemiology, established diagnostic approaches, emerging technologies, and evolving therapeutic approaches. Conventional microscopy and culture remain central to diagnosis, with molecular methods, sequencing, MALDI-TOF and noninvasive imaging offering advantages in sensitivity, speed and species-level identification. Novel diagnostic methods such as CRISPR-based tests, genome sequencing, artificial intelligence, biosensors and point-of-care diagnostics may provide rapid and accessible precision diagnosis. Therapeutic challenges include poor corneal drug penetration, antifungal resistance and prolonged treatment. Hence, the exploration of new antifungals, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, photoactivated therapies and antimicrobial peptides. These advances support a transition to integrated, rapid and precision-based management of FK collectively.

title: Natural and engineered bacteriophages against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: current landscape and clinical translation.
abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

title: Association of Xeroderma Pigmentosum group F (XPF) with epigenetic regulation of T helper cell differentiation in coronary artery disease-associated prostate cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coronary artery disease (CAD) and prostate cancer share common genetic and epigenetic risk factors. Xeroderma Pigmentosum group F (XPF), a DNA repair endonuclease, has been implicated in genomic stability and epigenetic regulation. This study investigated the association between XPF expression and epigenetic changes during T helper (TH) cell differentiation in CAD-associated prostate cancer (CAD-PC).
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: CD4+ T cells isolated from healthy controls and CAD-PC patients were subjected to CRISPR/Cas9-mediated XPF knockout or overexpression. TH cell differentiation, chromatin enrichment, global m6A RNA methylation, DNA methylation, R-loop formation, and tumor cell cytotoxicity were evaluated using molecular and functional assays.
RESULTS: XPF overexpression was associated with increased TH1 differentiation and elevated expression of XPF and TP53, whereas TH2, TH17, and Treg-associated markers were reduced. Increased enrichment of XPF and H3K4me3, together with reduced HDAC1, γH2A.X, and H3K27me3 enrichment, was observed at the TBX21 and IFNG loci. XPF overexpression was also associated with increased global m6A RNA methylation, reduced DNA methylation at TH1-associated loci, decreased R-loop accumulation, and enhanced tumor cell cytotoxicity in vitro.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that XPF expression is associated with a TH1-skewed epigenetic and immune profile in CAD-PC. However, the absence of disease-specific comparison groups and in vivo validation limits mechanistic interpretation, and further studies are required to establish causality. The present findings demonstrate an association between XPF and the observed TH1-associated epigenetic changes.

title: Synthetic mRNA engineering beyond prophylactic infectious disease vaccines: epigenomic and molecular reprogramming of diseased cells.
abstract: The clinical validation of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines in 2020-2021 accelerated the development of synthetic messenger RNA as a precision therapeutic platform beyond infectious disease prevention. Unlike gene therapy approaches that permanently modify genomic DNA, synthetic mRNA enables transient protein expression through programmable molecular engineering. This narrative review examines therapeutic applications of engineered mRNA, emphasizing its epigenomic potential. It discusses key engineering strategies, including nucleoside modifications, codon optimization, untranslated region engineering, cap chemistry, and advances in lipid nanoparticle and alternative delivery systems. Six therapeutic domains are explored: cancer immunotherapy, cardiac regeneration, monogenic diseases, genome and epigenome editing, autoimmune disease, and somatic cell reprogramming. Particular attention is given to mRNA-mediated replacement of chromatin regulators, dCas9-based epigenome editing, epigenetically derived tumor antigens, and transcription-factor-driven cellular reprogramming. The review distinguishes chemical nucleoside modifications from endogenous epitranscriptomic regulation and examines the differences between transient protein expression, heritable but reversible chromatin changes, and permanent genomic modifications. Clinical evidence, discontinued programs, and preclinical developments are critically evaluated. Despite promising advances, major challenges remain regarding delivery specificity, durability, safety, and clinical translation. Overall, synthetic mRNA represents an emerging platform for molecular and epigenetic therapeutic reprogramming beyond vaccination.

title: Macrophage-directed immunotherapy in Inflammatory bowel disease: advances in reprogramming intestinal phagocytes.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder characterized by dysregulation of the intestinal immune system, in which functional abnormalities of phagocytes such as macrophages play a critical role in pathogenesis. Although conventional therapies such as anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) antibodies are widely used in clinical practice, they have limitations including low response rates and significant side effects, creating an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. In recent years, macrophage-directed immunotherapy has emerged as a cutting-edge approach for IBD treatment by reprogramming intestinal phagocytes to restore immune homeostasis. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on the M1/M2 polarization framework, this review integrates recent single-cell discoveries of novel macrophage subsets (e.g. SPP1+ and TREM2+ macrophages), systematically examines the crosstalk among signaling, epigenetic, and metabolic regulatory layers, and critically evaluates translational barriers from preclinical models to clinical application. By evaluating preclinical and clinical studies, we assess the potential and challenges of these strategies. Through in-depth analysis, this review aims to provide a theoretical basis for the development of more precise and effective immunotherapies for IBD and to point out future research directions. (Literature search: PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase; January 2000-December 2025.).

title: Mathematical modeling in mRNA therapeutics: towards a pathway to individualized treatment protocols.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics represent a transformative pharmacological paradigm in which the delivery vehicle, genetic payload, and expressed protein form a tightly coupled system. This multicomponent structure introduces nonlinear, multiscale dynamics that challenge traditional pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic frameworks, making quantitative modeling essential.
AREAS COVERED: This review provides a structured biological framework for mRNA-LNP therapeutics, detailing the key processes governing delivery, endosomal escape, mRNA stability, and translation, and highlighting their associated temporal and spatial scales, providing the key aspects to consider for modeling. Building on this foundation, we summarize mathematical modeling approaches, including pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK), and quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models, used to represent these mechanisms. The literature was surveyed to identify representative preclinical and translational studies, focusing on model structure, assumptions, and their use in human projection and dose optimization.
EXPERT OPINION: Mathematical models are increasingly critical to interpret and predict mRNA therapeutic behavior, yet challenges remain in parameter identifiability, data availability, and model standardization. Future advances will depend on biologically grounded modeling frameworks, improved integration of mechanistic insight with quantitative approaches, and tighter coupling between experimental design and model development. These developments will support more efficient translation and enable precision medicine applications.

title: RIG-I is essential for radiation-induced IFN-β production and PD-L1/PD-L2 upregulation in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells.
abstract: The RIG-I pathway, a key component of the innate immune system that classically detects cytosolic viral RNA, has also been implicated in regulating tumor cell viability, radiosensitivity, and patient survival across multiple cancer types. However, these effects appear to be context-dependent and partly contradictory. Whether radiotherapy modulates tumor-intrinsic RIG-I signaling in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) depending on HPV status, and whether such modulation is associated with changes in the tumor immune phenotype, remains unknown. Four human HNSCC cell lines (two HPV-negative and two HPV-positive), along with siRNA-mediated RIG-I knockdown and a CRISPR/Cas9-generated RIG-I knockout derivative, were treated with radiotherapy. Tumor cells were analyzed for their immune phenotype, including RIG-I expression via Western blot and flow cytometry, IFN-β secretion via ELISA, and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression via flow cytometry. Radiotherapy, dose- and fraction-dependent, induced the upregulation of RIG-I expression and IFN-β secretion from HPV-negative HNSCC cells. The knockdown and knockout of the RIG-I-encoding gene DDX58 in the HPV-negative cell line HSC4 minimized both IFN-β secretion and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression. These effects could be replicated by pre-exposing HPV-negative cell lines to the RIG-I inhibitor RIG012 before irradiation. Interestingly, HPV-positive cells showed less radiotherapy-mediated modulation of RIG-I and of the tumor cell phenotype of immune-related surface markers and showed no significant reaction to the inhibitor treatment. The previously unrecognized RIG-I-IFN-β axis is a central regulator of RT-induced immune checkpoint modulation for HPV-negative HNSCC. These results provide new opportunities to reshape the immune response following RT in HNSCC.

title: Development of mRNA vaccines against herpes zoster.
abstract: Herpes zoster (HZ), caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), remains a substantial public health burden, particularly in aging populations, due to the risk of severe complications like postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). While existing vaccines (eg. Shingrix®) have advanced prevention efficiencies, they present notable limitations, such as high reactogenicity and complex manufacturing. mRNA vaccines represent a transformative alternative with rapid manufacturing, precise antigen design, and favorable safety. This review synthesizes the current landscape of mRNA vaccine development for HZ, focusing on the rational design of antigen constructs, innovations in lipid nanoparticle delivery systems, insights from preclinical immunogenicity studies, and the progress of leading candidates into clinical trials. In summary, this review highlights the potential of mRNA vaccines to address the limitations of current options, potentially offering a new paradigm for safer, highly efficacious, and scalable HZ prevention. Continued clinical validation is crucial to realize this potential and alleviate the global disease burden.

title: ADAR-mediated RNA editing of Influenza A virus genomes may be age-dependent and inversely correlates with viral load.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Seasonal influenza epidemics cause significant mortality, especially among the elderly. Influenza A virus triggers the host innate immune system through various mechanisms. Human enzymes belonging to the group of RNA-acting adenosine deaminases (ADARs) play a role in the innate antiviral immune response, partly by inducing mutations in viral RNA. The effect of this mechanismin influenza A virus infection remains unexplained in humans.
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess the clinical impact of ADAR-induced mutations on influenza A virus in hospitalised patients.
METHODS: Full-genome deep sequencing of Influenza A virus was performed on respiratory samples from 75 hospitalised, Influenza A(H3N2) virus infected patients, aged 41 to 95 years. ADAR-associated mutations in minor viral subpopulations were analysed in relation to demographic and clinical factors.
RESULTS: ADAR-associated mutations showed a significant inverse correlation with viral load (p < 0.0001) and age (p = 0.0051), especially in patients older than 75 years. The association between ADAR-associated mutations and viral load was independent of age, inflammation, and disease severity (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: We found an association between ADAR-induced mutations and viral load, which may indicate an antiviral function of ADAR on influenza A virus. The lower mutation rate and associated higher viral load in the elderly suggest an age-dependent reduced ADAR activity, which may contribute to increased disease severity.

title: PRIDA: Cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction based on biological language models and conditional domain-adversarial learning.
abstract:
MOTIVATION: The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein-RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein-RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance.
RESULTS: In this study, we propose PRIDA (Protein-RNA Interaction prediction based on Domain-Adversarial learning), a protein-RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening.
AVAILABILITY: The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub (https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA) and Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23644677).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Redirecting full-length FLT1 expression towards its soluble isoform by targeting alternative polyadenylation promotes postischaemic angiogenesis.
abstract:
AIMS: Vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs) and their endothelial tyrosine kinase receptors are crucial mediators of vasculogenesis and angiogenesis, with FLT1 (VEGFR1) acting as a decoy receptor for VEGFs. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) of Flt1 transcripts produces a truncated mRNA transcript encoding soluble (s) FLT1, which contains only the extracellular ligand-binding domain. The relative roles of full-length (fl) FLT1 and sFLT1 in angiogenesis are incompletely understood. Alternative polyadenylation is an important post-transcriptional mechanism of gene regulation that is increasingly recognized to affect the expression of many genes related to cardiovascular diseases. However, there are no in vivo models available to target APA and to examine the physiological roles of gene isoforms.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We here generated mice by introducing silent mutations into the Flt1 exon 13/intron 13 5' splice site through homology-directed repair with CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Embryonic development, postnatal retinal vascular development, and reparative angiogenesis were evaluated in models of hindlimb ischaemia and myocardial infarction, complemented by assessments of cardiac functional recovery and cell phenotypes through snRNAseq, as well as in vitro assays examining endothelial cell phenotype and function. The introduction of specific splice site mutations within Flt1 to activate APA led to a complete loss of flFLT1 and an increase in sFLT1 expression. Using this mouse model, we demonstrate that sFLT1 alone is sufficient for developmental vasculogenesis, whereas the specific loss of flFLT1 enhances reparative revascularization and angiogenesis and improves cardiac recovery after myocardial infarction.
CONCLUSION: Our findings show that APA can be effectively targeted to modulate FLT1 isoform expression in vivo. Our mouse model may help to understand diseases driven by an imbalance in FLT1 isoform expression. Given the widespread presence of APA signals, our approach could furthermore serve as a model for studying the function of other truncated gene isoforms.

title: Baseline characteristics of patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy in the CARDIO-TTRansform trial of eplontersen.
abstract:
AIMS: Eplontersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that suppresses hepatic production of circulating transthyretin (TTR) by targeting TTR mRNA. We present baseline data from an ongoing trial, CARDIO-TTRansform, evaluating eplontersen in patients with TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and compare findings across previous ATTR-CM trials.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We evaluated 1432 patients enrolled in CARDIO-TTRansform from March 2020 to July 2023 who received ≥1 dose of study intervention (eplontersen or placebo) and had ≥1 post-baseline measurement. Mean (standard deviation) age was 76.4 (7.1) years; 9.4% were female; 88.8% were White. A total of 211 (14.7%) patients had hereditary/variant ATTR-CM (ATTRv-CM); Val122Ile (p.Val142Ile) was the most common genotype (n = 130). Patients spanned New York Heart Association functional classes I (n = 192), II (n = 997), and III (n = 243); 62.6% were National Amyloidosis Centre disease stage 1. Median (interquartile range) N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide was 2025 (1296-3465) pg/ml; n = 51 measured >8500 pg/ml. Median (interquartile range) high-sensitivity troponin T was 50 (35-69) pg/ml and mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 55.7% (9.7%). At baseline, 57.2% were on TTR stabilizer; 18.4% were on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors.
CONCLUSION: The baseline characteristics of CARDIO-TTRansform were consistent with previous ATTR-CM trials; however, CARDIO-TTRansform evaluated patients with a wide range of disease severity and receiving the contemporary standard of care for ATTR-CM. Overall, blinded baseline data suggest that CARDIO-TTRansform provides a unique opportunity to determine the clinical benefits of eplontersen in a contemporary setting and in clinically relevant subgroups of patients with ATTR-CM.

title: Yeast-Based Platforms for Next-Generation Human Health Applications.
abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

title: Genetic principles enabling the creation of bacteria-based therapeutics.
abstract: Genetic engineering can transform bacteria (including Salmonella, Escherichia coli, Listeria, and Yersinia) from naturally occurring microbes into programmable therapeutics. Unlike passive platforms, engineered bacteria can localize to defined biological niches, sense environmental cues, regulate programmed activity in situ, interact with host tissues in novel ways, and persist for controlled periods. These properties make bacteria versatile medicines but require genetic control of precision, safety, stability, and activity under clinical conditions. Major design layers include strain or "chassis" selection, attenuation and biocontainment, control of therapeutic activity, targeting and persistence, and genotype-to-phenotype stability during manufacturing and in vivo use. These features also create liabilities, including off-target behavior, unstable expression, and evolutionary loss of function under selection. Progress depends on safe, clinically translatable chassis with integrated, bounded, and durable behaviors. This review examines the genetic design principles and liabilities of bacteria-based therapeutics, approaches used to produce clinical and near-clinical candidates, and the emergence of programmed bacteria delivering complete gene editing systems to therapeutically relevant cells.

title: IL-15/IL-15Rα-targeted CRISPRa boosts NK cell effector function against HIV-infected cells.
abstract: Like many other immune cell types, natural killer (NK) cells exhibit impaired functionality in people with HIV (PWH), limiting their ability to efficiently target and eliminate HIV-infected cells and contributing to the persistence of the HIV reservoir. Recently, adoptive NK cell therapy using activated or engineered NK cells has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer; however, its application to HIV remains in the early stages of development. NK cells primarily rely on interleukin-15 (IL-15) signaling for their development, survival, and maintenance, and dysregulated IL-15 signaling has been reported in PWH. We hypothesized that simultaneous enhancement of IL-15 and IL-15 receptor alpha (IL-15Rα) expression would improve NK cell effector function and promote clearance of HIV reservoir. Utilizing dCas9-VPR-mediated multiplex CRISPR activation (CRISPRa), we successfully upregulated both IL-15 and IL-15Rα expression in the same primary NK cells without altering the genomic sequence. CRISPRa-treated NK cells displayed increased IL-15 and IL-15Rα transcript levels, as measured by RT-qPCR and significantly elevated surface expression of IL-15Rα, as determined by flow cytometry. Enhanced IL-15/IL-15Rα expression increased NK cell metabolic activity and cytotoxicity against target K562 cells, a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line, indicating improved effector function. Furthermore, in co-culture experiments using an HIV-positive T-cell line, IL-15/IL-15Rα-CRISPRa-treated NK cells demonstrated enhanced target cell elimination and increased secretion of IFN-γ. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept that multiplex CRISPRa can be used to enhance NK cell function, representing a novel strategy to improve persistence and therapeutic efficacy in HIV and other disease settings.

title: ATMLP regulates MDVs mediated inflammation induced by radiotherapy in lung cancer.
abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and radiotherapy, a commonly used treatment for lung cancer, is associated with a variety of complications while treating cancer, among which radiotherapy-induced pneumonia is a common complication whose underlying mechanism remains unclear and requires further investigation. To address this, cell lines with ATMLP overexpression and knockdown were created using gene editing techniques, and Western blot, immunofluorescence and trans-well co-culture were used to explore the role of mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs) in mediating radiotherapy-induced inflammation, as well as the effects of ATMLP, DRP-1 and PGAM5 on MDVs. Ionizing radiation promoted the expression of ATMLP and the release of ATMLP-mediated MDVs. Up-regulation of ATMLP expression led to increased levels of PGAM5 and activation of phosphorylation at the Ser616 site of DRP-1. The increased number of MDVs further promoted macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype. Overall, ionizing radiation induces ATMLP expression, which enhances MDVs release through the PGAM5/DRP-1 axis. This process leads to macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype, contributing to the inflammatory response.

title: The pentatricopeptide repeat protein EMBRYO DEFECTIVE 1417 is required for chloroplast RNA editing and intron splicing in Arabidopsis.
abstract: Post-transcriptional RNA processing is essential for chloroplast biogenesis. The pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) protein EMBRYO DEFECTIVE 1417 (EMB1417), which contains only two PPR motifs, was previously shown to be required for splicing of rpoC1 and ycf3.2 transcripts in chloroplasts. Here, we demonstrate that chemical-induced silencing of EMB1417 results in a yellow-leaf phenotype with markedly reduced chlorophyll content. RNA sequencing analyses revealed that EMB1417 is indispensable for efficient C-to-U editing at multiple sites, including rpoA-200, clpP-559, petL-5, psbZ-50, accD-1568, and ndhD-2. Protein-protein interaction assays demonstrated that EMB1417 physically interacts with multiple RNA editing cofactors, MORF2/8/9 and DG409, thereby facilitating RNA editing in chloroplasts. Strikingly, disruption of EMB1417 significantly also severely impairs the splicing of group II introns in ndhB, petB, and petD transcripts. We further identified a direct interaction between EMB1417 and the splicing factor CFM3A. These findings establish that EMB1417 participates in chloroplast RNA processing, providing critical insights into the mechanisms of RNA editing and splicing during chloroplast development.

title: NEAT1 remodeling rewires the MYC degradation pathway.
abstract: MYC is among the most frequently amplified oncogenes in human cancer, yet its intrinsically disordered nature has rendered it refractory to direct pharmacological targeting. Here, we demonstrate that the long noncoding RNA NEAT1_1 functions as a molecular gatekeeper that controls MYC protein stability by regulating its access to the E3 ubiquitin ligase UBR5. We show that NEAT1_1 forms a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex with both MYC and UBR5, and that NEAT1_1 suppression disrupts this interaction, leading to decreased MYC polyubiquitination and enhanced protein stability. To systematically map the regulatory architecture of NEAT1_1 without altering its abundance, we screened 88 antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) mixmers tiling across the transcript. Strikingly, this phenotypic screen identified region-specific mixmers that elicit bidirectional control over MYC, either driving robust MYC destabilization or promoting its stabilization in a strictly expression-independent manner. Mechanistically, MYC-destabilizing mixmers selectively enhance the interaction between MYC and UBR5 to accelerate proteasomal degradation. A focused CRISPR screen targeting the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway independently validated UBR5 as the essential E3 ligase mediating this mixmer-induced turnover. In vivo, our lead mixmer ASO_#24 significantly suppressed tumor growth in MYC-high xenografts, whereas MYC-low tumors remained unaffected. Our findings reveal that the functional output of a scaffold lncRNA is encoded in its sub-domain architecture rather than bulk transcript levels, establishing domain-specific RNA targeting as a tractable strategy to rewire protein turnover pathways for otherwise undruggable oncogenes.

title: Chemically stabilized long antisense oligonucleotides perturb RNA exosome function.
abstract: The interaction with intracellular proteins shapes the pharmacology and toxicity of RNA drugs like gapmers and siRNAs. Here, we identify the RNA exosome as a modification-sensitive interaction partner of long, chemically stabilized, single-stranded RNA drugs. Using proximity biotinylation proteomics, we observe preferential binding of the catalytic exosome subunits DIS3 and EXOSC10 to oligonucleotides stabilized by 2'-ribose modifications and phosphorothioate linkages. RNA drug binding correlates with exosome impairment as measured by dose-dependent stabilization of promoter upstream transcripts and accumulation of ribosomal RNA processing intermediates leading to reduced cell viability. Consistent with structural requirements for substrate threading through the exosome channel, oligonucleotides longer than 24 nucleotides can impair exosome function. Systematic variation of ribose and backbone chemistry reveals that exosome inhibition is highly sensitive to the spatial arrangement of chemical modifications and can be mitigated by incorporation of bulky 2'-MOE residues or alternative internucleoside linkages like mesyl phosphoramidate. In contrast to the clinically established RNA drug modalities, class-specific liabilities of emerging ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides remain poorly understood. Importantly, we demonstrate that ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides can be designed that preserve editing activity while minimizing exosome interference. These findings illuminate critical variables that must be considered in the safer design of next-generation RNA base editing therapeutics.

title: Fanconi anemia pathway disruption drives lomustine sensitivity in glioma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Therapeutic options for progressive glioblastoma remain limited, with chlorethyl-cyclohexyl-nitrosourea (CCNU, lomustine) among the approved treatments. Beyond MGMT gene promoter methylation, molecular determinants of CCNU sensitivity or resistance are ill- defined.
METHODS: We employed genome-wide functional knockout screening using the CRISPR-Cas9 technology to identify and subsequently validate modulators of response to CCNU in experimental glioma. We established an immunocompetent glioma mouse model to enable functional interrogation of Fanconi anemia pathway (FA) genes in tumor growth and synthetic lethal interactions in vivo using the RCAS/tv-a somatic gene delivery system.
RESULTS: Multiple FA pathway members recurrently emerged as potent synthetic lethal interactors of CCNU treatment. In vivo knockdown of Fancm accelerated tumor onset and significantly increased CCNU sensitivity. Consistently, FA pathway inhibition enhanced CCNU efficacy across in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo models.
CONCLUSION: Together, these findings identify FA pathway components as key synthetic lethal interactors of CCNU response and reveal a therapeutically actionable vulnerability in glioblastoma.

title: A versatile tool for gene editing in the diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana.
abstract: Diatoms are major contributors to marine primary production, with the centric diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana a powerful model for understanding biogeochemical processes including carbon fixation and silicification. While there are molecular tools available for fluorescent protein (FP) tagging and CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing in T. pseudonana, these require the delivery of multiple vectors or have limited versatility. Additionally, scarless endogenous tagging, that results in a FP fusion expressed from its native genomic location, has yet to be developed. Here, we describe a versatile modular Golden Gate-based toolkit for T. pseudonana that through the delivery of a single-episome via bacterial conjugation enables: (i) FP tagging, (ii) dual FP tagging, (iii) CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, (iv) simultaneous FP tagging with gene editing, and (v) scarless endogenous FP tagging. We further expand the available parts for T. pseudonana by validating 3 additional FPs and 2 untested promoter/terminator pairs. We demonstrate the versatility of our system by knocking out diatom pyrenoid component 1 (DPC1) while simultaneously GFP tagging the rbcS (Rubisco small subunit), and by endogenously GFP tagging the bestrophin-like protein BST2. While DPC1 knockout does not result in a major pyrenoid structural defect due to unperturbed rbcS-GFP localization to the pyrenoid, we confirm that BST2 localizes to the pyrenoid and exhibits increased fluorescence under low CO2-supporting a role in diatom carbon fixation. Our developed genetic tools provide a robust framework for exploring cellular processes in diatoms, accelerating routine studies and enabling systematic, quantitative and large-scale studies.

title: CRISPR screening identifies GNPTAB as a noncanonical STING activator driving cellular senescence.
abstract: Cellular senescence is accompanied by profound lysosomal alterations, yet whether lysosome-associated factors actively drive aging remains unclear. Through a focused CRISPR/Cas9 screen in human mesenchymal progenitor cells (hMPCs), we identified N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase subunits alpha and beta (GNPTAB), an enzyme responsible for lysosomal hydrolase targeting, as a positive regulator of cellular senescence. Genetic ablation of GNPTAB attenuated senescence, whereas its overexpression accelerated senescence. This pro-senescent function occurred independently of GNPTAB's canonical enzymatic role. Instead, GNPTAB binds to the innate immune adaptor stimulator of interferon genes (STING) through an interface involving the critical residue E1119, leading to activation of STING and its downstream TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), as well as pro-inflammatory gene expression. A STING-binding-deficient GNPTAB mutant (E1119A) preserved canonical lysosomal functions but failed to induce senescence, while STING depletion abolished GNPTAB-driven senescence. Together, these findings uncover a new signaling pathway wherein GNPTAB engages STING to facilitate its activation, suggesting that the GNPTAB-STING interaction interface may serve as a potential therapeutic target for ameliorating age-related cellular dysfunction.

title: Dysregulation of macrophage colony stimulating factor in Paget's disease of bone.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine if common genetic variants at the chromosome 1p13 locus which predisposes to Paget's Disease of Bone (PDB) regulate Macrophage Colony stimulating factor (M-CSF) expression in bone cells and to determine if there is dysregulation of M-CSF in patients with PDB.
METHODS: The regions surrounding single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) previously associated with PDB at a genome wide significant level were deleted in clones of MG63 osteoblast-like cells using CRISPR/Cas and levels of M-CSF mRNA and protein were evaluated in cells with and without deletions. Serum M-CSF was measured by ELISA in PDB and controls and values in patients were related to clinical features of PDB and biochemical markers of bone remodelling.
RESULTS: Deletion of the region surrounding rs484959 increased expression of M-CSF mRNA by 1.31 fold [95%,1.04-1.58], p = 0.026 and M-CSF protein by 1.91 fold [1.25-2.57], p = 0.013, compared with control cells. Serum M-CSF was significantly elevated in PDB versus controls (mean ± SD = 781.7 ± 678 vs. 541 ± 491 pg/mL, p < 0.001). Furthermore, M-CSF levels were associated with number of affected bones (p = 0.029), bodily pain assessed by SF-36 (p = 0.026) and biochemical markers of bone turnover.
CONCLUSION: The rs484959 SNP is a regulatory variant which modulates M-CSF mRNA and protein expression in osteoblasts. Serum M-CSF is increased in PDB, is associated with pain, disease extent and biochemical markers of bone remodelling. This suggest that there is dysregulation of M-CSF in PDB and that this cytokine may play a role in pathogenesis of the disease.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle-Formulated Synthetic Messenger RNA Induces Reversible Hematopoietic Bias via Type I Interferon Responses Under Upper-Bound Inflammatory Conditions in Preclinical Animal Models.
abstract: Synthetic messenger RNA (mRNA) formulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) is increasingly used for vaccines and therapeutics, yet the consequences of high-dose systemic exposure for bone marrow hematopoiesis remain poorly defined. We previously reported that intramuscular mRNA/LNP administration transiently alters circulating reticulocytes and bone marrow erythroid cellularity in mice; here, we investigated the mechanistic basis and cross-species generalizability of this hematopoietic bias in murine and non-human primate models. Animals received intramuscular LNP-formulated mRNA encoding SARS-CoV-2 spike protein or firefly luciferase at deliberately supra-clinical, upper-bound doses, and type I interferon signaling was interrogated by interferon-α/β receptor blockade. Bone marrow was assessed by histopathology, bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, and trajectory analysis. LNP-formulated mRNA induced reversible erythroid-lineage suppression with concomitant granulocytic expansion, irrespective of the encoded antigen. These effects were absent after naked mRNA and only modestly induced by LNP alone, indicating that formulation of synthetic mRNA within the LNP was required to elicit the full phenotype. Single-cell analysis showed biased hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell differentiation toward granulopoiesis with broad induction of interferon-stimulated genes, and the bias resolved within two weeks. Interferon-α/β receptor blockade mitigated both changes, demonstrating type I interferon dependence. High-dose LNP-formulated synthetic mRNA can therefore drive reversible, type I interferon-dependent hematopoietic lineage bias in preclinical animal models.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated Mutagenesis of Two Alleles Encoding a Glutathione S-Transferase Confirms Their Identity as Fhb7 Conferring Fusarium Head Blight Resistance in Wheat.
abstract: Fhb7 is a gene derived from the homoeologous group-7 chromosomes of tall wheatgrass (Thinopyrum species), which confers resistance to Fusarium head blight (FHB) in wheat. Two resistance alleles at the Fhb7 locus (Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2) were identified from Th. ponticum and Th. elongatum, respectively, and introgressed into the wheat genome by homoeologous recombination. Fhb7Thp was first cloned and reported to encode a glutathione S-transferase (GST), which detoxifies trichothecenes through de-epoxidation. However, a recent study has questioned the role of GST in Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. To decipher the function of two GST-encoding alleles, Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2, in FHB resistance, we generated haploid plants from three spring wheat lines (CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80) carrying Fhb7Thp or Fhb7The2 through wide hybridizations with transgenic maize expressing Cas9 and guide RNA (gRNA) targeting GST. Of 57, 35, and 74 haploid plants derived from CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80, respectively, 16, 5, and 9 had an insertion/deletion at the target sites of GST. Greenhouse evaluation of doubled haploid (DH) lines derived from the haploid plants for FHB resistance indicated that the GST-edited DH lines were significantly more susceptible and accumulated more deoxynivalenol (DON) than their corresponding wildtypes and non-edited DH lines, confirming GST as the causal gene for Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. This study also demonstrated the power of wheat × maize hybridization coupled with genome editing in validating gene function in wheat.

title: A High-Sensitivity RPA/Cas12a Assay for Rapid Detection of the Select Agent Ralstonia solanacearum R3b2.
abstract: Ralstonia solanacearum is a globally distributed, soil-borne species complex that causes bacterial wilt in many economically important crops. Race 3 biovar 2 (R3b2) is a cold-tolerant, highly aggressive subgroup within this complex that is responsible for an estimated $1 billion in annual global losses. Because R3b2 remains exotic to North America, it is classified as a USDA Select Agent due to its high potential to devastate U.S. solanaceous crops and ornamental industries. However, current diagnostic methods for this pathogen involve trade-offs among cost, sensitivity, specificity, and ease of use, particularly for point-of-care (POC) detection in field settings. CRISPR-based detection platforms have recently emerged as promising tools for high-sensitivity POC diagnostics. Here we developed an isothermal recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)/Cas12a assay for specific, sensitive and rapid detection of R3b2. By targeting a genomic region associated with the cool-virulence phenotype, the assay reliably differentiates R3b2 from plant hosts and other diverse R. solanacearum strains. Incorporation of a dual-guide RNA system and an 8-mer single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) fluorescent reporter further improved sensitivity and reduced detection time. Using dilution series of R3b2-spiked Pelargonium DNA extracts, the assay detected as few as 4 CFU per reaction. To facilitate POC applications, the system was adapted into a one-pot, contamination-resistan¬t format compatible with portable fluorescence readers such as Genie III device and P51 viewer. By improving both sensitivity and portability, this assay enhances current diagnostic capabilities and, pending validation in real-world conditions, supports early surveillance efforts aimed at preventing the introduction of R3b2 into the United States.

title: ADAR1 Inhibits ZBP1-Driven Neuronal Necroptosis After Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Necroptosis is a critical response to secondary brain injury following intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Z-DNA Binding Protein 1 (ZBP1) binds to dsRNA and promotes the activation of Receptor-Interacting Protein Kinase 3 (RIPK3). This study investigated whether Adenosine Deaminase Acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) inhibits neuronal necroptosis after ICH. ADAR1-knockdown mice and ZBP1flox/flox/Thy1-Cre+/- mice were subjected to collagenase VII-induced ICH. Brain edema and neurobehavioral deficits were assessed. The expressions of ADAR1 and ZBP1 were investigated by qPCR, western blot, immunofluorescence, and ELISA. Protein interactions were performed using co-immunoprecipitation. ADAR1p150 was reduced in both ICH patients and mice. ZBP1 and ADAR1 both bound to dsRNA. ADAR1p150 suppressed ZBP1 activation, potentially through functional antagonism and dsRNA editing, although causality remains to be established. Knockout of ZBP1 resulted in increased ADAR1p150 expression and reduced brain edema. Etanercept and shRNA-mediated ADAR1 knockdown promoted ZBP1 expression. Complementation of the ADAR1 Zα truncation did not reduce ZBP1 in ADAR1-knockdown cells. The inhibitory effect of ADAR1 on ZBP1 was attenuated in ADAR1Zα-/- cells. These data show that the Zα domain is required for ADAR1 to suppress ZBP1, but they do not establish whether this suppression depends on RNA editing or on dsRNA binding alone.

title: Hypoxia-Driven CA2 Promotes Trophoblast Dysfunction in Preeclampsia.
abstract: Explore the potential function of Carbonic Anhydrase 2 (CA2) in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia. Peripheral blood and placental samples were collected from healthy pregnant women and patients with preeclampsia. Placental CA2 expression was validated in independent clinical cohorts and experimental mouse models. HTR-8/SVneo cells were cultured and transfected with a CA2 overexpression plasmid to evaluate trophoblast dysfunction. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed to identify downstream genes associated with CA2 overexpression, followed by VEGFA rescue experiments. Hypoxia-related regulation of CA2 was investigated. Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated siRNA against CA2 was constructed in an L-NAME-induced PE model to evaluate therapeutic effects. CA2 expression was significantly increased in placental tissues and maternal serum from women with PE and was also elevated in experimental PE mouse models. CA2 predominantly localized in trophoblast cells, and correlated positively with serum creatinine and urea and correlated negatively with fetal birth weight. CA2 overexpression markedly suppressed trophoblast proliferation, migration, and invasion, without affecting apoptosis. Transcriptomic analysis suggested that vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) acted as a downstream mediator of CA2, and VEGFA overexpression partially rescued CA2-induced trophoblast dysfunction. CA2 expression was upregulated under hypoxic conditions and regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). LNP-mediated CA2 silencing partially improved placental structure and fetal outcomes in vivo. CA2 is upregulated in the preeclamptic placenta and is associated with placental dysfunction and adverse fetal outcomes. Mechanistically, CA2 may act downstream of HIF-1α and contribute to trophoblast dysfunction partly through modulation of VEGFA signaling, and CA2 silencing partially improved maternal and fetal outcomes, highlighting CA2 as a potential therapeutic target for preeclampsia.

title: Gene Therapy: Routes of Inner Ear Delivery.
abstract: Gene delivery and the various routes of administration used to deliver viral vectors constitute a rapidly evolving field, with recent success in restoring hearing in children with OTOF variants in ongoing clinical otoferlin trials. With the rise of gene therapy for major hereditary hearing disorders, both syndromic and nonsyndromic, there has been parallel progress in the development of new delivery methods. Advances in intratympanic injection of antibiotics and corticosteroids, along with nearly half a century of experience in cochlear implantation surgery, have enabled multiple local and systemic approaches to access the inner ear. Recent industry investment in gene therapy and delivery technologies has accelerated scientific progress, underscoring the need for continuous evaluation of the most suitable gene delivery strategies for different causes of hearing loss. Although most gene delivery in animal models has been performed via round window membrane injection, yielding promising results in cochlear hair cell transduction, potential drawbacks remain for clinical translation-particularly limited vector distribution, which may result in a basal-to-apical gradient. Venting procedures such as stapes footplate fenestration or canalostomy have been explored to mitigate these limitations, and recent intrathecal or even in utero injections have been investigated as alternative approaches. Hearing loss can be inherited in multiple ways, and patient treatment with gene delivery, or even the type of gene therapy itself, may vary with the recent success of CRISPR/Cas-based editing tools. Understanding the genetic etiology of inner ear disorders has facilitated the identification of therapeutic targets and innovative delivery approaches. This review summarizes the current understanding of delivery routes for gene therapy, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations as demonstrated in translational and clinical research to date. Furthermore, it examines advances in drug delivery and clinical applications in the context of emerging therapeutics, providing an integrated overview and perspective on the future direction of gene delivery strategies.

title: Emerging Therapies for Genetic Deafness: The Rise of Precision Gene Editing.
abstract: Hearing loss is a prevalent sensory disorder with profound social and health impacts. Although hearing aids and cochlear implants can significantly restore auditory perception, they do not address the underlying genetic causes. Inherited forms of hearing loss, often monogenic, are ideal candidates for gene therapy, particularly since over 150 genes have been linked to deafness. Advances in vector engineering and genome editing technologies now enable precise targeting of auditory cells within the inner ear. Technologies such as Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats-Cas systems, base editing, and prime editing offer powerful tools to correct pathogenic variants at their native genomic loci. This review summarizes the current landscape of gene editing approaches for both hereditary and acquired hearing loss, emphasizing key preclinical studies in mouse models encompassing dominant and recessive forms of deafness. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different editing techniques, vector delivery systems, and administration routes, and explore obstacles including editing efficiency, cell-specific targeting, and the translation of these therapies to humans. Collectively, these advances represent a pivotal step toward variant-specific, durable, and potentially curative treatments for hearing loss.

title: RNA-Targeted Therapeutics in Cardiovascular Risk Reduction: From Gene Silencing to Precision Cardiology.
abstract: Advances in cardiovascular prevention and treatment have substantially improved patient outcomes. However, residual cardiovascular risk remains a major clinical challenge. Traditional lipid-lowering and antihypertensive therapies, although effective, remain limited by suboptimal adherence, adverse effects, and persistent residual cardiovascular risk. RNA-targeted therapeutics have emerged as a transformative therapeutic paradigm, offering durable and highly specific gene silencing through small interfering RNA and antisense oligonucleotide platforms. This review evaluates the current evidence on RNA-targeted therapeutics for cardiovascular risk reduction, with an emphasis on their mechanisms of action, clinical efficacy, safety, and emerging therapeutic applications. A review was conducted using PubMed, Embase, Scopus, ScienceDirect, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to June 2026. A total of 154 eligible studies were included and narratively synthesized by therapeutic class and molecular target. Inclisiran reduced low-density lipoprotein cholesterol by approximately 50% with twice-yearly dosing, while pooled ORION analyses suggested a reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events. Pelacarsen, olpasiran, and lepodisiran achieved 80-98% reductions in lipoprotein(a), whereas zilebesiran lowered systolic blood pressure by more than 15 mm Hg with sustained effects for up to 24 weeks. Across studies, RNA therapeutics demonstrated favorable safety profiles, with predominantly mild injection-site reactions. Although definitive cardiovascular outcome data remain unavailable for several emerging agents, RNA-targeted therapeutics represent a promising advance in precision cardiovascular medicine by providing durable, mechanism-based therapies capable of addressing important residual cardiovascular risk.

title: The small protein PhrS-P, encoded by the dual-function small RNA PhrS, augments fitness of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the presence of aminoglycosides.
abstract: PhrS (Pseudomonas Hfq-binding RNA S) is a dual-function small RNA of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The base-pairing small regulatory RNA PhrS-R positively regulates pyocyanin biosynthesis. PhrS-R stimulates the production of the Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) by indirectly activating the translation of pqsR mRNA, encoding the quorum sensing regulator PqsR (MvfR), and by inhibiting the synthesis of the anthranilate degradation regulator AntR. Furthermore, PhrS-R was shown to promote biofilm formation, swarming motility and CRISPR-Cas immunity. In addition, PhrS encodes a 37 amino acid long and conserved small protein (PhrS-P), the function of which remained unknown. Here, we provide evidence that PhrS-P is an inner membrane protein which does not contribute to the known physiological roles of its RNA counterpart. RNA-Seq-based transcriptome analyses revealed that multiple aminoglycoside resistance genes, including those of the AmgR regulon, are differentially expressed depending on PhrS-P. AmgR is the response regulator of the AmgRS two-component system (TCS), which affects aminoglycoside and zinc resistance in P. aeruginosa. A PhrS-P-deficient mutant strain exhibited reduced fitness when exposed to sub-inhibitory concentrations of the aminoglycosides tobramycin and amikacin as well as zinc. Based on our findings, we present a working model wherein PhrS-P positively regulates the AmgRS TCS activity through an unknown mechanism, leading to increased bacterial fitness in the presence of aminoglycosides.

title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems.
abstract: In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage-encoded anti-defence against bacterial anti-phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co-folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti-CRISPR-Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD+. Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD+ from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti-PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti-Septu). Phages counteract toxin-antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti-defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

title: CRISPR screens identify ACSL4 as a key regulator in macrophage activation and metabolic inflammation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pro-inflammatory macrophages drive obesity-associated metabolic inflammation. Identifying key regulators of their activation is crucial for new therapies. This study aimed to identify novel regulators of pro-inflammatory adipose tissue macrophage (ATM) activation and assess their therapeutic potential.
EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: We combined genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening with scRNA-seq data from human adipose tissue and identified long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 4 (ACSL4) as critical for pro-inflammatory ATM activation. Validation used myeloid-specific Acsl4 knockout mice (Acsl4fl/fl Lyz2Cre) and shRNA-mediated knockdown in macrophage cell lines (RAW264.7, THP-1, and iBMDM). Mechanisms were explored via mutagenesis, immunostaining, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and transcriptional activity assays. A high-throughput screen of 8,685 DrugBank compounds was performed to identify candidates targeting ACSL4.
KEY RESULTS: ACSL4 deficiency markedly reduced pro-inflammatory factor expression (Tnfα, Il1β, and Il6). Myeloid ACSL4 deletion protected against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory ATMs and enhanced adipocyte lipolysis and thermogenesis, without affecting food intake, water intake, or locomotor activity in mice. However, glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity were not significantly affected. Mechanistically, ACSL4 contributed to inflammation independent of its enzymatic/ferroptotic functions (Thr328 mutation, troglitazone insensitivity). Instead, ACSL4 translocated to the nucleus in a karyopherin β1 (KPNB1)-dependent manner. DrugBank screening identified abemaciclib as a potential inhibitor of the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction. Notably, abemaciclib treatment reduced macrophage inflammation and attenuated HFD-induced obesity in mice.
CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: ACSL4 promotes pro-inflammatory macrophage activation through its KPNB1-dependent nuclear translocation and cooperation with IRF5. Targeting the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic inflammation.

title: An inhibitor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain exerts synergistic anti-tumour effects when combined with alkylating agents.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Cancer cells exhibit the Warburg effect, but oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is also important for cancer cell proliferation. Metabolic reprogramming from glycolysis to OXPHOS is one mechanism of resistance to anti-tumour drugs. Here, we have synthesized and characterized OPB-111077, a novel, first-in-class orally available small-molecule compound, and investigated its anti-tumour activity and therapeutic potential in combination with alkylating agents.
EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Inhibition of mitochondrial function by OPB-111077 were assessed by measuring the oxygen consumption rate, ATP production and Complex I enzymatic activity. anti-tumour effects were evaluated in human haematological and solid tumour cell lines and in cell line-derived xenograft and lymphoma patient-derived xenograft models. Mechanistic studies included CRISPR screening, metabolomic analyses, and measurements of the oxygen consumption and extracellular acidification rates. Effects of OPB-111077 combined with alkylating agents were also assessed in mice.
KEY RESULTS: OPB-111077 inhibited mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I, suppressed OXPHOS, and exerted anti-tumour effects in several models. OPB-111077 demonstrated synergism with the alkylating agent bendamustine, with simultaneous inhibition of both OXPHOS and glycolysis. Bendamustine reprogrammed cancer cells into an OXPHOS-dominant state, thereby enhancing the efficacy of OPB-111077.
CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Based on these findings, we propose a novel anticancer therapeutic strategy of combining OXPHOS inhibitors with alkylating agents. OPB-111077 has demonstrated potential in combination therapy and was recently evaluated with bendamustine and rituximab in a Phase 1 clinical trial for patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (NCT04049825).

title: Challenges in Gene-Directed Therapies for Rare Neurodevelopmental Disorders Using HNRNPU as an Exemplar.
abstract: Next-generation sequencing has radically transformed the diagnostic capability of rare neurodevelopmental disorders (RNDDs), yet translating these molecular insights into viable therapeutics remains a hurdle. While gene-directed modalities, specifically viral-mediated supplementation, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and CRISPR-based activation or precision editing, offer a means to rescue loss-of-function phenotypes, successful clinical implementation requires moving past the reductive framework of merely increasing the expression of the target gene towards approaches that account for spatial, developmental, and therapeutic windows. This review uses HNRNPU-related rare neurodevelopmental disorder (HNRNPU-RNDD), a condition marked with global developmental delay and refractory epilepsy, as an exemplar to discuss these translational hurdles. We discuss the homeostatic boundaries of this scaffold attachment factor, where unregulated overexpression risks localised cytotoxicity, and altered chromatin dynamics compromise editing safety. Furthermore, we assess how cell-type sensitivity and narrow developmental windows may dictate clinical efficacy. By using HNRNPU-RNDD to critically analyse the challenges of using each therapeutic platform, we hope to inform the creation of gene-directed therapies that aim to treat disorders resulting from structural pleiotropic dosage-sensitive proteins.

title: Chromatin Modifications Orchestrate DNA Repair Pathway Choice: Epigenetics Strategies for Enhancing CRISPR-Cas9-Mediated Knock-In Efficiency.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated precise gene knock-in relies on homology-directed repair (HDR) at low frequencies in most mammalian cells, limiting precise gene editing in both research and therapeutic applications. Although multiple strategies have been developed to increase knock-in efficiency, their application can be restricted by technical complexity, limited applicability, or potential safety concerns. In this review, we propose a shift in focus from conventional strategies toward epigenetic methods to increase knock-in efficiency. It has been proved that histone modifications such as H3K36me3, H3K9me3, H4K20me2, and H2AK15ub are involved in DNA damage signallings and the recruitment of key HDR and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) factors. We further discuss conceptual strategies for transient chromatin modulation to bias repair pathway choice and highlight associated technical challenges and safety considerations. Together, these findings and insights highlight the essential role of histone modification in shaping chromatin states and orchestrating DNA repair dynamics. Accordingly, epigenetic regulation emerges as a compelling strategy to facilitate high-fidelity gene knock-in, offering valuable mechanistic clues and actionable epigenetic targets to gene editing for basic research and therapeutic translation.

title: Beyond Dendritic Cells: A Cellular Pharmacology Agenda for mRNA Cancer Vaccines in Hematologic Malignancies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: mRNA-based vaccines are emerging as a promising platform for cancer immunotherapy, including in hematologic malignancies. Current vaccine development has largely focused on antigen selection, mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, and combination with established immunotherapies. However, increasing evidence indicates that the cellular and tissue distribution of antigen expression may critically influence the quality and durability of the immune response. In this context, the term "cellular pharmacology" refers to the principle that the pharmacodynamic effect of an mRNA vaccine is shaped not only by the encoded antigen and formulation but also by the cell types in which antigen expression occurs.
OBJECTIVES: Here, we propose a cellular pharmacology framework for mRNA vaccines in hematologic malignancies, moving beyond the traditional dendritic-cell-centric model and considering antigen expression as a determinant of immune activation, tolerance, and T-cell exhaustion.
DISCUSSION: Three functionally distinct compartments can be considered: professional antigen-presenting cells, immunogenic non-immune cells at the injection site, and tolerogenic tissues, particularly hepatocytes. This tripartite model is intended as a simplified functional framework rather than a complete anatomical or cellular classification. While antigen expression in dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells supports effective T-cell priming, antigen production by skeletal myocytes and stromal cells may provide a sustained source of antigen for uptake and cross-presentation. Importantly, myocytes should not be regarded as professional antigen-presenting cells, but rather as potential antigen-producing cells whose antigens can be presented by professional APCs. Conversely, hepatic antigen expression may promote peripheral tolerance and impair antitumor CD8+ T-cell responses. Recent preclinical evidence indicates that microRNA-guided hepatocyte detargeting may enhance vaccine-induced immunity and tumor control in experimental models, although its clinical relevance in hematologic malignancies remains to be established. This concept may be particularly relevant in hematologic malignancies, characterized by disseminated disease, chronic antigen exposure, immune dysfunction, and frequent treatment-related organ vulnerability. We discuss how cellular targeting could be incorporated into mRNA vaccine strategies for lymphomas, acute leukemias, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and multiple myeloma, as well as into combination approaches with CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
CONCLUSIONS: The therapeutic potential of mRNA vaccines in hematologic malignancies may depend not only on the antigen encoded but also on the cellular compartment in which it is expressed. Incorporating tissue biodistribution and cell-type specificity into vaccine design could represent a new strategy to improve immunogenicity while limiting tolerogenic signals and potentially reducing unwanted tissue exposure. At present, however, hepatocyte detargeting should be considered a promising and testable translational strategy rather than a clinically validated approach. Prospective clinical studies integrating biodistribution, immune correlates, and tissue-specific antigen expression will be essential to translate this cellular pharmacology concept into clinical practice.

title: A guide to studying tumour-T-cell interactions using in vitro coculture assays.
abstract: T cells are central mediators of antitumour immunity and are the cellular basis of many successful cancer immunotherapies, including immune checkpoint blockade, T-cell receptor (TCR)-engineered therapies and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. However, clinical responses remain variable, and many tumours evade or resist T-cell-mediated control. Understanding how T cells recognise tumour cells, deliver cytotoxic signals, produce inflammatory cytokines and shape tumour cell fate is therefore essential for improving modern immunotherapies. In vitro tumour T-cell coculture systems provide a powerful experimental framework for dissecting these processes under controlled conditions. They allow investigators to manipulate antigen specificity, HLA/MHC restriction, tumour genotype, T-cell activation state, cytokine exposure and drug-mediated perturbation in ways that are difficult to achieve in vivo. However, these systems require careful design, because assay outcomes are strongly influenced by tumour model, antigen expression, effector-to-target ratio, assay duration and readout. This guide provides a practical framework for studying tumour T-cell interactions in vitro, with a focus on CD8+ T-cell-mediated tumour recognition and killing. It discusses commonly used mouse and human antigen-specific models, how antigen expression and presentation can be experimentally controlled, T-cell activation and coculture conditions, cytotoxicity assays, immune synapse imaging, competition assays, cytokine-mediated bystander killing, transcriptional profiling, CRISPR perturbation strategies, therapeutic testing and patient-derived models. The aim is to help researchers choose the most appropriate model, experimental setup and readout for the biological question being asked and to avoid common interpretive pitfalls when studying tumour immune sensitivity, resistance and therapeutic response.

title: Clinical Prospect of Novel Therapies for Functional Cure in Chronic Hepatitis B.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global health problem. Functional cure is defined as sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroclearance with undetectable HBV DNA 24 weeks after cessation of therapy. It has emerged as a clinically meaningful endpoint, associated with regression of liver fibrosis, reduced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk, and a lower treatment burden. However, current CHB therapies, including nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUCs) and pegylated interferon-α (Peg-IFNα), rarely lead to functional cure despite adequate viral suppression, leading to a notable portion of patients remaining at risk for adverse liver-related outcomes, including hepatic decompensation and HCC. Hence, novel therapeutic agents are aimed at accelerating towards functional cure. They are categorized as virus-targeting and immunomodulatory therapies.
METHODS: This review summarizes the clinical evidence for emerging therapies aimed at acheiving functional cure, with a particular focus on RNA-targeting therapies. It also discusses practical considerations relevant to treatment selection.
RESULTS: Among these novel therapies, RNA-targeting therapies are currently the most promising, with bepirovirsen (an unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide) standing out as the only agent completed in Phase III study showing efficacious results. Combination regimens that use RNA-targeting therapies as backbone are increasingly pursued, leveraging potential synergistic effects to achieve higher rates of HBsAg seroclearance.
CONCLUSION: RNA-targetting therapies and combination regimens offer promising approaches in attaining functional cure in CHB. Further research should emphasize on the long-term efficacy and safety for these novel agents.

title: RNA binding by ADARs prevents RNA interference from attacking self-produced dsRNA.
abstract: The ability of an organism to identify self and foreign RNA is central to eliciting an immune response in times of need while avoiding autoimmunity. As viral pathogens typically employ double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), host identification, modulation, and response to dsRNA is key. However, dsRNA is also abundant in host transcriptomes, raising the question of how these molecules can be differentiated. Two host pathways that regulate dsRNA are A-to-I RNA editing by adenosine deaminases (ADARs), and RNA interference (RNAi). Both mechanisms are important for normal organism development and function by regulating gene expression. Herein, we studied the structure and amount of siRNAs at editing sites and the ability of ADARs to prevent exogenous RNAi using the model organism, Caenorhabditis elegans. We found that the number of siRNAs targeting edited genes is significantly upregulated in ADAR mutant animals. We also found that despite an almost complete depletion of primary siRNAs generated from editing sites in wildtype animals, secondary siRNAs are generated from edited transcripts, suggesting ADARs antagonize only the first step of RNAi processing. We show that ADARs interfere with the efficacy of exogenous RNAi in vivo, probably to prevent trans-silencing, and have indications that ADR-2 binding to the dsRNA is needed for the efficient prevention of RNAi. This work sheds light on how the RNA editing process protects self-produced dsRNAs from aberrant recognition by the immune processes in the cell and from by-product degradation.

title: A B1 SINE element within the mouse Malat1 long noncoding RNA acts as an internal ribosome entry site mediating micropeptide translation.
abstract: In most cells, Malat1 long noncoding RNA localizes to the nucleus where it affects splicing and chromatin function. In mouse neurons, Malat1 is exported to the cytoplasm where it is translated to generate the M1 micropeptide. Here, we characterize an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) required for M1 translation that is sufficient to induce cap-independent expression of a downstream open reading frame. In vivo chemical probing and structural modeling defined a three-stem-loop RNA secondary structure that encompasses the active IRES segment and coincides with a mouse B1 SINE (short interspersed element) repetitive element. In affinity purification experiments, a minimal IRES/B1 RNA selectively bound ribosomal subunits, translation factors, and the known IRES cofactors Rack1 and hnRNP A2/B1. Depletion of Rack1 and hnRNP A2/B1 inhibited IRES-dependent translation of the reporter and expression of the endogenous M1 peptide. Our study identifies an unexpected functional unit hidden within a widely studied long noncoding RNA.

title: FOSL1-associated condensates modulate superenhancer-mediated selected IL-1 family gene activation in psoriasis.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)-SE regulating IL1A, IL1B, and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE-centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

title: In situ CAR-M engineered by liposomal mRNA nanomedicine remodels fibrotic microenvironment for ameliorating liver fibrosis.
abstract: Liver fibrosis is a severe complication of diverse chronic liver diseases characterized by a dysregulated hepatic microenvironment, and effective clinical therapeutic strategies for this condition remain lacking to date. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) hold considerable therapeutic potential for liver fibrosis via antigen-specific recognition and efferocytotic activity, yet their clinical translation is largely hindered by the sophisticated ex vivo preparation procedures. Herein, we report an in situ CAR-M engineering strategy that uses a phosphatidylserine (PS)-incorporated, macrophage-targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for the codelivery of CAR messenger RNA (mRNA) and Cas9 mRNA in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that this engineered LNP achieves efficient targeting of liver-resident macrophages. Transfection with fibroblast activation protein α (FAPα)-CAR mRNA equips macrophages with the capacity to specifically target activated hepatic stellate cells (aHSCs), whereas Cas9-mediated follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL-1) gene editing enhances the efferocytotic function of macrophages in liver tissues. Consequently, functional CAR-Ms are generated in situ, which elicits robust antifibrotic effects, including reduced collagen deposition, restored sinusoidal architecture and enhanced immune-mediated antifibrotic activity. Collectively, our customized LNP-mediated in situ engineering of liver macrophages into CAR-Ms enables precise antifibrotic intervention for liver fibrosis and circumvents the cumbersome ex vivo CAR-M preparation process.

title: Cas9 nickase-mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington's disease mouse model.
abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington's disease (HD) patient-derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient-derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non-cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.
