title: A multivalent mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine containing eight hemagglutinin antigens elicited broad neutralizing antibody responses and protected against influenza A virus challenge in swine.
abstract: The diversity within H1 and H3 subtype influenza A viruses (IAVs) in swine prevents effective vaccine control approaches with inactivated whole-virus vaccines. We addressed the challenge of controlling co-circulating hemagglutinin (HA) clades of swine IAV with the development of a multivalent messenger RNA (mRNA)-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing eight HA proteins to maximize genetic coverage. We applied a computational approach to select eight HA genes that represented 95% of the observed IAVs detected in the United States between 2022 and 2025. Piglets were vaccinated and boosted intramuscularly with either individual HA mRNA-LNP or an 8-HA multivalent mRNA-LNP. Serum was collected to evaluate systemic antibody levels. Twenty-one days post-boost, pigs were challenged with a field-relevant H1 1A.3.3.3-c3 IAV strain. The 8-HA multivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine induced neutralizing antibodies against all eight antigens, and vaccinees were protected against lung lesions, with lesion scores similar to non-challenged animals. Homologous monovalent vaccination significantly reduced IAV detection in nasal secretions and in the lungs. Heterologous monovalent vaccination was not cross-protective but did not induce vaccine-associated enhanced respiratory disease. We provide evidence that monovalent and multivalent mRNA-LNP influenza vaccines elicited neutralizing antibody responses in pigs and protected against viral challenge. The versatility and capacity for rapidly updating the mRNA-LNP vaccine platform make it an appealing tool to improve animal health and minimize the circulation and diversity of IAV in swine.IMPORTANCEInfluenza A virus (IAV) is an important respiratory pathogen in swine, and zoonotic transmission of swine strains to humans remains a public health risk. Control strategies against IAV in swine herds rely heavily on biosecurity measures and vaccination. However, the antigenic diversity of IAV circulating in swine challenges current vaccination programs, and there is a need for broadly protective vaccines or platforms that can rapidly update components to reflect circulating diversity. mRNA-LNP vaccines have emerged as promising vaccine platforms, offering simultaneous delivery of multiple antigens, rapid development, scalable manufacturing, and potent immunogenicity. In this study, we assessed the immunogenicity and protective capacity of monovalent and multivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines encoding eight representative IAV hemagglutinin (HA) antigens. To our knowledge, this is the first study to objectively select multiple representative endemic swine IAV strains by quantifying genetic diversity within the phylogeny and to apply this selection to rationally design and evaluate a multivalent HA mRNA-based influenza vaccine in the swine model.

title: Revisiting mRNA capping in Mononegavirales: a promising, yet underexplored antiviral target.
abstract: mRNA capping is a co-transcriptional, nuclear process in eukaryotes that adds a cap onto the 5' end of RNA to confer stability, efficient translation, and nuclear export. Viruses have evolved diverse strategies by mimicking or subverting host pathways to install an mRNA cap for efficient gene expression and evasion of the host innate immune response. The conventional mRNA capping pathway, employed by many RNA and DNA viruses, is mediated by dedicated RNA 5'-triphosphatase, guanylyltransferase, and methyltransferase enzymes. In contrast, many RNA viruses utilize unconventional capping mechanisms that diverge from the canonical pathway, offering unique opportunities to develop virus family-specific antiviral therapeutics. Among negative-sense RNA viruses, members of the order Mononegavirales harbor a unique capping domain, polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase), embedded within the viral RdRp large (L) protein. Unlike the conventional guanylyltransferase-mediated mechanism, PRNTase catalyzes mRNA capping through the formation of a covalent L-pRNA intermediate rather than the canonical GMP-enzyme intermediate. The HR motif in PRNTase, involved in covalent linking to mRNA, is highly conserved in non-segmented negative-strand RNA viruses. This review focuses on structural and functional insights into Mononegavirales capping, highlighting the conserved motifs and domain architecture that make it a promising therapeutic target.

title: Preliminary stability studies of a β-SARS-CoV-2 virus-like particle vaccine.
abstract: We aimed to study the stability of a Beta (β)-SARS-CoV-2 virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine in a series of preliminary experiments using selective stabilizing excipients. β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were produced and purified using established methodologies. The thermostability of VLPs was tested at 4°C and -30°C in the presence or absence of stabilizers polysorbate 80, sorbitol, or L-histidine in the presence of a physiological NaCl concentration of 137 mM. The integrity of VLPs was assessed using ELISA, Western immunoblot, and dynamic light scatter (DLS). β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were stable at 4°C for 14 days, and the addition of stabilizing excipients improved stability compared to VLPs in PBS alone. Storage of VLPs at -80°C maintained particle integrity by DLS analysis for up to 2 years. Excipients helped to maintain the antigenicity of the VLPs by ELISA and Western immunoblot, and DLS analysis revealed that VLPs retained their particulate structure.IMPORTANCESARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally and cause significant illness. The problem of waning immunity to mRNA/LNPs has necessitated frequent boosters to keep pace with emerging variants. The development of alternative vaccines, therefore, remains a priority. Protein- based vaccines, like VLPs, offer a safe alternative able to produce longer-lasting immune responses. In this preliminary stability analysis, the β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were found to be stable at 4°C, and the addition of excipients improved VLP stability. Storage of VLPs at -30°C and -80°C also showed that the VLPs are stable for extended periods. Our findings will be of importance for the ongoing development of a SARS-CoV-2 VLP-based vaccine.

title: Non-canonical function of SCIMP restricts JAK1 activity to counteract immune evasion in bladder cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite the fact that immunotherapy is reshaping the therapeutic landscape of bladder cancer, immune evasion remains a major obstacle to durable clinical benefit. Therefore, elucidating the mechanisms underlying immune resistance is essential for developing novel therapeutic strategies.
METHODS: In this study, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in bladder cancer cells co-cultured with CD8+ T cells and identified the SLP adaptor and CSK-interacting membrane protein (SCIMP) as a key gene that enhances CD8+ T cell antitumor immunity.
RESULTS: SCIMP serves as a favorable prognostic biomarker in patients with bladder cancer treated with immunotherapy. Mechanistically, SCIMP restricts JAK1 phosphorylation in an adaptor-independent manner, suppressing the IFN-γ/JAK1/STAT5A/PD-L1 signaling axis. Meanwhile, YTHDF2 destabilizes the m6A-tagged SCIMP transcripts to reduce their expression. Remarkably, SCIMP synergizes with PD-1 blockade in suppressing tumor growth.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unexplored non-canonical role of SCIMP in preventing immune evasion and provide a potential therapeutic target for bladder cancer.

title: T Cell Receptor-Engineered T Cell Therapy in Solid Tumors: Where We Stand and What's to Come.
abstract: T cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising adoptive cellular therapy for solid tumors by enabling recognition of intracellular antigens presented via human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules. Unlike chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy, TCR-T cell therapy targets a broader antigen repertoire, including cancer-testis antigens, neoantigens, and viral antigens. Recent clinical advances, highlighted by the approval of afamitresgene autoleucel in synovial sarcoma, demonstrate meaningful antitumor activity. However, several limitations remain, including HLA restriction, antigen heterogeneity, toxicity related to on-target/off-tumor effects, and mechanisms of resistance such as antigen loss and T cell exhaustion. Advances in antigen selection, gene editing, and synthetic biology are improving both safety and efficacy. Combination strategies and next-generation engineered constructs are expected to overcome current barriers. This review summarizes the biological rationale, clinical evidence, safety considerations, and resistance mechanisms of TCR-T cell therapy in solid tumors and discusses future directions to optimize their therapeutic potential.

title: Alternative and Synergistic Strategies Against Antibiotic-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus in Clinical and Environmental Settings.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) poses a serious global health threat, undermining treatment outcomes and necessitating the development of innovative therapeutic strategies. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major contributor to this burden, with increasing prevalence in hospitals, contaminated food, and environmental sources. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further intensified S. aureus resistance due to widespread antibiotic misuse. Biofilm formation, which facilitates the horizontal transfer of resistance genes such as mecA (methicillin resistance gene A), plays a central role in the development of resistance. To counteract antibiotic-resistant S. aureus, alternative approaches have emerged, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), photodynamic therapy (PDT), and drug repurposing guided by artificial intelligence (AI). Cutting-edge technologies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based gene editing and engineered bacteriophages offer promising avenues for targeting resistant strains. Natural compounds such as thymol and chlorogenic acid (CGA) have also shown potential in reducing resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. Effective management of AMR requires strengthened antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs), robust surveillance systems, and public health measures such as proper hand hygiene and environmental sanitation. Combining antibiotic adjuvants (AAs) with existing antibiotics and leveraging bioactive peptides (BAPs) can enhance antibiotic efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-drug-resistant (PDR) S. aureus. This review investigates the prevalence and resistance mechanisms of S. aureus in clinical, food, and environmental contexts, explores promising alternative therapies, and emphasizes the urgent need for global antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) and sustainable intervention strategies.

title: Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells in Rare Neurological Disorders: Opportunities and Challenges for Disease Modeling and Drug Discovery.
abstract: Rare disease is a condition that affects a small fraction of the population. In most cases, it has a known genetic cause but could also be associated with other contributing factors. As the affected individuals may exhibit diverse symptoms due to the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, non- or misdiagnosis of rare diseases is common. Their low incidence and prevalence present an obstacle to developing new therapies despite a major unmet need with only a few treatment options available. This is particularly relevant to rare neurological disorders as there are major difficulties in studying the mechanisms of initiation and progression of the central nervous system (CNS) disorders. Recent advances in biotechnology, specifically the use of human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for modeling diseases, have been instrumental in providing a flexible platform that not only reflects the effects of genetic disturbances on the development of CNS disorders but also is capable of providing insights into complex multifactorial disorders. Whether the human iPSCs are harvested from the affected individuals or using the gene-editing tools on cells from healthy individuals, valuable models can now be made available for studying these orphan conditions. In this narrative review, we explore the benefits of using human iPSC models over the existing platforms of other primary cell lines and animal models for the disease modeling and drug discovery and discuss the limitations and future aspects of the iPSC use in the investigation of rare neurological disorders.

title: ETV6 Rearrangement Suppresses CDKN1B Transcription by Disrupting an Intragenic Super-enhancer in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: ETV6-rearranged acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is associated with poor prognosis in adults. Previously, a super-enhancer (SE) located within the ETV6 intragenic region (ETV6-SE) was identified in a rare fusion gene, ETV6::ACSL6; however, further work is needed to determine whether ETV6-SE is broadly present in ALL and how ETV6 rearrangements affect the SE function. In this study, we demonstrated that ETV6 functions as a regulatory element via ETV6-SE in ALL, with CDKN1B as a key target. CRISPR interference and knockout experiments revealed the core enhancer region within ETV6-SE responsible for CDKN1B regulation. ETV6 rearrangements disrupted ETV6-SE and impaired long-range chromatin interaction with the CDKN1B locus, leading to its downregulation that in turn activated the NF-κB pathway and increased expression of antiapoptotic proteins BCL-2/BCL-XL. In patient-derived xenograft models, pharmacologic inhibition of BCL-2/BCL-XL using venetoclax or navitoclax showed additive effects when combined with dexamethasone. Collectively, these findings establish the ETV6-SE-CDKN1B regulatory axis as a mechanism contributing to treatment resistance in ETV6-rearranged ALL.
SIGNIFICANCE: ETV6 comprises a super-enhancer that activates CDKN1B expression and is lost in ETV6-rearranged acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which contributes to glucocorticoid resistance via downstream activation of the NF-κB pathway.

title: A syngeneic murine glioma model recapitulates key molecular, immunologic, and functional features of human glioblastoma to enable therapeutic development.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of novel therapies. Here we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

title: DNMT3B Plays Antagonistic Roles with SMARCB1 and Is a Targetable Vulnerability in Rhabdoid Tumors.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Rhabdoid tumors (RT) are highly aggressive pediatric cancers driven by the biallelic inactivation of the SMARCB1 tumor-suppressor gene, the sole recurrent genetic alteration. SMARCB1 encodes a core subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex; its loss disrupts epigenetic gene regulation, supporting the classification of RT as prototypical epigenetically driven cancers and highlighting the therapeutic potential of targeting epigenetic modifiers. Notably, previous studies have reported the overexpression of DNMT3A and DNMT3B, enzymes responsible for de novo DNA methylation, in RT.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: Using patient samples, cell lines, and an ex vivo brain organoid system, combined with immunohistochemistry and bioinformatics, we investigated the role of DNMT3 enzymes in RT progression.
RESULTS: In a composite tumor case, SMARCB1-deficient and -proficient regions displayed distinct methylation profiles. SMARCB1 loss correlated with increased DNA methylation and DNMT3A/B overexpression. To assess their respective roles in RT, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to knock out DNMT3A/B in a SMARCB1-inducible RT cell line. DNMT3B loss impaired viability more strongly than DNMT3A. DNMT3B knockout and SMARCB1 reexpression regulated overlapping gene programs related to development and cell adhesion at methylation and transcriptional levels. We next demonstrated that the cytotoxicity of the DNMT inhibitor decitabine, which impairs RT cell growth in human induced-pluripotent stem cell-derived cerebral organoids, is primarily mediated by DNMT3B.
CONCLUSIONS: These results show that DNMT3B plays a key role in the cascade of epigenetic effects following SMARCB1 loss and is pivotal to RT sensitivity to decitabine; our study, therefore, supports the development of DNMT3B-specific inhibitors for RT.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Intratumoral MEDI1191, an IL12 mRNA Lipid Nanoparticle, plus Intravenous Durvalumab in Patients with Advanced Solid Tumors: A First-in-Human Study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: MEDI1191 is a lipid nanoparticle-formulated messenger RNA (mRNA) designed to induce local interleukin (IL) 12 production and intensify antitumor T-cell responses. We report dose-escalation results from a first-in-human, open-label, phase I study of intratumoral MEDI1191 plus intravenous durvalumab (NCT03946800).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients were ≥18 years with advanced/metastatic solid tumors and had progressed on ≥1 line of prior therapy (immunotherapy permitted). Cutaneous/subcutaneous (parts 1A and 1B) or deep-seated lesions (part 1D) were injected; patients had ≥1 noninjected lesion measurable per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST v1.1). Target lesions were noninjected. MEDI1191 and durvalumab were given sequentially (part 1A) or concurrently (parts 1B and 1D). Primary objectives were safety and determination of maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Secondary objectives included efficacy.
RESULTS: As of February 27, 2023, 61 patients were treated. Patients had a median of four prior regimens (range, 1-17); 39 (63.9%) received prior anti-programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death ligand 1 [PD-(L)1] immunotherapy. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) occurred in 96.7% of patients, and 41.0% experienced grade 3/4 TEAEs. There were no dose-limiting toxicities. The MTD was not reached. The objective response rate was 9.8%, including 1 confirmed complete response and 5 confirmed partial responses (PR). The duration of response was 2.7 to 22.3 months; the median was not reached. Responses occurred in injected lesions, local noninjected lesions, and distant lesions. Three of the 39 patients with prior anti-PD-(L)1 therapy had PRs.
CONCLUSIONS: MEDI1191 and durvalumab were tolerated. Preliminary antitumor activity was encouraging in these heavily pretreated patients, including patients previously treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.

title: Danvatirsen plus Pembrolizumab versus Pembrolizumab for Recurrent and/or Metastatic Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (PEMDA-HN): A Randomized, Phase II Trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is important in promoting a pro-oncogenic tumor microenvironment. This first randomized trial of a STAT3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide with pembrolizumab assessed whether this first-line combination would improve outcomes compared with pembrolizumab alone in recurrent/metastatic (R/M) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This multicenter, randomized, open-label, controlled study (NCT05814666) enrolled patients with previously untreated R/M HNSCC with positive PD-L1 expression [combined positive score (CPS) ≥1]. Patients were stratified by CPS (1-19; ≥20) and randomized 2:1 to danvatirsen 3 mg/kg intravenously weekly (with two loading doses in week 1) plus pembrolizumab 200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks or pembrolizumab alone. Patients received 21-day treatment cycles until progressive disease, unacceptable toxicity, or voluntary withdrawal. Primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR; partial + complete response per RECIST v1.1).
RESULTS: Sixty-nine patients were randomized, and 66 were treated [51 (77.3%) male]: 45 with danvatirsen + pembrolizumab and 21 with pembrolizumab alone. Enrollment was stopped due to lack of response in the CPS 1 to 19 cohort after ≥1 scan (∼6 weeks of treatment) and in the CPS ≥20 cohort after ≥2 scans (∼12 weeks). In the final analysis, ORRs were 15.6% and 14.3%, respectively (risk difference 1.3; P = 1). The treatment-emergent adverse event rate was increased in the combination arm (97.8% vs. 85.7%), and the combination side effect profile was similar to previous danvatirsen studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Combination danvatirsen + pembrolizumab did not improve ORR compared with pembrolizumab alone in first-line treatment of R/M HNSCC. Further exploration of STAT3-targeted approaches is needed within the context of immunotherapy.

title: Dual Inhibition of PARP and ATR Induces Synthetic Lethal Vulnerability in Prostate Cancer with CDK12 Deficiency.
abstract: Prostate cancers harboring CDK12 alterations exhibit aggressive clinical behavior and poor responses to current therapeutic strategies. Although CDK12 is categorized as a homologous recombination repair (HRR)-related gene, clinical evidence indicates limited benefit of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor monotherapy in CDK12-defective tumors. To clarify the functional consequences of CDK12 loss and identify a mechanistically rational therapeutic approach, we generated CDK12-knockout (KO) prostate cancer cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 and assessed cell-cycle regulation, DNA damage repair, and replication stress via flow cytometry, γH2AX immunofluorescence, and DNA fiber assays. CDK12 KO abrogated the G0-G1 checkpoint, permitting cell-cycle progression into the M-phase despite the persistence of unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks (DSB), and reduced ATM transcription, resulting in a DSB response phenotype resembling ATM deficiency. CDK12 loss also increased intrinsic replication stress and sensitized prostate cancer cells to ATR inhibition. In patient-derived xenograft models harboring CDK12 alterations, combined PARP and ATR inhibition led to enhanced DSB accumulation and selectively suppressed tumor growth in CDK12-defective models. These findings highlight the importance of interrogating individual genes within the HRR pathway to define distinct mechanistic vulnerabilities and provide a strong rationale for combined PARP and ATR inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with CDK12-altered prostate cancer.

title: Preclinical modeling of trastuzumab deruxtecan in a mouse model of brain metastatic triple-negative breast cancer identifies two contributors to efficacy.
abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in advanced HER2-low to -ultralow breast cancer. We employed a mouse model of triple-negative breast cancer in the difficult-to-treat brain metastasis setting to determine T-DXd efficacy and investigate mechanism(s). T-DXd (10 and 3 mg/kg) was compared to an identical ADC except HER2-nonbinding (control) in a hematogenous model of HER2-ultralow brain-tropic triple-negative breast cancer, MDA-MB-231-BR7 (231-BR). The roles of HER2 and the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) were determined by CRISPR-Cas9 deletion and shRNA knockdown, respectively. 231-BR cells exhibited HER2 0+ staining, with occasional membrane expression. T-DXd at 10 mg/kg reduced 231-BR brain metastases by 49% (P=0.002), while a dose reduction showed a 30% (ns) metastasis reduction, each compared to the control-ADC. HER2-specific and -nonspecific ADC uptake into metastases was accompanied by a 23-47% tumor cell Ki-67 decline, and 5-fold increase in tumor apoptosis. A HER2 CRISPR-Cas9 knockout 231-BR formed multiple brain metastases but was insensitive to T-DXd in vivo. 231-BR tumor cells expressed FcRn, potentially enabling nonspecific ADC uptake. Analysis of human tumors showed TNBC tumors expressed FcRn mRNA. T-DXd failed to inhibit brain metastases in two 231-BR FcRn knockdown clones compared to a 231-BR clone transduced with a scrambled shRNA where T-DXd inhibited brain metastases (67% reduction, P=0.01). Despite ultralow HER2 expression, the HER2 binding capacity of T-DXd is a significant contributor to its efficacy. Breast cancers variably express FcRn, suggesting that nonspecific tumor cell uptake of T-DXd via FcRn is also a potential mechanism of T-DXd action.

title: Cullin-5 RING E3 ligase limits CD8⁺ T-cell persistence and effector responses during chronic antigen stimulation.
abstract: T-cell exhaustion limits durable antitumor responses and remains a barrier to adoptive cell therapies (ACT) in solid tumors. To identify regulators of T-cell persistence, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in primary human CD8⁺ T cells expressing an NY-ESO-1-specific T-cell receptor and subjected them to repeated tumor cell rechallenge. These screens revealed enrichment of single-guide RNAs targeting components of Cullin-RING E3 ligases, particularly Cullin-5 (CRL5) assemblies comprising CUL5, RNF7, and ARIH2. Disruption of CRL5 genes in T cells preserved cytotoxic activity and enhanced cytokine production while sustaining effector-associated transcriptional programs and suppressing exhaustion-related signatures. Pharmacologic inhibition of cullin neddylation with the NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor MLN4924 recapitulated CRL5 loss and enhanced T-cell effector function in vitro. In a human melanoma xenograft model, ACT with CRL5-deficient T cells improved tumor control. Together, these findings identify CRL5 as a negative regulator of T-cell fitness and a potential therapeutic target to enhance ACT durability in solid tumors.

title: Immune Checkpoint Blockade Sensitivity Is Linked to Endogenous Retroelement Transcriptional Changes in Cancer.
abstract: Endogenous retrotransposable elements (ERE) can modulate immune responses. We explored ERE transcription in relation to response to immune checkpoint inhibition in advanced solid tumors. ERE expression was measured in pre- and on-treatment samples from patients treated in a clinical trial with pembrolizumab. We evaluated immune cell infiltration and correlated ERE expression with interferon (IFN)-stimulated gene profiles and cytolytic activity. Two independent datasets were retrospectively analyzed as external validation. ERE transcription, notably Alu repetitive elements followed by long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE), is upregulated in immunotherapy responders, and higher ERE expression correlates with durable clinical benefit and improved long-term outcomes. In responders, this dynamic increase correlates with CD8+ T-cell infiltration and cytolytic activity, particularly during treatment. A trend toward increased A-to-I RNA editing was observed in responders. External validation in melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer cohorts confirmed a consistent pattern in ERE transcription. Therefore, ERE transcription is emerging as a potential biomarker for personalized immunotherapy in solid tumors.

title: Therapy-Persistent Leukemia Is Selectively Vulnerable to SLC23A1 Restoration via Targeting KHSRP.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is prone to relapse driven by therapy-persistent residual cells. To discover specific vulnerabilities in this population, we performed genome-wide CRISPR interference screens in leukemia cells treated with multiple agents. KHSRP was the top hit, the depletion of which sensitized AML cells to therapy and substantially prolonged survival in treated AML-bearing mice. Analysis of in vivo residual disease after venetoclax/azacitidine treatment identified downregulation of the vitamin C and uric acid transporter SLC23A1, which mediated resistance to multiple therapies. KHSRP depletion restored SLC23A1 expression by preventing its ZC3H4-mediated nuclear mRNA degradation. KHSRP depletion therefore enhanced the synergistic cytotoxicity of vitamin C and uric acid, particularly in therapy-persistent leukemia cells. Re-expression of TET2 overrode the chemosensitizing effect of KHSRP depletion in TET2-mutant leukemia, suggesting that KHSRP-linked phenotypes were related to vitamin C- and uric acid-mediated TET activation. These findings suggest targeting KHSRP to enhance treatment efficacy and selectively eradicate residual AML.
SIGNIFICANCE: Residual AML cells that persist following therapy have distinct biological properties compared with initial disease or overt relapse. Here, we nominate KHSRP as a target to improve therapy efficacy and exploit selective vulnerabilities of AML residual disease.

title: Optimizing Perfusates for Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion: A Pharmaceutic Perspective on Formulations, Functions, and Future Innovations.
abstract: Ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) is now an established normothermic machine-perfusion strategy in lung transplantation, primarily enabling structured donor lung assessment, short-term preservation, and selective rehabilitation outside the recipient. Because the supply of transplantable lungs remains limited, clinically implemented EVLP protocols have increased donor-lung utilization by allowing transplant teams to evaluate marginal grafts under near-physiological ventilation and perfusion rather than relying exclusively on static cold storage. The perfusate is central to this process because it stabilizes colloid osmotic pressure, electrolytes, buffering capacity, metabolic substrates, and oxygen transport according to protocol requirements. This review critically summarizes the development of EVLP perfusates and separates clinically validated roles from experimental repair strategies. We first distinguish EVLP perfusates from cold preservation solutions and compare acellular, red blood cell-containing, and whole-blood approaches with attention to their physiological rationale, logistical constraints, and level of evidence. We then discuss protocol-specific additives, including anti-inflammatory agents, antioxidants, antimicrobials, anticoagulants, hormones, nutritional substrates, and cellular or gene-based therapies. Emerging interventions such as polymerized hemoglobin, cytokine adsorption, mesenchymal stromal cell-derived products, CRISPR-Cas-mediated interleukin-10 modulation, and prolonged or intermittent EVLP illustrate the expanding therapeutic potential of the platform. However, most of these strategies remain preclinical or early translational. Future perfusate development should therefore prioritize standardized outcome measures, evidence-based component selection, and careful separation of organ preservation, organ assessment, and organ rehabilitation.

title: Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Inducing Kinase- and Inhibitor of Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Kinase Subunit Beta-Binding Protein Promotes Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy by Regulating Inhibitor of Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Kinase Subunit Beta-Mediated Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Activation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is a major risk factor for heart failure. NIBP (NF-κB [nuclear factor kappa-B] inducing kinase- and inhibitor of NF-κB kinase subunit beta-binding protein) is a key regulator of cytokine-induced NF-κB signaling, but its role in cardiac hypertrophy remains unknown.
METHODS: We established transverse aortic constriction-induced cardiac hypertrophy in mice and phenylephrine-induced hypertrophy in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes. Genetic interventions included generation of whole-body Nibp knockout mice via CRISPR-Cas9; creation of cardiomyocyte-specific Nibp knockout mice using adeno-associated virus serotype 9-delivered Cre and single-guide RNAs in Rosa26-LSL-Cas9 mice; and cardiac-specific Nibp overexpression via adeno-associated virus serotype 9delivery. In neonatal rat ventricular myocytes, NIBP was knocked down or overexpressed using adenoviruses. Phenotypes were assessed by echocardiography, histology (wheat germ agglutinin, picrosirius redstaining), and molecular analyses. Mechanisms were investigated via RNA-sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and Western blotting for key signaling molecules.
RESULTS: NIBP protein was upregulated in hypertrophic hearts and cardiomyocytes. Both Nibp-knockout and cardiomyocyte-specific Nibp knockout attenuated transverse aortic constriction-induced cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibrosis, whereas Nibp overexpression exacerbated these pathologies. Consistently, in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes, NIBP knockdown mitigated, while its overexpression aggravated, phenylephrine-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, NIBP directly interacted with IKKβ (inhibitor of NF-κB kinase subunit beta), enhanced its phosphorylation, and drove hyperactivation of the downstream NF-κB pathway. Overexpression of a kinase-dead IKKβ mutant reversed the hypertrophic effects of NIBP.
CONCLUSIONS: NIBP promotes pathological cardiac hypertrophy by activating the IKKβ/NF-κB axis, identifying it as a potential therapeutic target for cardiac remodeling and heart failure.

title: Characterizing NaV1.7 antisense analgesia through antagonist binding, mRNA expression, and neuraxial distribution.
abstract: Genome-targeting strategies to address NaV1.7-mediated signaling in nociceptive afferents are of great clinical interest given its high selectivity and persistent analgesic outcomes. In the present work, we analyze concentration-dependent effects of suppressing primary afferent NaV1.7 using the intrathecal delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) on pain behaviors and demonstrate that NaV1.7 ASOs are likely to modulate pain traffic by blocking afferent signaling at the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) level. Intrathecal NaV1.7 ASOs induced a concentration-dependent gradient of knockdown in DRGs (lumbar to cervical) of Scn9a mRNA and ATTO488-ProTx-II binding in small DRG neurons, and a suppression of pain behaviors initiated by mechanical compression, inflammation, and the NaV1.7 agonist OD-1. The rostro-caudal reduction in mRNA correlated with ASO distribution, with implications for dose-related analgesic profiles. Marked reduction in DRG NaV1.7 binding was seen after intrathecal delivery of an ASO optimal dose, with high selectivity for small DRG neurons. Changes in sciatic nerve NaV1.7 binding were not detected, indicating a pain traffic modulation likely happening due to a block of afferent signaling at the DRG level.

title: A single liver-sparing myotropic AAV ameliorates muscular dystrophy in humanized mice by base editing.
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, most of which are large exon deletions that result in loss of dystrophin protein. Adenine base editing (ABE) enables permanent gene correction by modifying splice sites to cause exon skipping and restoration of the DMD open reading frame. We previously demonstrated that adeno-associated virus 9-mediated (AAV9-mediated) delivery of adenine base editors allows efficient gene editing in mouse models of DMD. However, conventional AAV-based gene delivery approaches are complicated by their limited packaging capacity and high-dose-related toxicity. Here, we describe a single AAV vector encoding a compact adenine base editor, SlugABE8e, and a single-guide RNA, which enable efficient editing in a humanized DMD mouse model at a lower dose using the muscle-tropic MyoAAV4 capsid. Systemic MyoAAV4A delivery in juvenile DMD mice efficiently restored dystrophin expression in the heart and skeletal muscles. This molecular rescue was accompanied by reduced serum creatine kinase activity and diminished muscle pathology. A liver-detargeted MyoAAV4E-off capsid eliminated viral entry and editing in the liver. We also explored a high-fidelity base editor, SlugHF-ABE8e(V106W), which showed similar on-target and off-target editing to SlugABE8e. Together, these findings establish an all-in-one AAV strategy that efficiently mitigates DMD disease progression.

title: Beyond Viruses: Transposons and CRISPR-Programmable Nonviral Systems for Genome Engineering.
abstract: Human gene therapy has been transformed by repurposing mobile genetic elements as tools for efficient gene delivery and precise genome modification. Viruses, transposons, and retrotransposons mobilize genetic material through distinct mechanisms with distinct advantages for genome engineering platforms with therapeutic potential. This review describes the mechanisms, performance characteristics, and translational relevance of nonviral methods of gene transfer and genome engineering, with emphasis on engineered systems such as the Sleeping Beauty (SB) and piggyBac (PB) DNA transposons, R2 retrotransposon-based platforms, CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs), and prime editing (PE). Clinical trials using both SB- and PB-engineered cells have shown feasibility by demonstrating sustained therapeutic effect through stable transgene integration, such as CD19-directed CAR-T cell therapy for hematological malignancies. These transposon-based vectors enable robust gene transfer for cell engineering, but are fairly promiscuous with respect to where in the genome they insert their genetic cargo. On the contrary, R2-derived systems and CASTs represent promising technologies for programmable insertion, but are still under preclinical development. CRISPR-based PE provides a distinct route to precise sequence correction without double-strand breaks and is particularly attractive for the correction of monogenic disorders. Taken together, these technologies define a continuum from natural genome mobility to clinically relevant genome engineering. Continued optimization of delivery, targeting, and editing fidelity will determine how rapidly these approaches move from experimental innovation into routine clinical use.

title: Novel Technologies and Clinical Breakthroughs: The Evolving Landscape of Gene Therapy in China.
abstract: Gene therapy offers a fundamental approach to treating genetic disorders, malignant tumors, and refractory chronic diseases by directly modifying or replacing defective genes at the molecular level. Driven by policy support, increased investment, and technological innovation, China has achieved remarkable progress in adenoviral and adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors, gene editing, genetically engineered immune cells, oncolytic microorganisms, and small nucleic acid drugs. This review provides a comprehensive narrative overview of the technical principles, product pipelines, and clinical advances in these fields. Notable achievements include the approval of AAV-based gene therapy products in China, the entry of multiple in vivo and ex vivo gene editing therapies into clinical trials, a leading number of CAR-T trials worldwide with expansion into solid tumors and autoimmune diseases, encouraging efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy in liver cancer and melanoma, and positive clinical data of small interfering RNA/antisense oligonucleotide drugs for chronic hepatitis B and hypercholesterolemia. However, challenges remain including suboptimal tissue specificity, off-target risks, limited cargo capacity, high production costs, and poor accessibility. Future directions should focus on tissue-selective vectors, precise editing tools, off-the-shelf cell products, scalable manufacturing, and improved regulatory frameworks. With abundant clinical resources and strong manufacturing capabilities, China is poised to play a significant role in the global gene therapy landscape.

title: Efficient Generation of Single- and Multigene CRISPR-Cas9 Knockout in Human Cells.
abstract: The CRISPR-Cas9 system has revolutionized genome editing, but generating multiple gene knockouts (multi-KOs) remains challenging. This study presents an improved method for efficient generation of multi-KOs using sgRNA DNA strands and the CRISPR/Cas9 system. The method was tested on genes involved in the apoptosis pathway of HEK293T cells. The crRNA for each target gene was designed from Exon 1, near the starting codon ATG, such that a small deletion or insertion in this region would lead to a premature STOP codon and functional knockout. The T7 endonuclease I assay confirmed the high editing efficiency of sgRNAs in both single- and multiple-gene knockouts. Deep sequencing analysis revealed frameshift mutations and premature stop codons, indicating successful loss-of-function mutations. Using the sgRNA DNA strands provided a more uniform and efficient editing profile compared to other methods. This improved protocol offers a simpler, faster, and cost-effective approach for generating multigene knockout clones, with implications for functional genomics, therapeutic development, and synthetic biology.

title: Liver concentrations of JNJ-73763989 siRNA triggers in patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB): The INSIGHT study panel 3 results.
abstract: BackgroundJNJ-73763989 is a 2:1 combination of 2 N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated short interfering RNAs (siRNA) targeting the S (daplusiran) and X (tomligisiran) regions of the hepatitis B virus genome. In phase 2b studies, 48 weeks of JNJ-73763989-based combination treatments led to dose-dependent reductions in viral markers, including hepatitis B surface antigen. The objective of the INSIGHT study Panel 3 was to quantify intrahepatic concentrations of the siRNAs in human livers during and after treatment.MethodsIn the open-label, single-arm, single-center study, participants with chronic hepatitis B received 48 weeks of treatment with JNJ-73763989 200 mg every 4 weeks and nucleos(t)ide analog, with optional pegylated interferon α2a 180 µg weekly added after Treatment Week (TW) 40. Core liver biopsies were collected at TW12, TW40, and at Follow-up Week (FUW) 24.ResultsLiver biopsies were available from all 4 participants at TW12 and from 3 at TW40 and FUW24. Between TW12 and TW40, liver concentrations of daplusiran and tomligisiran increased 1.5- to 2.6-fold, consistent with intrahepatic accumulation. Twenty-eight weeks after the last injection of JNJ-73763989, the triggers were still measurable in 2 of 3 participants with 4.5- to 15-fold reduced concentrations from peak levels; the estimated liver half-life ranged from approximately 2.9 to 16.1 weeks.ConclusionsIn this first study to assess liver concentrations of GalNAc-siRNA in humans with sequential biopsies, long persistence of JNJ-73763989 triggers in human livers may partially explain the prolonged suppressive effect on viral parameters observed in phase 2 studies.

title: Huntington's disease clinical trials update: August 2026.
abstract: In this edition, we highlight several important developments across the Huntington's disease therapeutic pipeline. We discuss the launch and subsequent discontinuation of POINT-HD, the first-in-human phase I study of RG6496 (Hoffmann-La Roche), an allele-selective antisense oligonucleotide designed to selectively lower mutant huntingtin while largely preserving wild-type huntingtin expression. We also discuss the launch of two phase III efficacy trials: INVEST-HD, evaluating votoplam (Novartis Pharmaceuticals), and PRECISE-HD, evaluating pridopidine (Prilenia). In addition, we summarise recent advances across the field, including preclinical updates for LQT-23 (LoQus23), SRP-1005 (Sarepta Therapeutics) and HRN001 (Harness Therapeutics); interim 12-month clinical results from SKY-0515 (Skyhawk Therapeutics); the announcement by uniQure that 3-year data from the phase I/II AMT-130 study may support a Biologics License Application seeking accelerated approval and Roche's discontinuation of the phase II GENERATION HD2 study of tominersen. Finally, we provide an updated listing of registered and ongoing clinical trials in Huntington's disease.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotides that Are Toxic to Prion-Infected Mice Share an Emergent Mechanism.
abstract: Some, but not all, gapmer antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) delivered into cerebrospinal fluid exhibit fatal subacute toxicity in late-stage prion-infected mice but not in uninfected mice. Here, we performed a battery of in vivo studies demonstrating that the toxicity is compound- and disease- stage-dependent, and not predicted by behavioral or molecular measurements in uninfected animals. A panel of toxic ASOs all elicited a consistent transcriptomic response signature in prion-infected mice, which emerged over the course of 7 days post dose. This signature, driven chiefly by decreased expression of a specific set of astrocyte-expressed genes, was absent in uninfected mice receiving the same ASOs, was absent, less intense, and/or more transient in infected mice receiving tolerated ASOs, and was distinct from the transcriptomic effect of prion disease itself. Our data argue that the toxicity is an interaction between ASO and prion disease at high doses for specific compounds, and does not represent an exacerbation of ASO toxicity nor of prion disease.

title: Considerations of Gene Expression Analysis Methods for Gapmer Antisense Oligonucleotide-Treated Samples.
abstract: Probe-based PCR assays are commonly used to evaluate gene expression in antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-treated samples, but assay design and postextraction processing may introduce substantial measurement bias. We investigated workflow-dependent differences in measured knockdown across PCR-based and RNA-sequencing assays using an allele-specific gapmer ASO, targeting a linked single nucleotide polymorphism of a dominant-negative SPTAN1 variant. Exogenous ribonuclease H (RNase H) activity during reverse transcription or ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-depletion inflated apparent knockdown and reduced RNA-sequencing coverage at the ASO-binding site. In droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), allele-specific detection probes overlapping the ASO-binding site produced substantially greater apparent knockdown than nonoverlapping probes, particularly following workflows with active RNase H. Spike-in experiments showed that this bias was not reproduced by adding ASO to purified RNA before complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis or to cDNA before ddPCR, but emerged when ASO was present during rRNA depletion. Together, these findings show that exogenous RNase H activity during RNA processing and ASO-probe overlap can distort measurements of gapmer-mediated transcript reduction. Poly(A)-based RNA sequencing, reverse transcriptase with reduced RNase H activity, and nonoverlapping PCR detection probes can minimize measurement bias when evaluating gapmer ASO-mediated knockdown.

title: Improved Efficacy and Tolerability of Antisense Oligonucleotide with Guanidine-Bridged Nucleic Acid.
abstract: Guanidine-bridged nucleic acid (GuNA) is a bridged nucleic acid analog with high binding affinity toward complementary strands along with high nuclease resistance. GuNA has been developed to improve pharmacokinetics and safety profiles of phosphorothioate modified gapmers. Here, we evaluated antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) modified with combination of GuNA and 2'-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) and found that the dual-modification strategy could significantly improve knockdown activity in vitro and in vivo. Long-term efficacy evaluation showed that intracerebroventricularly administered GuNA-modified gapmers stayed active for over 24 weeks in mouse brain. Furthermore, we observed that GuNA-modified gapmers could evade lymphocyte-derived immune responses and kept ASO-induced toxicity in check. Taken together, the results of this study demonstrate that GuNA modification can improve the functional potential of ASOs, especially in the central nervous system.

title: Recombinant Fusion of Polyglutamic Acid Enhances Cell-Penetrating Peptide-Mediated CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery.
abstract: Genome editing has been revolutionized by Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology. However, efficient intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) remains a major challenge, particularly in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods. Integrating viral vectors carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas physical methods such as electroporation are not well suited for in vivo or clinically relevant applications. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a promising alternative for direct RNP delivery, although their efficiency is often limited by endosomal entrapment and limited cytosolic release. In this study, we developed two recombinant CPP-fused Cas9 proteins, polyglutamate (PE)-trans-activator of transcription (TAT)-nuclear localization signal (NLS)-Cas9 (PETATCas9) and TAT-NLS-Cas9 (TATCas9), designed to improve solubility, membrane penetration, RNP complex formation, and nuclear targeting. PE tag in PETATCas9 was introduced to optimize charge balance and reduce nonspecific electrostatic interactions between TAT and guide RNA (gRNA), thereby enhancing RNP stability and delivery performance. Both recombinant proteins were expressed, purified, and assembled with gRNA into functional RNP complexes for delivery into SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. The optimized CPP-Cas9 RNP system enabled efficient intracellular delivery and glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) gene editing in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings establish PETATCas9 as a scalable, transient, nonviral, and self-delivering RNP platform for CRISPR-based genome editing in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods.

title: USP22 is a novel vulnerability regulating MEIS1 protein abundance and gene transcription in KMT2Ar acute leukemia.
abstract: Patients with acute leukemias harboring translocations involving gene lysine methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A) have a poor prognosis due to chemotherapy resistance with rapid relapse following standard treatments. The resulting KMT2A fusion proteins dysregulate gene expression, leading to an upregulation of leukemogenic transcription factors such as HOXA9 and MEIS1, which drives leukemic transformation. Although menin inhibitors are proving to be promising new therapeutics for patients with KMT2A-rearranged (KMT2Ar) acute leukemia, resistance mechanisms have already been described and new therapeutic approaches for this patient subgroup must be identified. Here, a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen in a KMT2Ar B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia cell line identified the deubiquitinase ubiquitin-specific peptidase 22 (USP22) as a novel regulator of MEIS1 protein stability. USP22 is a member of the Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase multiprotein complex, which has crucial functions in shaping the chromatin landscape and modulating transcription. Genetic depletion of USP22 impaired cellular growth and proliferation in KMT2Ar acute leukemia models. Chromatin immunoprecipitation revealed cooperative binding between USP22 and MEIS1 at critical oncogenic target genes, suggesting that USP22 safeguards leukemogenic transcription by protecting MEIS1 from proteasomal degradation. Genetic or chemical inhibition of USP22 led to the polyubiquitination of MEIS1, resulting in proteasomal degradation and downregulation of the expression of target genes. Our study identifies USP22 as a novel regulator of MEIS1 protein stability that could potentially be exploited as a therapeutic target in the future in KMT2Ar leukemias.

title: Reduced SRSF1 expression correlates with LCK exon skipping and impaired Treg induction in immune thrombocytopenia.
abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by antibody-mediated platelet destruction and impaired regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, yet its molecular basis remains poorly defined. Here, we show that CD4+ naive T cells from patients with ITP exhibit diminished T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling and impaired in vitro Treg induction relative to healthy controls. RNA sequencing revealed widespread dysregulation of alternative splicing, most notably exon 8 skipping in LCK, a kinase central to TCR signaling and Treg differentiation. Using an LCK minigene combined with RNA pull-down mass spectrometry and RNA immunoprecipitation assays, we identified the splicing factor SRSF1 as a direct upstream regulator of LCK exon 8 skipping. Notably, SRSF1 expression was reduced in CD4+ naive T cells from patients with ITP, and its overexpression restored in vitro Treg induction capacity. Antisense oligonucleotide-mediated blockade of SRSF1 binding to LCK enhanced exon 8 skipping and attenuated TCR activation in Jurkat cells. Although murine Lck lacks the human-specific recursive splicing sites required for exon 8 exclusion, the adoptive transfer of CD4+ naive T cells expressing the exon 8-skipped murine Lck into CD61-knockout mice significantly reduced Treg proportions and platelet counts in an active ITP model. Mechanistically, Jurkat cells engineered to express only the exon 8-skipped LCK variant showed markedly reduced binding to ZAP70 and CD3ζ, which may partly account for the attenuated TCR signaling and downstream FOXP3 induction. Together, these findings define a novel SRSF1-LCK splicing axis that may regulate Treg development in ITP.

title: A phase 2a study with SPL84: A novel RNA-targeted approach to restore CFTR function in people with CF carrying the 3849+10 kb C→T mutation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The 3849+10 kb C→T mutation in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene leads to aberrant splicing and the inclusion of a cryptic exon harboring a premature stop codon, resulting in the production of non-functional CFTR protein. SPL84 is an inhaled antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) designed to correct CFTR splicing and restore functional CFTR expression in people with CF (pwCF) carrying this mutation.
METHODS: This Phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, multiple ascending dose study evaluated safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and exploratory efficacy of inhaled SPL84 in pwCF carrying the 3849+10 kb C→T mutation. Participants received once-weekly inhalations of SPL84 (25 or 50 mg) or placebo for 9 weeks. Exploratory efficacy measures included changes in ppFEV1, ppFEF25-75, and CFQ-R respiratory symptom score.
RESULTS: Seventeen participants were included in the analysis, with fifteen completing all treatments. SPL84 was well tolerated with no drug-related serious adverse events. Most adverse events were mild or moderate and consistent with the underlying CF disease. Improvements in lung function, defined as change from baseline in ppFEV1≥5, were observed in up to 70% of the treated participants per cohort, accompanied by improvement of additional efficacy outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Inhaled SPL84 demonstrated a favorable safety profile together with encouraging signals of clinical benefit in pwCF carrying the 3849+10 kb C→T mutation. These findings represent, to our knowledge, the first evidence of potential clinical benefit from a nucleic acid-based therapy targeting RNA in a pulmonary disease, supporting further evaluation of SPL84 as a mutation-specific, RNA-targeted treatment.

title: Muco-obstructive lung disease exhibits distinct hypoxic and inflammatory airway epithelial gene pathways.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intraluminal obstruction produces chronic airway epithelial hypoxia. We investigated how chronic airway epithelial hypoxia and inflammatory stimuli interact in human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cultures and resected human bronchiectatic lungs to produce an airway epithelial environment characteristic of muco-obstructive disease.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: HBE cultures were exposed to normoxia or hypoxia (1% O2) for 5 days, followed by administration of supernatants from cystic fibrosis (CF) lung-derived mucopurulent material (SMM) or PBS for 24 h. A reverse order protocol with SMM followed by hypoxia was also performed. Bulk RNA-sequencing and functional (Na+ transport) studies were performed. HIF1A and EPAS1-mediated transcriptional responses were characterised in CRISPR knockdown HBE cells. RNA in situ hybridisation studies of excised bronchiectatic lungs and bioinformatic analyses of published datasets tested for relevance of in vitro findings to in vivo conditions.
RESULTS: Hypoxia and SMM regulated largely separate airway epithelial transcriptional programmes regardless of treatment order. PTGS2 (COX-2), CCL20, MUC5B, and CXCL8 (IL-8) represented a small number of genes upregulated by both hypoxia and SMM. HIF1A knockdown and EPAS1 knockdown produced distinct, often opposing, effects on hypoxia-responsive pathways. HIF1A dominated upregulation of glycolytic pathway signalling. EPAS1 regulated genes that increase mucus concentration under hypoxia (e.g., SCNN1G). An EPAS1 inhibitor blocked hypoxia-induced upregulation of Na+ transport.
CONCLUSION: Chronic hypoxia and inflammation regulated distinct genes/pathways that combine to produce a complex diseased environment in muco-obstructed airway epithelia. HIF1A and EPAS1 regulated distinct hypoxia-induced transcriptional responses. EPAS1 inhibition may exhibit a favourable therapeutic ratio for treatment of muco-obstructive lung diseases.

title: Immortalisation of human airway epithelial cells for genome editing applications.
abstract:
AIM: In vitro air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures of human airway epithelial cells are widely used to study respiratory biology and disease, as they recapitulate key features of the pseudostratified airway epithelium and reduce reliance on animal models and repeated patient biopsies. However, the limited proliferative capacity of primary airway basal cells restricts long-term studies and genome editing. This study aimed to generate stable, immortalised human airway basal cell lines that retain differentiation capacity and support genetic manipulation.
METHODS: Human airway epithelial basal cells from bronchial and nasal origin were immortalised by lentiviral expression of human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) followed by polyclonal expansion. A panel of cell lines derived from three independent nasal donors was established. Differentiation capacity was assessed in ALI cultures and compared with primary airway epithelial cells. Suitability for genetic manipulation was evaluated using lentiviral overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout and knock-in strategies.
RESULTS: All immortalised cell lines displayed sustained proliferative capacity and efficiently differentiated into major airway epithelial cell types, including multiciliated and secretory cells. Differentiation patterns and functional characteristics closely resembled those of primary airway epithelial cultures. The cell lines supported efficient lentiviral transduction and CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, enabling stable gene overexpression, targeted gene disruption, and precise genomic modification.
CONCLUSIONS: hTERT-immortalised human airway basal cell lines preserve key features of primary airway epithelium while enabling long-term culture and versatile genome editing. This resource provides a robust platform for airway biology research, disease modelling, and therapeutic development.

title: From molecular pathways to nanocarrier design: a translational framework for lipid-based nanoparticles in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease, being a complicated neurodegenerative disoder affects cognitive as well as memory functions. Characterised by amyloid-β aggregation, along with tau hyperphosphorylation, and cholinergic dysfunction, this disease is also associated with oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. Conventional clinical interventions, like acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and novel monoclonal antibodies predominantly rely on symptomatic alleviation of symptoms. Nevertheless, these conventional treatments come across considerable constraints, like temporary effectiveness, lesser therapeutic reach due to the blood brain barrier, apart from additional adverse effects. To overcome these delivery obstacles and achieve intracellular targeting, lipid nanoparticles, such as liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, and drugs, that can effectively traverse biological barriers, and facilitate precise intracellular release. This review introduces a translational, pathway-integrated framework that connects key molecular mechanisms of the disease with rational design strategies of lipid nanocarriers. The review also illustrates how essential internal factors, such as lipid composition, ionizable lipid pKa, selection of helper lipids, PEG density, along with methods of endosomal escape, and the protein corona, affect brain targeting efficacy and toxicity. It further focuses on pathway-enforced nano lipidic therapeutic approaches, where nanocarrier design is tailored to cater to specific biological targets. Nano lipidic delivery of siRNA, miRNA, mRNA, monoclonal antibodies, and along with other neuroprotective agents has been emphasised. Additionally, advancements in surface functionalization, intranasal administration, as well as receptor-mediated transcytosis, and focused ultrasound-driven blood-brain barrier penetration have also been highlighted in this review. Therefore, it aims to bridge the gap between molecular pathology and formulation design through alignment of design principles that emphasize on nanocarrier properties and its relevance to disease-specific requirements, an approach that has never been comprehensively addressed in previous literature.Registration number of clinical trial: Not applicable.

title: Characterization of the organelle genomes of mycoheterotrophic Thismia angustimitra and evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Our knowledge about mitochondrial genome evolution in plants is lacking far behind our knowledge of plastome evolution. In heterotrophic plants, it is well-known that plastome degradation and reduced or lost photosynthesis go hand in hand, and there is little if any difference between plastome evolution in mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites. The mitochondrial genome appears less affected by a heterotrophic lifestyle, although exceptions occur. In contrast to plastome evolution, mitochondrial evolution may differ between mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites, in particular with regards to the occurrence of horizontal gene transfer. However, data from mycoheterotrophs are scarce, and complete mitogenomes are only known from three of ten clades.
RESULTS: Here we present data from the complete plastome and mitogenome from Thismia angustimitra, representing a fourth clade of mycoheterotrophs. The 18,215 bp plastome is much reduced and includes only few genes. The mitogenome has a multicircular structure consisting of 22 chromosomes with a total length of 422,400 bp. The gene content and the pattern of RNA editing are normal. The mitogenome includes only few repeats and recombinational activity is limited. A search for foreign DNA did not reveal any fungal sequences, the content of plastid DNA is low, but a large proportion of intergenic DNA shows similarity to distantly related angiosperms. Just a few plastid inserts appear to have originated through intracellular transfer, whereas others most likely stem from horizontal gene transfer. Synteny patterns of the intergenic sequences suggest that horizontal transfer may happen in either direction.
CONCLUSION: The highly reduced plastome of T. angustimitra fits completely the general picture of plastome degradation in heterotrophic plants. Whereas the mitogenome in many aspects appears unaffected by the lifestyle, the recombinational activity is unusually low. Surprisingly, we find evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer, indicating that this phenomenon may be more common among mycoheterotrophic plants than previously thought.

title: The advances and challenges of mRNA-LNP application in fields of hematology and oncology therapeutics.
abstract: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.

title: Innovations and emerging trends in adoptive cell therapies for solid tumors: engineering strategies and clinical translation.
abstract: Cancer remains a formidable challenge in global oncology, with conventional treatments often failing to achieve durable responses in advanced stages. Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), despite its revolutionary success in hematological malignancies, faces critical bottlenecks in solid tumors, including a hostile immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), restricted cellular trafficking, and the rapid onset of T-cell exhaustion. This review systematically explores the evolution of ACT platforms, ranging from foundational tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to precision-engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T and T-cell receptor (TCR)-T therapies. We highlight how innovative engineering strategies such as the integration of "armored" CARs, synthetic gene circuits, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing have been employed to enhance the persistence and polyfunctionality of effector cells. Beyond T-cell-centric approaches, we examine the emerging landscape of diverse immune effector cells, including CAR-natural killer (NK) cells, and CAR-macrophages (CAR-M), which offer unique advantages in antigen recognition and safety profiles. Furthermore, we detail the synergistic potential of multimodal combination regimens, where ACT is paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), localized radiotherapy, or nanotechnology-based delivery systems to dismantle TME barriers and achieve systemic anti-tumor immunity. By tracing the journey of therapeutic cells from ex vivo expansion to intratumoral infiltration and cytotoxicity, this review illuminates the molecular mechanisms governing therapeutic efficacy. Finally, we discuss the current clinical trial landscape, manufacturing hurdles, and the regulatory pathways essential for transitioning these sophisticated cellular products from bench to bedside.

title: RNA N4-acetylcytidine modification in health and cancer: molecular mechanisms, cellular plasticity, and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: N⁴-acetylcytidine (ac⁴C) is an evolutionarily conserved RNA modification that was initially identified in transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA). Increasing evidence has subsequently expanded its functional landscape to messenger RNA (mRNA) and multiple classes of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). As the best-characterized ac⁴C writer in mammals, N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10) orchestrates RNA structure, stability, processing, and translation, thereby governing fundamental physiological processes, including ribosome biogenesis, translational fidelity, proteostasis, cell fate determination, hematopoiesis, reproduction, and embryonic development. Cancer cells exploit the NAT10-ac⁴C axis to selectively stabilize or enhance the translation of oncogenic transcripts, reprogram tRNA and rRNA-dependent translational programs, and cooperate with non-canonical NAT10 functions, including R-loop regulation, protein acetylation, and RNA binding, to sustain uncontrolled proliferation, cancer stemness, metabolic reprogramming, DNA damage repair, invasion and metastasis, resistance to regulated cell death, and immune evasion. Consequently, the NAT10-ac⁴C axis has emerged as a central molecular hub linking RNA fate, the translational machinery, and adaptive tumor reprogramming. Therefore, phenotypes resulting from NAT10 depletion or pharmacological inhibition should not be indiscriminately attributed to reduced ac⁴C deposition in the absence of catalytic rescue experiments and site-specific validation. In this Review, we comprehensively summarize the molecular basis of ac⁴C, its substrate landscape, catalytic mechanisms, and determinants of substrate selectivity, as well as its physiological functions in normal tissues and pathological roles in cancer. We further compare the shared and context-dependent mechanisms by which the NAT10-ac⁴C axis drives malignant progression and therapeutic resistance across diverse cancer types. In addition, we critically evaluate current ac⁴C detection technologies, the hierarchy of substrate evidence, NAT10 inhibitors, targeted protein degradation strategies, rational combination therapies, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and therapeutic windows. Finally, we propose that future research should move beyond broad NAT10 inhibition toward identifying tumor-specific NAT10 dependencies and selectively disrupting oncogenic NAT10-RNA regulatory circuits through high-confidence ac⁴C atlases, site-specific RNA editing technologies, and precision delivery strategies.

title: CRISPR-enhanced microalgae for carbon sequestration and carotenoid production: opportunities and fundamental constraints.
abstract: Microalgae represent a promising biological platform for CO2 sequestration and the sustainable production of high-value metabolites, particularly carotenoids such as lutein and astaxanthin. However, industrial performance remains constrained by low carbon conversion efficiency, reduced photosynthetic performance, and competing metabolic fluxes that limit product yield. The emergence of CRISPR/Cas-based genome engineering has enabled precise and multiplexed modulation of microalgal metabolic networks, offering new opportunities to overcome these limitations. This review critically evaluates CRISPR-enabled engineering strategies for improving carbon assimilation, photosynthetic efficiency, and carotenoid biosynthesis in microalgae. We discuss advances in transformation and delivery systems across diverse species, CRISPR interference, CRISPR activation, and multiplexed pathway rewiring. Targeted modifications of light-harvesting complexes, carbon concentrating mechanisms, and key carotenoid biosynthetic enzymes are discussed with their reported impacts on biomass accumulation, CO2 fixation, and pigment productivity. Emerging evidence indicates that while pathway-specific genetic interventions can significantly enhance metabolic accumulation, these improvements are often not proportionally reflected in whole-cell carbon fixation, revealing underlying constraints imposed by energy allocation, redox balance, and regulatory network coupling. Finally, we highlight the potential of synthetic regulatory circuits and programmable transcriptional control as next-generation tools for dynamic regulation of metabolic fluxes rather than static gene-level modifications. By integrating molecular engineering strategies with physiological and system-level constraints, this review provides a critical framework for developing robust microalgal cell factories for sustainable bioproduction and climate mitigation.

title: Antifungal resistance landscapes in major fungal pathogens in Zhejiang, China.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal infections caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and other pathogenic fungi represent a major global health threat, with treatment increasingly complicated by the emergence of antifungal drug resistance. Azole antifungals serve as the first-line therapy for aspergillosis, but resistance rates vary substantially across geographical regions. This study aimed to characterize the antifungal resistance landscape among clinical fungal isolates from Hangzhou and Yiwu cities in Zhejiang Province, Eastern China, and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus.
RESULTS: We analyzed 110 Aspergillus clinical isolates for antifungal susceptibility. Among A. fumigatus strains, 8.6% exhibited azole resistance, with half of these harboring the tandem repeat mutation TR34/L98H in the cyp51A gene. One resistant strain carried the TR46/Y121F/T289A mutation combination. Minimum inhibitory concentration testing revealed that 8.6% of A. fumigatus isolates were resistant to amphotericin B We identified one resistant isolate without known resistance mutations and characterized it through whole-genome sequencing and transcriptomic analysis. Novel mutations S437F in cyp51A and P298T in hmg1 were discovered; however, functional validation using CRISPR-Cas9 demonstrated these mutations do not directly confer resistance. Instead, transcriptomic profiling revealed significant upregulation of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway genes and efflux transporter genes, suggesting alternative resistance mechanisms. Among non-A. fumigatus species, all A. niger isolates displayed resistance to itraconazole and posaconazole.
CONCLUSIONS: This comprehensive regional surveillance reveals concerning patterns of antifungal resistance among major human pathogenic fungi in Zhejiang Province, China. The identification of both classical resistance mutations and novel transcription-mediated resistance mechanisms highlights the complex and evolving nature of antifungal resistance. These findings emphasize the critical need for continued surveillance programs and rapid resistance detection methods to inform clinical treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes.

title: Advances in therapeutic oligonucleotide conjugates.
abstract: Oligonucleotide therapeutics (ONTs) have revolutionized the medical landscape by enabling the precise modulation of genetic pathways. This perspective highlights the major conjugation strategies for ONTs, using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) as representative modalities. We describe diverse classes of targeting ligands, including small molecules, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs), antibodies, and aptamers. For example, triantennary N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) conjugation has enabled a number of approved oligonucleotide therapeutics. Meanwhile, other emerging conjugation technologies have expanded oligonucleotide delivery to extrahepatic tissues to address a broader range of diseases. We further summarize the clinical translation of these delivery platforms, highlighting approved therapeutics alongside emerging clinical candidates. Finally, we provide an outlook on challenges and opportunities for the next generation of oligonucleotide therapeutics.
