title: Cancer nanomedicine and RNA/Lipid nanoparticle platforms in oncology: developmental evolution, translational barriers, and precision-therapy opportunities.
abstract: Nanomedicine has become an important translational platform in oncology by enabling altered pharmacokinetics, controlled exposure, reduced systemic toxicity, intracellular delivery of nucleic acids, and improved handling of complex therapeutic payloads. Early cancer nanomedicines, including pegylated liposomal cytotoxics and albumin-bound drug products, demonstrated that nanoscale formulation design could improve the clinical utility of established anticancer agents. More recently, lipid nanoparticles, RNA therapeutics, individualized neoantigen vaccines, gene-regulatory approaches, and immune-modulating delivery systems have expanded the role of nanoparticles from passive drug carriers to programmable oncology platforms. This narrative review examines the developmental evolution of cancer-focused pharmaceutical nanoparticles, with emphasis on liposomes, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), albumin-bound systems, polymeric particles, polymeric micelles, nanocrystals, nanoemulsions, solid lipid nanoparticles, inorganic particles, extracellular vesicles, and hybrid delivery technologies. Each platform class is treated systematically, covering representative approved products, formulation characteristics, route of administration, clinical evidence, and the specific development risks that limit it. There view connects platform design with oncology-specific barriers, including tumor heterogeneity, variable enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effects, dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, mononuclear phagocyte clearance, protein-corona formation, endosomal escape, immune activation, and the difficulty of translating animal tumor models into clinical benefit. These barriers are organized as a sequential delivery cascade, and the behavior of each platform class is compared step by step rather than described as a set of universal phenomena. Nanoparticle candidates that accumulated well in preclinical tumors but failed in clinical trials are examined alongside approved products, because the contrast between the two is where most of the transferable lessons sit. A product-development perspective is used to discuss critical quality attributes (CQAs), manufacturing scalability, potency testing, sterility strategy, stability, release methods, regulatory expectations, commercial feasibility, and clinical differentiation. A development-to-translation framework is proposed for comparing cancer nanomedicine platforms across formulation maturity, analytical maturity, manufacturing maturity, biological rationale, clinical evidence, regulatory readiness, and commercial feasibility; regulatory and commercial maturity are scored separately, the criteria behind each level are defined explicitly, and the resulting rankings are presented as a heuristic aid to discussion rather than a validated quantitative metric. Future progress in oncology nanomedicine will depend not only on novel materials or targeting claims, but also on disciplined product design, biologically meaningful potency assays, scalable manufacturing, patient-selection strategies, and clear integration with precision oncology.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated transcription factor EB mRNA delivery for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent disorder characterized by excessive hepatic lipid accumulation, frequently progressing to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Transcription factor EB (TFEB) coordinates lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy, and lipid catabolism, and therefore represents a potential therapeutic target; however, safe and direct strategies for selectively enhancing hepatic TFEB activity remain limited. Here, liver-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) were developed to deliver mRNAs encoding wild-type TFEB or the constitutively active TFEB S211A mutant, and their efficacy was evaluated in cellular and choline-deficient, L-amino acid-defined high-fat diet (CDAHFD)-induced mouse models of MASLD. LNP-mediated delivery increased hepatic TFEB expression, enhanced autophagic flux, and reprogrammed metabolic pathways toward fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A and ACOX1) while suppressing the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g., FASN, ACC, and SREBP1). Consequently, targeted TFEB mRNA therapy significantly reduced hepatic triglyceride content, attenuated steatosis, lowered MASLD activity scores, and decreased fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling, ChIP-qPCR, promoter-reporter assays, and targeted knockdown models indicated that TFEB exerts its protective effects against lipid accumulation at least partly by transcriptionally activating the fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings establish LNP-mediated TFEB mRNA delivery as a useful preclinical approach for investigating hepatic biology and provide a targeted, transient, and non-integrating genetic strategy with potential for the treatment of MASLD.

title: A patient-derived missense mouse model of Kabuki syndrome 1.
abstract: Kabuki syndrome type 1 (KS1) is a rare cause of intellectual disability resulting from heterozygous pathogenic variants in the gene encoding the histone methyltransferase KMT2D. A previously established loss-of-function mouse model of KS1 exhibits key phenotypic features, and therapeutic trials in this mouse model suggest postnatal malleability of neurological symptoms. However, 15-30% of individuals with KS1 carry missense variants. To investigate whether missense variants lead to similar phenotypic presentation in mice, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce the KS1 patient variant R5179H, corresponding to R5230H in mice, into C57BL/6NTac animals. Computational and in vitro testing suggested that the R5230H variant does not impair protein stability or enzyme function of KMT2D. Despite a distinct mechanistic basis, our new mouse model (Kmt2d+/R5230H) recapitulated most phenotypes of our prior loss-of-function model, including growth deficiency, craniofacial anomalies and IgA deficiency, but not altered neurological function. Kmt2d+/R5230H mice showed perinatal lethality and a high frequency of unilateral kidney agenesis, a novel phenotype in KS1 mouse models. Kmt2d+/R5230H mice provide a unique opportunity to understand the impact of missense variants on KMT2D function and uncover developmental and perinatal abnormalities in KS1.

title: Human-relevant disease models to accelerate the development of nucleic acid-based therapies and other advanced therapeutics.
abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

title: Diverse RNA Editing Systems Across Heterolobosea (Discoba).
abstract: Mitochondrial RNA editing events were previously reported in only three unrelated species within the phylum Heterolobosea (Discoba): Naegleria gruberi and Acrasis kona (which performs C-to-U substitutions) and Pharyngomonadida sp. BB2 (which inserts single nucleotides by a yet unknown mechanism). We present novel high-quality genome assemblies obtained via a combination of whole-genome and targeted sequencing approaches and predicted proteomes for two species, Paravahlkampfia ustiana and Heteramoeba clara, representing an understudied clade of the phylum. Surprisingly, we discovered RNA editing events of C-to-U substitutions and mononucleotide insertions co-existing in the mitochondria of P. ustiana, while the two systems were both absent in H. clara. In addition, P. ustiana also exhibits A-to-I editing sites in rRNA transcripts encoded in multicopy circular rDNA plasmids. RNA editing events in P. ustiana were verified by proteomics, Illumina short RNA reads, ONT long cDNA and direct RNA reads. We elaborate on the potential mechanisms of mitochondrial insertional editing by investigating several aspects of the RNA transcription machinery and base modifications in template DNA and mRNA products. We report additional cases of C-to-U RNA editing in other species of Heterolobosea and explore the distribution of various putative components of the C-to-U editosome, including the DYW domain-containing pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, across the phylum expanding the understanding of the evolutionary dynamics underlying this phenomenon, which remains understudied outside land plants. The comparative analysis of available sequence data from Heterolobosea revealed that C-to-U RNA editing was acquired relatively deep in the evolution of Heterolobosea and subsequently underwent repeated losses.

title: Improving the dynamic range of a trimethoprim-responsive self-amplifying RNA.
abstract: Self-amplifying mRNA (SAM) is a potential platform for protein replacement, as it enables recipients to transiently produce a therapeutic protein for 4-8 weeks. To obtain external control over the level and duration of protein expression, synthetic SAM constructs that switch OFF in the presence of a small molecule such as trimethoprim (TMP) have been developed in the past. Here, we increase the ON-state protein expression of such a TMP-responsive SAM by fusing the effector protein L7Ae to a TMP-responsive destabilizing domain (DD) on both terminals. We also lower the OFF-state by adding a duplicate of the SAM 3'UTR downstream from the DD-L7Ae subgenomic ORF. We demonstrate that fusing two DDs to L7Ae has a beneficial effect on the response rate and level of protein production after removal or addition of TMP. We further demonstrate that overexpression of DD-L7Ae results in microscopic abnormalities. These insights are implemented in a mechanistic model, and further improvements of the platform are highlighted.

title: Cellular signal-responsive m5C editing by an inducible split CRISPR platform.
abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

title: PNLDC1 deadenylase affects translational rate and cell proliferation in mESCs.
abstract: PNLDC1 is a member of the DEDD deadenylases, known for its specificity in poly(A) tail removal during mRNA turnover. While initially characterized for its function in pre-piRNA trimming critical to spermatogenesis and transposon silencing, its broader deadenylase activity which is especially pronounced during early development and silenced during differentiation, remains poorly understood. In this study, we mapped the epigenetic regulation of Pnldc1 during mESC differentiation, uncovering its promoter methylation pattern associated with transcriptional repression. Pnldc1-knockout mESC models established via CRISPR/Cas9 were shown to retain viability and pluripotency. RNA-seq and subsequent polysome profiling revealed that Pnldc1 deficiency leads to the downregulation of gene networks involved in translation and a lower overall translational rate. Notably, PNLDC1 has been linked to epigenetic changes in various cancers and is associated with oncogenic signaling pathways. Using a homology model based on the related PARN deadenylase, we conducted virtual screening of compound libraries and selected 12 candidates for experimental testing. Experimental validation revealed that two compounds significantly impacted genes involved in stress response and signal transduction, while also suppressing aberrant proliferation. These findings highlight PNLDC1's role in regulating mRNA stability during differentiation and proliferation and as a candidate for targeted therapeutic intervention.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotides with 5'-decoy technology triggers nonsense-mediated decay of SCN9A to elicit long-lasting analgesia.
abstract: The voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7 (SCN9A) is a genetically validated target for pain therapy, but achieving therapeutic isoform selectivity remains a formidable challenge for small-molecule inhibitors. Here, we overcome this bottleneck through a highly selective RNA-targeted strategy that dictates SCN9A alternative splicing. We first identified ASO50 as the most potent baseline candidate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO). Subsequent 5'-decoy (5D) sequence screening yielded an upgraded candidate, L9C-ASO50, which is engineered to competitively intercept U1 snRNA, achieving a cooperative spatial hindrance that robustly suppresses exon 5 recognition. This targeted exon exclusion introduces a frameshift that triggers robust, obligate transcript clearance via the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, ensuring complete functional silencing without cross-reacting with homologous NaV channels. Mechanistically, we define the underlying cis-trans regulatory architecture, revealing a homeostatic tug-of-war where the RNA-binding protein ELAVL2 enforces exon inclusion, paradoxically antagonized by the canonical SR protein family. Crucially, CNS-restricted delivery of L9C-ASO50 produces profound and sustained mechanical and thermal analgesia. These findings establish splice-modulated transcript degradation as a viable therapeutic paradigm for chronic pain and provide a broadly applicable blueprint for engineering targeted RNA therapeutics.

title: Detection of the RNA-Editing Enzyme ADARB1 in Primary Auditory Neurons and Anti-ADARB1 Immunofluorescence as a Means for Automated Counting.
abstract: Spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the primary auditory afferents in the inner ear, are vulnerable to degeneration from neuropathies, concussion, and aging, among other causes. Accurate quantification of SGNs is critical for assessing degeneration and therapeutic interventions, but manual counting is arduous due to dense cellular crowding and unreliable nuclear markers. Because SGNs receive input from GluA2-containing AMPA receptors, the transcripts for which must be RNA-edited for calcium impermeability, we hypothesized that SGNs express high levels of the RNA-editing enzyme ADARB1. Here, we confirm enriched expression of Adarb1 transcripts in SGNs and show that anti-ADARB1 antibodies robustly label the nuclei of type I and type II SGNs from young and aged mice, adult macaques, and adult humans. Neuronal versus glial specificity was confirmed using antibodies against neurofilament heavy chain (NFH), human antigen D (HuD), GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3), and SRY-box 2 (SOX2). A blinded investigator manually counted mouse SGNs via NFH, and these were compared to automated counts of ADARB1-positive nuclei using the analyze particles function in ImageJ. A concordance correlation coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated strong agreement between the manual and automated counts. Together, these results suggest broad utility of ADARB1 immunolabeling for automated counts of SGNs across species.

title: Deficiency of placental GDF15 causes fetal growth restriction by inhibiting fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 axis.
abstract: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, we show that growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) levels are significantly reduced in the placenta and fetal circulation in mouse and pig FGR models and correlate positively with fetal weight. Placenta-specific GDF15 deficiency causes FGR, while placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA delivery through targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) effectively alleviates FGR. Mechanistically, placental GDF15 is a major contributor to the fetal circulating GDF15 pool and enters the fetal compartment, where it activates the hepatic STAT3 signaling pathway to stimulate IGF2 production during pregnancy. Placental GDF15 deficiency decreases hepatic STAT3 phosphorylation and IGF2 levels in fetuses. Inhibition of STAT3 in primary mouse fetal hepatocytes blocks GDF15-induced IGF2 upregulation. Placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA-LNP administration rescues the decreased hepatic p-STAT3 and IGF2 levels in FGR fetuses. Collectively, our findings identify a placenta-fetal liver metabolic axis where placental GDF15 promotes fetal growth by activating the fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 pathway, revealing a potential therapeutic target for FGR.

title: Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis.
abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

title: Unveiling the functional landscape of A-to-I RNA editing associated with Marek's disease in chickens.
abstract: Genetic improvement of disease resistance against viral infections represents a longstanding and formidable challenge in animal breeding. The antiviral innate immune response is highly regulated at the RNA level, especially through RNA modifications. Adenosine-to-Inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing modifies the mRNA sequence. Growing evidence shows that this type of RNA editing plays a key role in mediating cellular responses to viral infections and disease resistance. However, the role of RNA editing in cellular response to MD remains unclear. In this study, we examined A-to-I editing in CD4+ T cells during Marek's disease virus (MDV) infection. By comparing MD-resistant and susceptible chicken lines, we identified 642 A-to-I RNA editing events in CD4+ T cells, most of which were located within repeat elements, particularly in the CR1 family. We observed differences in RNA editing levels and counts between the two chicken lines with different infection statuses, indicating distinct editing patterns across genetic backgrounds and infection states. Additionally, ADAR (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA) expression was correlated with RNA editing frequency. We identified 21 RNA editing sites (RESs) associated with gene expression and 42, 14, and 38 RESs with predicted effects on amino acid sequences, alternative splicing, and miRNA-target binding, respectively. A comparative analysis revealed 131 group-specific RESs and 21 RESs shared across groups. Functional enrichment analysis of genes associated with group-specific RESs highlighted several terms related to MD resistance, including the MHC class I protein complex in non-infected MD-resistant birds. Significantly, we identified two L63-specific candidate RNA editing sites, chr6:26,600,122 in MXI1 and chr16:1,716,632 in MHCY57, which were predicted to affect gga-miR-1759-3p binding and amino acid sequence, respectively. Our findings reveal the landscape of A-to-I RNA editing in CD4 ⁺ T cells during MDV infection and provide new insights into its potential association with immune regulation and MD resistance.

title: Genetic background determines allele-specific Pfkelch13- mediated artemisinin tolerance and persistence in Plasmodium falciparum.
abstract: Artemisinin-based combination therapies are the frontline treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria, but their efficacy is threatened by Artemisinin partial resistance (ART R ). ART R in Plasmodium falciparum is mediated by Pfkelch13 ( k13 ) mutations but remains rare in West Africa. A critical question is whether short-term drug survival intrinsically predicts long-term evolutionary persistence. Here, using CRISPR-Cas9 editing, and nanopore-assisted allele tracking in a contemporary Senegalese isolate, we evaluated ART R receptivity using the ring-stage survival assay (RSA), a proxy for clinical resistance. We demonstrate that ART R survival and drug-free persistence are biologically separable traits. While the WHO-validated Asian I543T mutation conferred the RSA phenotype, it was rapidly counter-selected during drug-free growth. In contrast, emerging African alleles (R561H, M579I) and a regional novel variant (C473S) establish stable resistance without a competitive penalty. These findings reveal that a parasite's genetic background acts as a strict evolutionary filter, uncoupling short-term tolerance from long-term persistence and establishing that genomic context determines allele-specific resistance trajectories.

title: Research Progress of Stem Cell Therapy for Premature Ovarian Insufficiency.
abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a heterogeneous reproductive and endocrine disorder characterized by impaired ovarian function before the age of 40 years. Conventional management, particularly hormone therapy, addresses hypoestrogenic symptoms and long-term health risks but does not reliably restore endogenous ovarian activity or fertility. Stem cell-based strategies have therefore attracted considerable interest because of their potential paracrine, immunomodulatory, anti-apoptotic, angiogenic, and microenvironment-remodeling effects. This review summarizes current evidence on stem cell sources, therapeutic mechanisms, preclinical models, clinical studies, extracellular vesicle-based approaches, biomaterials, gene-editing strategies, and translational challenges in POI. Particular emphasis is placed on the distinction between mechanistic and animal evidence, uncontrolled or pilot human studies, and controlled clinical evidence. Across preclinical models, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) frequently improve ovarian histology, hormone profiles, follicular parameters, and reproductive performance; however, these findings cannot be assumed to represent restoration of ovarian reserve or fertility in humans. Clinical evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from small non-randomized studies, with outcomes ranging from menstrual recovery and changes in AMH, FSH, estradiol, or antral follicle count to a small number of reported pregnancies. These surrogate changes should be distinguished from clinically meaningful endpoints such as ovulation, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth. Emerging approaches involving extracellular vesicles, biomaterials, and gene editing may improve cell retention or therapeutic potency, but most remain preclinical or early translational strategies. Overall, stem cell therapy should currently be regarded as an investigational approach for POI. Progress toward clinical translation will require standardized cell products, clearly defined dosing and administration routes, appropriate comparator groups, clinically meaningful reproductive endpoints, rigorous long-term safety surveillance, and adequately powered controlled trials.

title: Potential Therapeutic Applications of Spherical Nucleic Acids (SNAs) in Cancer: Key Observations and Insights.
abstract: Spherical nucleic acids (SNAs) are a unique class of nucleic acid nanotherapeutics characterized by densely packed, radially arranged oligonucleotides surrounding a nanoparticle or molecular core, or core-free nanoscale structures. Compared with conventional linear nucleic acids, SNAs exhibit excellent cellular uptake, resistance to nuclease degradation, and efficient target recognition without the help of transfection agents. This review summarizes SNAs' structural diversity, design principles, and the multiscale delivery barriers they encounter. We mainly focus on liposomal SNAs (LSNAs) as programmable platforms for cancer immunotherapy. We emphasize how lipid chemistry, membrane architecture, and anchor stability control lymphoid distribution, immune-cell uptake, antigen presentation, and strong antitumor immunity, rather than seeing lipids as inert carriers. Furthermore, we also discuss current developments in gene silencing, CRISPR-based genome editing, and stimulus-responsive multimodal therapies, highlighting the significant therapeutic advancements of SNAs like clinical trial NU-0129 and LSNAs like cavrotolimod. Finally, we describe present translational obstacles and potential prospects by using SNAs as next-generation precision immunotherapeutics.

title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Brain-Targeted Drug Delivery for Methamphetamine Use Disorder: Advances, Challenges and Translational Perspectives.
abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) poses a significant global health challenge, lacking FDA-approved pharmacotherapies. Despite extensive exploration of therapeutic targets and interventions, effective treatment remains scarce due to challenges in delivering therapeutic agents to relevant brain regions at effective concentrations. Nanoparticle-mediated delivery offers a promising approach for transporting various therapeutic cargos to the central nervous system, including small molecules, nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and gene-editing systems. However, the application of nanomedicine strategies in addressing the unique pathophysiological characteristics of MUD has not been systematically assessed. This review presents a problem-focused analysis of how lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, biological, and hybrid nanocarriers tackle successive delivery obstacles such as systemic stability, blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, brain region-specific distribution, and controlled release of intracellular cargo. We compare preclinical nanotherapeutic approaches encompassing small-molecule neuroprotective agents, anti-METH vaccines, gene-silencing RNAs, neurotrophic proteins, and emerging gene-editing methods, outlining their respective benefits, limitations, and design considerations. Additionally, we explore key factors influencing nanomedicine performance in MUD, including protein corona formation, the impact of METH-related BBB dysfunction and neuroinflammation on nanoparticle distribution, and the disparity between acute animal models and chronic human MUD with relapse tendencies. In conclusion, we present a systematic framework for aligning nanocarrier characteristics with distinct delivery obstacles and therapeutic needs. We also emphasize forthcoming avenues such as disease-triggered nanocarriers, targeted delivery to specific regions, combined nanomedical approaches, theranostic strategies, and standardized assessments of biodistribution, effectiveness, safety, and translational potential.

title: Nanotechnology-Enabled Immunotherapy for Colorectal Cancer: Overcoming the "Cold" Tumor Microenvironment in Microsatellite-Stable Disease.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the management of mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the ~95% of patients with mismatch repair-proficient/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) disease derive little benefit owing to an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), poor T-cell infiltration, myeloid dominance, TGF-β-enriched stroma, and the systemically immunosuppressive milieu imposed by hepatic metastases. Clinically tested combinations-multikinase inhibitor plus anti-PD-1, Fc-enhanced dual checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy- or antiangiogenic-ICI regimens-have so far produced modest, largely non-durable response rates that are further attenuated in liver-metastatic disease, motivating approaches that pharmacologically remodel the TME rather than only release checkpoint restraint.
OBJECTIVE: To provide an evidence-stratified synthesis of nanotechnology-enabled immunotherapy in CRC that explicitly separates (a) clinically established evidence, (b) strategies under early-phase clinical investigation, and (c) concepts that remain preclinical or are extrapolated from other tumor types, and to derive from this appraisal a biomarker-enriched translational research agenda.
METHODS: Narrative, integrative (non-systematic) review. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ASCO/ESMO/AACR proceedings were searched from January 2010 through April 2026. Each strategy was appraised according to the highest available level of evidence, the tumor type and model system in which the evidence was generated, and its demonstrated CRC specificity.
RESULTS: In current clinical practice, nanomedicine in CRC is essentially limited to nanoparticle-formulated cytotoxics exploited for pharmacokinetic advantage (e.g. liposomal irinotecan), whereas nano-enabled immunotherapy is confined to a small number of early-phase trials-most notably lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in ctDNA-positive resected CRC and hafnium-oxide nanoparticle radioenhancers-none of which has yet demonstrated a progression-free or overall survival benefit in MSS CRC. Against this background we critically appraise six classes of strategy: (i) LNP-based mRNA neoantigen vaccines; (ii) polymeric and inorganic nanocarriers for STING and TLR agonists; (iii) tumor-associated macrophage-repolarizing nanoparticles; (iv) nano-radiosensitizers and photothermal/photodynamic platforms priming immunogenic cell death; (v) nano-formulated checkpoint inhibitor delivery; and (vi) locoregional nano-strategies directed at hepatic metastasis-specific immunosuppression. For categories (ii)-(vi) the supporting evidence is predominantly murine (largely subcutaneous CT26/MC38 models) or extrapolated from immunologically "hot" tumors such as melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer, in which both the underlying biology and the checkpoint backbone differ materially from MSS CRC. Recurrent translational barriers include low, highly heterogeneous nanoparticle accumulation in human tumors, dense TGF-β-rich stroma and elevated interstitial pressure, mononuclear phagocyte system clearance, liver-metastasis-specific tolerance that subcutaneous models do not reproduce, unresolved manufacturing/CMC and regulatory pathways, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers of intratumoral immune conversion.
CONCLUSION: Nanotechnology offers a mechanistically coherent and experimentally testable-but at present clinically unproven-set of strategies for converting "cold" MSS CRC into immune-responsive disease. We therefore position nano-enabled immunotherapy as a research priority rather than an imminent standard of care, and argue that its clinical value can only be established through biomarker-enriched, paired-biopsy early-phase trials with pharmacodynamic endpoints of immune conversion and prospective stratification by metastatic site (particularly hepatic involvement) and consensus molecular subtype.
LIMITATIONS: This is a narrative rather than systematic review; it is therefore subject to selection and publication bias, and much of the evidence synthesized is preclinical and of limited direct translational certainty.

title: Sonodynamic Therapy in Periodontitis: From Mechanisms to Biomaterial-Based Innovations.
abstract: Periodontitis is a common chronic inflammatory disease driven by pathogenic biofilms, leading to progressive periodontal tissue destruction and systemic health risks. Conventional therapies often fail to eradicate biofilms in deep periodontal pockets, promote antimicrobial resistance and offer limited regenerative potential. Although SDT has emerged as a promising alternative, its clinical efficacy is constrained by several material- and microenvironment-related barriers that have not been systematically addressed in previous reviews. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) employs low-intensity ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inducing mechanical disruption of biofilms, with advantages of deep tissue penetration, broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and low risk of resistance. Nevertheless, conventional sonosensitizers often exhibit poor water solubility, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and suboptimal ROS generation, while hypoxia, continuous fluid turnover, and mechanical disturbance within periodontal pockets further compromise local retention and therapeutic efficacy. Advances in biomaterials address these barriers by engineering high-performance sonosensitizers to enhance ROS efficiency, developing delivery systems to improve solubility and prolonged retention and integrating multimodal antibacterial and regenerative functions. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of SDT with recent advances in sonosensitizer engineering, local delivery platforms, synergistic therapies, and multifunctional biomaterials, thereby linking antimicrobial performance to periodontal tissue regeneration. We further identify hypoxia, delivery efficiency, biosafety and the lack of standardized evaluation as key translational challenges, and propose future directions including AI-guided sonosensitizer design, precision delivery systems, and CRISPR-assisted antimicrobial combination strategies to accelerate the clinical translation of SDT for periodontitis management.

title: The "Invisible Killer" of Neurodegeneration: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Disorders, Mechanisms, Emerging Pathways and Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) place substantial burden on global public health. Mounting evidence identifies mitochondrial dysfunction as a central contributor to neuronal damage and progressive brain functional decline. As a narrative review, this work aims to dissect mitochondrial‑associated pathological features across these major neurodegenerative disorders, summarize under‑recognized emerging mechanisms, and highlight translational bottlenecks for mitochondrial‑targeted therapies. Mitochondria sustain neuronal survival by mediating oxidative‑phosphorylation‑driven energy production, biomolecule biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, and apoptotic regulation. In PD, aggregated α‑synuclein (α‑syn) damages respiratory‑chain complex I, perturbs mitochondrial dynamics and blocks PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy. In AD, amyloid‑β together with hyper‑phosphorylated tau (p-Tau) impairs respiratory complex activity, axonal mitochondrial trafficking and mitophagic clearance. Mutant huntingtin induces multiple mitochondrial lesions in HD, while inflammation‑triggered oxidative stress secondarily compromises mitochondrial function in MS. Pathogenic mutations in ALS disrupt respiratory‑chain assembly, mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy. Beyond classic mitochondrial defects including respiratory‑chain impairment, dynamic imbalance and defective mitophagy, emerging mechanisms such as mitocytosis, mitochondrial aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (mt‑aaRS) dysfunction and mitochondria‑associated membrane (MAM) disruption are discussed. Mitochondrial dysfunction drives neurodegeneration via energy exhaustion, aggravated oxidative stress, pathological protein aggregation and excessive neuronal apoptosis. We further recapitulate mitochondrial‑oriented therapeutic approaches including small‑molecule regulators, mitophagy activators, mitochondrial biogenesis promoters, gene‑editing strategies and mitochondrial transplantation. Notable translational obstacles remain, including limited blood‑brain‑barrier penetration of candidate drugs, narrow therapeutic time‑window post‑symptom onset, and prominent disease heterogeneity. By synthesizing basic experimental findings and pre‑clinical and clinical trial progress, this review provides updated insights into the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases and facilitates the development of precise mitochondrial‑targeted therapeutic regimens.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-based Genome Editing in Inherited Diseases: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Advances, Safety and Clinical Translation.
abstract: Gene therapy has transformed modern biomedical research by enabling curative strategies that target the molecular basis of disease. Among genome-editing technologies, the CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a versatile and efficient platform due to its programmability, simplicity, and precision. This review summarizes the evolution of gene therapy and highlights the therapeutic potential of CRISPR-based genome editing. CRISPR/Cas9 has demonstrated significant potential in correcting disease-causing mutations across multiple inherited disorders, including sickle cell disease, β- thalassemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, phenylketonuria, muscular dystrophies, and cystic fibrosis. Emerging technologies such as base editing and prime editing further improved editing precision and reduced unintended genomic alterations. However, challenges including off-target effects, DNA repair pathway bias, immune responses, and vector-associated toxicities remain major limitations. The review highlights the rapid progress of CRISPR-mediated therapeutics and emphasizes the importance of improving editing accuracy, delivery efficiency, and long-term safety. Advances in vector engineering and genome-editing platforms are expected to overcome current technical and ethical barriers, facilitating broader clinical applications. CRISPR/Cas9 and related genome- editing technologies represent promising disease-modifying and potentially curative therapeutic approaches. Continued optimization of precision, safety, and delivery systems will be essential for successful translation into routine clinical practice.

title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 Rnps Into Cells.
abstract: The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPRassociated protein 9 (Cas9) system has revolutionized genome editing through its precision, simplicity, and programmability. The clinical translation of CRISPR/Cas9 Ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) remains constrained by major delivery challenges, including large molecular size, instability in biological fluids, and limited cellular penetration. Nanoparticle-mediated, non-viral delivery systems have emerged as a compelling strategy to overcome these barriers by providing targeted, transient, and biocompatible transport of Cas9 RNPs into cells. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in lipid-based, polymeric, peptide, and exosome-derived nanocarriers, focusing on their design principles, mechanisms of uptake, and endosomal escape strategies. Particular attention is given to receptor-mediated targeting, intracellular trafficking, and the emerging translation of lipid nanoparticle systems such as NTLA-2001, which exemplify clinical progress in genome editing. Despite these advancements, several challenges persist. Nanoparticle systems exhibit trade-offs between efficiency, biocompatibility, and scalability. For example, lipid nanoparticles may trigger anti- PEG immune reactions, exosome production faces manufacturing constraints, and polymeric systems risk cytotoxicity or limited degradability. Pre-existing immunity to Cas9 proteins and unpredictable immune responses to nanoparticle components remain significant translational hurdles. By integrating current preclinical and early clinical evidence, this review highlights both the promise and the limitations of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 RNP delivery. Understanding these biological, immunological, and engineering challenges will be crucial for developing safe, efficient, and clinically scalable genome editing platforms.

title: SMART Nanocarriers for siRNA Delivery: Stimuli-Responsive Platforms for Targeted Gene Silencing.
abstract: Despite the remarkable specificity of small interfering RNA (siRNA)-based treatments for gene silencing, biological limitations like poor stability, rapid systemic clearance, immunogenicity, and inefficient intracellular delivery hinder their clinical translation. A promising strategy for overcoming these challenges and enabling precise, site-specific gene silencing is the use of SMART nanocarriers, including stimuli-responsive, adaptable, and multifunctional delivery platforms. Controlled siRNA release, enhanced cellular uptake, and effective endosomal escape are enabled by these novel nanocarriers' ability to respond dynamically to exogenous triggers such as light, ultrasound, and magnetic fields as well as endogenous stimuli such as pH gradients, redox potential, enzymatic activity, and hypoxia. Recent advances have combined rational material design, surface functionalization with targeted ligands, and modular architectures to gain spatiotemporal control over gene silencing while limiting unintended targets and systemic toxicity. This study examines the critical design concepts, fabrication methodologies, and molecular pathways governing SMART nanocarrier-mediated siRNA distribution, with a focus on polymeric, lipid-based, inorganic, and bioinspired platforms. The article highlights key preclinical and emerging clinical breakthroughs, as well as issues with scalability, repeatability, immunocompatibility, and regulatory translation. This review emphasizes the critical significance of stimulus-responsive nanocarriers in developing siRNA treatments towards precision medicine applications in oncology, neurological disorders, and inflammatory illnesses by consolidating recent studies and future prospects.

title: Post-Transcriptional Silencing of PHD2 by CRISPR-Cas13d Enhances Pro-Angiogenic Signaling in Human Endothelial Cells.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) reduces tissue perfusion and causes ischemia, conditions in which hypoxia-responsive pathways have an important adaptive role. Hypoxia- inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α), a central regulator of this response, is tightly controlled by prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2 (PHD2), encoded by EGLN1. Here, we used an RNA-targeting CRISPR-Cas13d system to downregulate EGLN1 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) under normoxia and hypoxia.
METHODS: A PHD2-knockdown (PHD2-KD) HUVEC line was generated by lentiviral delivery of an EGLN1-targeting RNA guide, alongside non-transduced (CTRL) and non-targeting gRNA (NTG) control lines. Molecular and functional assays assessed hypoxia-related signaling, metabolic activity, migration, and sprouting responses under normoxia and hypoxia.
RESULTS: Western blotting confirmed a marked reduction in PHD2 protein abundance in PHD2-KD cells relative to both CTRL and NTG cells. PHD2-KD HUVECs exhibited increased VEGFA transcript levels (6.5-fold under normoxia and 5.3-fold under hypoxia) and secreted VEGF concentrations (6.6-fold and 9.4-fold, respectively), together with early increases in HIF1A transcript and HIF-1α protein levels and lower TNF-α concentrations. Functional assays showed higher metabolic activity, faster wound closure (2.0-fold under normoxia and 2.2-fold under hypoxia), and enhanced sprouting, with up to 7.2-fold more sprouts per bead and sprouts up to 2.7-fold longer than those formed by CTRL.
DISCUSSION: CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated EGLN1 targeting reduced PHD2 protein abundance and was associated with higher endothelial metabolic activity, faster wound closure, enhanced sprouting behavior, and lower TNF-α secretion.
CONCLUSION: CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated downregulation of EGLN1/PHD2 was associated with increased pro-angiogenic signaling and improved angiogenesis-related endothelial responses in vitro, supporting RNA-targeting strategies to modulate hypoxia-responsive pathways.

title: Cell-Based Therapeutic Strategies for Correcting Mitochondrial DNA Mutations and Mitigating Oxidative Stress.
abstract: Mitochondria are essential structures that produce energy in cells through mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and are one of the primary sources of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) cause a wide range of hereditary illnesses with multisystem clinical symptoms, poor cellular bioenergetics, and decreased mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Effective treatment approaches have been hampered by the genetic complexity associated with mtDNA disorders, including heteroplasmy and tissue-specific diversity. The relationship between mutations in the mitochondrial DNA and oxidative stress is multidimensional and snowballing, with structural malfunction of the electron transport chain encouraging the development of ROS that causes further damage to mitochondrial DNA, lipids, and proteins. Under carefully regulated experimental conditions, cell-based disease models, in particular induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and standard transmitochondrial cybrids, have become useful tools for studying disease mechanisms, simulating mutation-specific phenotypes, and assessing possible therapeutic interventions. This review provides the key roles of mutations and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of the disease in the context of the primary role of the mitochondrial genome, its maternal inheritance, and the most common disorders, i.e., mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) and myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF). We outline the use of cell-based models to study mitochondrial pathologies, including patient-derived primary cells and iPSCs, which could be differentiated into cell types of interest to the disease, and cybrid systems, which could isolate the contribution of single mutations in the mitochondrial DNA to an underlying background of controlled nuclear genetic backgrounds. Besides, the review focuses on innovative technologies to mend mutations in mitochondrial DNA, such as allotopic expression, mitoTALENs and mitoZFNs, and the new base-editing systems like DdCBEs. Included are the free cell-based therapies like mitochondrial transfer and nuclear transfer procedures. Finally, we discussed the measures to be taken to minimize oxidative stress, and these actions are standard: mitochondria- targeted antioxidants, mitophagy, and autophagy regulation. The study also looks at the present level of proof supporting these therapy techniques and discusses the advantages and disadvantages of existing experimental models. Although several gene editing and mitochondria replacement technologies have shown promising results in clinical and cellular research, their clinical translation is still restricted and needs more confirmation in terms of long-term therapeutic efficacy, safety, and delivery efficiency.

title: Antiangiogenic Drug Testing Using Proangiogenic and Hypoxia Zebrafish Model.
abstract: Zebrafish is an excellent in vivo model for high-throughput antiangiogenic drug testing, commonly known as the zebrafish angiogenesis assay. Conventional zebrafish angiogenesis assays are performed in wild-type zebrafish to evaluate the vascular changes in intersegmental and subintestinal vessel regions of the zebrafish larvae at 2 and 3 dpf stages, respectively. However, wild-type zebrafish larvae do not adequately mimic the hypoxia microenvironment and ectopic vessel branching characteristics of cancer. To overcome this limitation, we developed a genetically engineered zebrafish model with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway by targeting the vhl, a tumor suppressor, by negative regulation of the hypoxia pathway, using CRISPR mutagenesis. This model exhibits robust ectopic blood vessel branching throughout the larval body, thereby recapitulating pathological angiogenesis. The utility of this zebrafish model system for drug screening was validated with the sorafenib treatment, a known antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Overall, this proangiogenic hypoxia zebrafish model provides a physiologically relevant platform for testing antiangiogenic drugs. Key features • Generate a vhl mutant zebrafish line with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway using CRISPR-CAS9 mutagenesis. • The generated model exhibits extensive ectopic neovascular branching and abnormal vascular growth resembling pathological angiogenesis observed in solid tumors. • Mimics the chronic hypoxic microenvironment commonly associated with cancer progression and angiogenesis. • Provides an economical alternative to mammalian tumor models for early-stage antiangiogenic drug testing.

title: High Ubiquitin-like Protein 3 Expression Is Associated With Prolonged Recurrence-free Survival in Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Current clinicopathological factors inadequately capture the biological heterogeneity of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). This study investigated the prognostic significance of ubiquitin-like protein 3 (UBL3), a molecule involved in extracellular vesicle sorting and immune regulation, in NMIBC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Following an exploratory analysis of public RNA-sequencing databases, we evaluated tissue samples from patients who underwent transurethral resection for primary NMIBC. A discovery cohort (n=37) was assessed for UBL3 mRNA via qRT-PCR and protein expression via immunohistochemistry (IHC) quantified using digital H-scores (QuPath). A separate internal validation cohort (n=192) was subsequently evaluated by IHC. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival (RFS).
RESULTS: The database analysis indicated that high UBL3 expression was associated with longer RFS in early-stage bladder cancer. In the discovery cohort, higher UBL3 mRNA levels were associated with prolonged RFS [hazard ratio (HR)=0.33, p=0.004]. mRNA levels also were associated with digital H-scores (ρ=0.39, p=0.018). In the separate internal validation cohort, elevated UBL3 protein expression was associated with a reduced risk of recurrence. A multivariable Cox regression confirmed that a higher UBL3 H-score (HR=0.95 per 10-point increase, p=0.023), alongside a negative preoperative urine cytology and immediate intravesical chemotherapy, remained independently associated with RFS.
CONCLUSION: Elevated UBL3 expression was associated with prolonged RFS in patients with NMIBC following transurethral resection of bladder tumor. While UBL3 has potential as a prognostic biomarker, establishing its definitive clinical utility will require mechanistic investigations and validation across independent, multicenter cohorts.

title: Sex- and Ketogenesis-Dependent Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Diet-Induced Fatty Liver Disease.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Intermittent fasting (IF) improves metabolic health, yet whether hepatic ketogenesis is required for mediating its effects remains unclear. Here, we investigated how ketogenesis contributes to the systemic and liver-specific metabolic effects of IF in male and female mice. Fasting increased circulating ketone bodies in both sexes, with females showing a greater increase, indicating intrinsic sex differences in ketone metabolism. IF reduced body weight gain and adiposity in both sexes, and these benefits persisted when Hmgcs2 expression was knocked down in adult mice, using an antisense oligonucleotide approach to inhibit ketogenesis. In contrast, hepatic benefits were sex- and ketogenesis-dependent. IF markedly reduced steatosis and fibrosis in male mice, but these improvements were attenuated when Hmgcs2 expression was suppressed. In contrast, female mice showed minimal hepatic benefit from IF and had heightened susceptibility to steatosis, fibrosis, and inflammatory activation upon Hmgcs2 knockdown. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified neutrophils and myofibroblasts as key responders to hepatocyte-derived ketone bodies. IF suppressed neutrophil-driven inflammatory signaling in an Hmgcs2-dependent manner, and ketone bodies attenuated low-grade inflammation in cultured neutrophil-like cells. This ketogenesis-inflammation-fibrosis axis was further supported by human Genotype-Tissue Expression liver coexpression analyses. Together, these findings demonstrate that although body weight and antiobesity actions of IF are largely ketogenesis-independent in both sexes of mice, its hepatic antisteatotic and antifibrotic effects are sexually dimorphic and ketogenesis-dependent in male mice.
ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS: We investigated whether ketogenesis is required for the metabolic benefits of intermittent fasting (IF) and whether these effects differ between sexes. We specifically asked whether ketogenesis drives IF-mediated protection against obesity and fatty liver disease in male and female mice. We found that IF reduced adiposity independently of ketogenesis in both sexes, but its antisteatotic and antifibrotic effects were ketogenesis-dependent in male mice and minimal in female mice. These findings reveal a sex-dependent ketogenesis-inflammation-fibrosis axis and highlight the need to consider sex and ketone metabolism when designing dietary or therapeutic interventions.

title: The Role of miRNAs in Regulating Cellular Senescence: A Potential Strategy for Overcoming Drug Resistance in Ovarian Cancer.
abstract: Ovarian cancer remains one of the most lethal gynecological malignancies, largely due to late diagnosis and the frequent development of resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy and taxanes. Increasing evidence implicates microRNAs as key regulators of drug response through their control of DNA damage response and repair, apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and therapy-induced cellular senescence. Senescence is a double-edged process characterized by irreversible cell-cycle arrest and the secretion of pro-inflammatory factors collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, which may suppress tumor growth but also promote chemoresistance and disease recurrence. This review summarizes current evidence on microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulation of therapy-induced cellular senescence and its role in drug resistance in ovarian cancer. We integrate data from mechanistic studies, preclinical models, and clinical observations, focusing on senescence-associated miRNAs and their regulatory networks. miRNAs including miR-34a, miR-21, miR-146a, miR-200c, miR-506, and miR-433 regulate key senescence pathways, notably p53/p21 and p16-RB signaling, and modulate the senescence-associated secretory phenotype by controlling inflammatory mediators, extracellular matrix remodeling, and angiogenic factors. Several of these miRNAs are also associated with resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy, taxanes, poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, and immunotherapies through effects on PI3K/AKT and Hippo signaling pathways, as well as DNA repair mechanisms. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to modulate or eliminate senescent cells using miRNA mimics, inhibitors, or gene-editing approaches, including nanoparticle-based delivery systems. Although preclinical studies suggest that these approaches may restore chemosensitivity, clinical translation remains limited by delivery challenges, off-target effects, and the context-dependent role of senescence. Targeting miRNA-senescence regulatory axes may represent a strategy for addressing drug resistance in ovarian cancer and warrants further investigation as part of combination treatment strategies.

title: HNRNPH2-R114W remodels RNA splicing and neurodevelopmental gene programs in isogenic cerebral organoids.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder has been linked to disrupted RNA processing during corticogenesis, yet variant-specific mechanisms remain difficult to resolve. Isogenic cerebral organoids derived from a patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) line carrying the HNRNPH2-R114W variant and its CRISPR-corrected counterpart serve as a human developmental model to investigate variant-associated RNA dysregulation. Imaging quantification and exploratory bulk RNA sequencing, performed at a single developmental time point on a pooled organoid RNA from each genotype, identify coordinated remodeling of neuronal and metabolic programs, along with junction-centered splicing dysregulation involving 6,310 differentially used junctions. Computational structural docking situates HNRNPH2 RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) 1-3 within a spliceosomal context and locates residue R114 near a predicted RNA-contact interface, indicating that the R114W substitution may alter RNA engagement. Integration of differential expression with event- and isoform-level analyses identifies regulatory hubs enriched for axon guidance and synaptic signaling pathways. Single-cell-reference-based deconvolution suggests modest compositional shifts that are unlikely to account for the extent of transcriptional and splicing alterations observed. Collectively, these findings imply HNRNPH2-R114W in widespread RNA rewiring and define candidate isoform-level endpoints for mechanistic and therapeutic investigation in human cortical organoids. These molecular signatures open new avenues to examine how HNRNPH2-associated RNA dysregulation evolves across developmental time and recurs across independent biological contexts, providing a foundation for further mechanistic studies of this rare neurodevelopmental disorder.

title: CRISPR/Cas genome editing strategies to enhance abiotic stress tolerance in sugar crops.
abstract: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. Prominent candidate targets include transcription factors (TF), signaling components, raffinose biosynthesis genes implicated in freezing tolerance, regulators of salt and alkaline stress, and determinants of heavy metal tolerance and sequestration. Translational challenges, such as off-target effects, low transformation efficiencies, and editing multiple homologues or haplotypes, are being addressed such as DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, high-throughput screening, haplotype-specific target design, and haplotype-aware guide RNA engineering based on unique genetic variation sites across different gene haplotypes. Collectively, the integration of advanced CRISPR toolkits with enhanced genomic information resources and phenotyping capabilities holds significant potential for accelerating the development of precision-bred, multi-stress-resilient sugar crops that sustain yield, quality, and industrial value under abiotic stress conditions.

title: Engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells for hematological malignancies: genome editing, synthetic biology, and precision immunotherapy.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment by enabling engineered immune cells to selectively recognize and eliminate malignant targets, with CAR-T cells establishing the first major clinical success in this field. However, severe associated toxicities, logistical complexities of autologous manufacturing, and high rates of antigen-loss relapse have accelerated the development of alternative effector platforms such as CAR-NK cells. CAR-NK cells combine antigen-directed cytotoxicity with the innate antitumor functions of natural killer cells, offering a potentially safer and more readily available off-the-shelf therapeutic strategy. Nevertheless, the clinical efficacy of CAR-NK therapy is constrained by key biological and translational hurdles: brief in vivo persistence, inadequate trafficking and solid tumor infiltration, severe susceptibility to tumor microenvironment-mediated immunosuppression, and antigen escape driven by tumor heterogeneity. These biological constraints are compounded by technical bottlenecks, including cell source variability, limited large-scale expansion capacity, ex vivo functional exhaustion, and an absence of standardized manufacturing protocols. To address these multi-faceted barriers, recent advances in genome engineering, systems biology, and computational modeling provide promising routes forward. Given that prolonged exposure to immunosuppressive niches induces functional impairment, genome-editing strategies targeting inhibitory checkpoints and persistence programs are crucial; however, enhancing persistence requires stringent safeguards to mitigate toxicity risks from constitutive signaling or genomic instability. Thus, engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells necessitates balancing extended longevity, potent cytotoxicity, and safety. Multiomics approaches facilitate deeper characterization of CAR-NK functional states and tumor-immune interactions, whereas artificial intelligence-guided engineering integrates high-dimensional biological and manufacturing data to optimize receptor design, predict therapeutic performance, and accelerate translational workflows. Collectively, these innovations support a paradigm shift toward programmable CAR-NK cells that can dynamically sense, adapt, and respond to tumor evolution, driving the transition toward autonomous, highly scalable, and precisely controllable cellular immunotherapies in precision oncology.

title: Intranasal nano-immunotherapy for glioma: bypassing the blood-brain barrier, reprogramming the immune microenvironment, and bridging preclinical validation.
abstract: Glioma, particularly glioblastoma, remains difficult to treat because of limited drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, profound immune suppression, and insufficient intracranial exposure of systemic immunotherapies. Intranasal nano-immunotherapy is being explored as a potential strategy that may integrate noninvasive nose-to-brain delivery with nanocarrier-mediated immune reprogramming. Intranasal administration may partially bypass conventional vascular barriers through olfactory, trigeminal, mucosal, cerebrospinal-fluid, and perivascular transport routes, while nanoparticles are designed to protect immune-active payloads, support brain tumor targeting, and enable controlled release. Current evidence spans three distinct levels: direct intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy, intranasal glioma nanodelivery without demonstrated immune reprogramming, and non-intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy that provides mechanistic support for future intranasal adaptation. Across these evidence levels, investigated platforms include peptide-guided nanomicelles, lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic nanoparticles, ferritin-based nanovectors, spherical nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, bacterial outer membrane vesicles, and stimuli-responsive systems. These platforms can deliver immune-activating cargos, such as STING or TLR agonists; gene-regulatory cargos, such as siRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 components; and microenvironment-modulating cargos, such as chemokine-axis inhibitors, checkpoint-modulating agents, and combination payloads. Through these payloads, intranasal nanoplatforms may activate innate immune sensing, reverse myeloid-mediated suppression, enhance T-cell infiltration, and induce immunogenic cell death. However, translation remains limited by dosing uncertainty, species differences in nasal anatomy, mucosal and neurological safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and incomplete immune pharmacodynamic validation. This review summarizes recent advances in intranasal and brain-targeted glioma nano-immunotherapy, highlights key immune mechanisms, and proposes a preclinical validation framework for evaluating whether experimental efficacy can be advanced toward clinically testable treatment designs.

title: Specific residues modulate the antiviral activity of the extracellular vesicle-derived effector SH3b domain from Lactobacillus johnsonii N6.2.
abstract: Lactobacillus johnsonii N6.2-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) provide protection against murine norovirus (MNV-1) both in vitro and in vivo. Within the proteins enriched in EVs, the SH3b2 domain of Sdp was shown to be sufficient to recapitulate the antiviral effects shown by EVs. In this report, we compared the effects of six SH3b domains of Sdp and identified amino acids expected to be important for interactions with host proteins. We found that SH3b2 showed the highest activity in inducing NF-ĸB/AP-1 and IRF pathways in RAW macrophage reporter cell lines. Structure-guided site-directed mutagenesis of SH3b2 revealed residues in SH3b2 potentially responsible for interactions with host proteins. SH3b2-G501D had significantly lower stimulation of NF-ĸB/AP-1 and IRF pathways. In addition, SH3b2-G501D showed reduced IL10 and Oas1 mRNA levels, resulting in an impaired MNV-1 antiviral response in RAW 264.7 cells. mCherry fusions to SH3b2-G501D confirmed that the effects observed were not related to reduced uptake into macrophages, as quantified by confocal microscopy. Additionally, the role of the C-terminal linker sequence in Sh3b2, which is absent in SH3b6, in uptake or signaling in macrophages was evaluated. It was found that deletion of the C-terminal linker (SH3b2ΔC2 treatment) resulted in reduced promoter activity, while SH3b6::C2 partially regained function through restoration of uptake in macrophages. These results indicate that the C-terminal linker plays an important role in internalization by macrophages. We propose that once internalized, SH3b2 mimics eukaryotic SH3 domains involved in signal transduction to activate the cellular innate immune response in macrophages.

title: Phage-directed precision microbiome medicine: engineering pathobiont depletion, synbiotic succession, microbial-function editing, metabolite host signaling, neurophagomics, and durable ecological state control in gut dysbiosis associated diseases.
abstract: Bacteriophages are being investigated as strain-selective tools for modifying intestinal microbial communities, but the evidence supporting ecological reconstruction is substantially less mature than the evidence supporting targeted bacterial depletion. This review separates current knowledge into three domains: established and emerging experimental evidence, human translational evidence, and hypotheses proposed for future testing. Human studies show that orally administered natural or engineered phages can be recovered from the gastrointestinal tract and can alter selected bacterial populations without antibiotic-like loss of overall community diversity. Preclinical studies further demonstrate targeted suppression of inflammatory Klebsiella pneumoniae in inflammatory bowel disease models, cytolytic Enterococcus faecalis in alcohol-associated liver disease, evolutionary steering of Escherichia coli, in situ bacterial genome editing, local therapeutic-protein production, and phage-probiotic cooperation. These findings do not yet establish that an integrated phage-successor-prebiotic sequence can durably reprogram a human gut ecosystem. To organize this translational gap, we use Subtract-Seed-Feed-Lock as an explicitly proposed design framework. A phage or phage-derived platform first depletes, weakens, or edits a disease-relevant bacterial strain or function; a niche-matched successor is then introduced; a selectively utilized nutrient supports that successor; and durability is assessed after treatment withdrawal. Related terms used in this review-Functional Phageability, Minimum Ecological Dose, Ecological Vacancy Window, nutrient-conditioned phagogram, ecological pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (Eco-PK/PD), ecological pharmacovigilance, neurophagomic reverse translation, and microbiome-state digital twin-are hypothesis-generating operational concepts rather than validated clinical methods. Host signaling is likewise framed as predominantly indirect: phage-induced changes in bacterial abundance or function may alter lipopolysaccharide, short-chain fatty acids, indoles, bile acids, and other metabolites that subsequently engage inflammatory, barrier, hepatic, or neural pathways. The gut-brain application remains especially preliminary; targeting urdA-positive imidazole-propionate producers has not been validated with therapeutic phages. Clinical development will require reproducible good manufacturing practice, control of endotoxin and host-cell contaminants, product stability, resistance and immune-neutralization monitoring, environmental-shedding assessment, and regulatory strategies for genetically modified, dynamically updated, and multi-component products. The immediate opportunity is therefore precise microbial perturbation with evidence-matched endpoints; durable programmed reconstruction remains an experimentally testable objective.

title: Metabolic-epigenetic regulation of the HBV cccDNA reservoir: pathways underpinning viral persistence.
abstract: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a global public health burden, and functional cure represents the primary goal of clinical management. The nuclear covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) minichromosome stably maintained in infected hepatocytes constitutes the major barrier to HBV cure. Clinically, functional cure is defined as sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroclearance with undetectable serum HBV DNA after finite treatment, a definition that does not require complete cccDNA elimination. At the molecular level, functional cure is thought to be associated with stable transcriptional silencing of cccDNA and integrated HBV DNA, a state biologically distinct from physical cccDNA depletion. Accumulating data demonstrate that the persistence and transcriptional homeostasis of the cccDNA reservoir are controlled by viral proteins and dynamically shaped by host metabolic signaling and epigenetic remodeling. Here, we first outline key steps of the HBV life cycle to establish the mechanistic context for cccDNA formation and replenishment, and then focus our synthesis on the integrated host metabolic-epigenetic network that governs cccDNA establishment, transcriptional activity, stability, and clearance. We dissect how central carbon metabolites, bile acid signaling, histone post-translational modifications, and immune cytokines converge to modulate cccDNA reservoir homeostasis, and critically evaluate the strength of evidence supporting their physiological relevance in the chronically infected human liver. We also discuss mechanisms of HBV immune evasion, including hepatitis B virus X protein (HBx)-driven epigenetic reprogramming and subviral particle-associated immune tolerance. We summarize preclinical and clinical therapeutic strategies targeting the metabolic-epigenetic microenvironment, viral assembly, antigen secretion, and cccDNA modulation to achieve a functional cure for HBV infection. Finally, we outline key unresolved challenges in the field, including the undefined in vivo cccDNA turnover kinetics, the poorly characterized physiological relevance of cell-to-cell transmission, the inherent limitations of gene-editing technologies, and the urgent need for specific non-invasive biomarkers reflecting intrahepatic cccDNA activity.

title: Progress on therapeutic mRNA vaccines for cancer.
abstract: Therapeutic mRNA vaccines are a clinically validated cancer immunotherapy platform using in vitro transcribed mRNA encoding tumor antigens to induce durable anti-tumor immunity. Advances in mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery, and immunomodulatory combinations have propelled this approach from preclinical models to randomized trials with survival benefit. This review systematically examines vaccine efficacy through an antigen-delivery-immunomodulation tripartite framework. We trace the evolution from shared tumor-associated antigens to personalized neoantigens identified by computational pipelines, discuss ionizable lipid chemistry and LNP formulation for controlled tissue tropism and transfection, and analyze the bidirectional crosstalk between vaccine components and innate immune sensing that shapes adaptive T cell responses. Clinical evidence across melanoma, pancreatic cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, and other solid tumors is critically evaluated, alongside combination strategies-checkpoint blockade, oncolytic virotherapy, and adoptive cell therapy to overcome TME resistance. Persistent challenges include optimal neoantigen selection, standardized immune monitoring, and predictive biomarkers. We conclude that future research should prioritize systematic optimization of the tripartite design through multi-antigen targeting, tissue-specific delivery engineering, and rational combination immunotherapy, aiming to establish mRNA cancer vaccines as a standard-of-care modality.

title: The minipig as a programmable translational platform for experimental oncofertility.
abstract: Experimental oncofertility remains fragmented across models of cancer biology, treatment-associated gonadotoxicity, fertility preservation, and reproductive recovery. We propose extending the Oncopig concept into a translational platform that reconnects these states within one genetically defined, cancer-bearing host. The Oncopig provides the oncologic backbone, combining programmable cancer in an immunocompetent large-animal host with clinically scaled intervention and longitudinal sampling. High-resolution porcine genomics, CRISPR-based genome engineering, somatic-cell nuclear transfer for line generation, comparative experimental pathology, and mature reproductive biotechnology extend this architecture toward reproductive endpoints. Here, programmability refers to deliberate specification of the cancer state-genotype, cell lineage or induction strategy, and timing-whereas the reproductive phenotype is measured longitudinally rather than programmed. Distant-cancer modules can test whether cancer status modifies gonadotoxicity, while reproductive-organ modules require disease-specific alleles, appropriate cell-of-origin targeting, and pathology-led validation. Because porcine and human reproduction align in several endocrine and gonadal processes but differ in cycle organization, implantation, placentation, and pregnancy, translation should emphasize process-level endpoints rather than numerical equivalence. The platform is particularly suited to unresolved questions involving targeted therapies and immunotherapies, preservation timing, and pediatric or prepubertal patients. Porcine reproductive biotechnology provides functional endpoints from gonadal tissue and gametes to embryos and offspring. Rather than replacing rodent or human-based models, the Oncopig framework adds an integrated translational layer for questions requiring clinically scaled intervention, longitudinal physiology, and functional reproductive recovery.
