title: Inhibition of heat shock protein 90 in the mouse spinal cord enhances opioid antinociception via the upregulation of dual specificity protein phosphatase 15 (DUSP15) in CGRP neurons.
abstract: In an extended series of studies, we have shown that Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) has a novel role in regulating opioid signal transduction and antinociception in both the brain and spinal cord. Inhibition in the spinal cord enhances opioid antinociception, which led to the finding that an isoform-selective Hsp90 inhibitor could improve opioid therapy, both enhancing pain relief and reducing side effects. However, the signaling mechanisms for this activity are still not fully understood. We thus identified Dual Specificity Phosphatase 15 (DUSP15) from an earlier proteomic study as a protein enhanced in the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibition. Using male and female CD-1 mice, we confirmed that DUSP15 is upregulated in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibitor (17-AAG) treatment. Using CRISPR and siRNA-mediated knockdown, we showed that DUSP15 was necessary for the enhanced morphine antinociception after Hsp90 inhibitor treatment in both the tail flick and post-surgical paw incision pain models. Using immunohistochemistry (IHC) and behavioral tools, we placed DUSP15 upstream of both ERK MAPK and AMPK in the opioid signaling cascade. We then used IHC to demonstrate that DUSP15 upregulation occurs at least in part in CGRP neurons, and using cell-selective CRISPR, showed that DUSP15 in CGRP neurons is necessary for the enhanced antinociception observed with spinal Hsp90 inhibitor treatment. Together these studies further expand the known mechanisms by which Hsp90 regulates opioid signal transduction and pain relief and provide basic science insight into a potential strategy to improve opioid therapy using Hsp90 inhibitors.

title: Pharmacological reprogramming of myeloid suppression in solid tumors: mechanisms, evidence standards for immune conversion, and biomarker-informed combinations.
abstract: Myeloid cells regulate immune exclusion, T-cell dysfunction, angiogenesis, stromal remodeling, and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade in solid tumors. Pharmacological development has moved from nonspecific depletion toward recruitment or survival blockade, intracellular state reprogramming, restoration of antigen presentation, and tumor-selective phagocytosis. Clinical experience nevertheless shows a recurrent gap between biological activity and attributable therapeutic immune conversion. We introduce the Myeloid Immune Conversion Audit Trail (MICAT), a fixed four-level extension of the pharmacological audit trail that grades intratumoral target engagement, conversion of the intended myeloid state, propagation through the immune ecosystem, and randomized clinical attribution. Each level is scored as not demonstrated, partial, or demonstrated. Applying MICAT across representative trials shows that most programs stop at systemic pharmacodynamics or partial lineage effects; few establish ecosystem propagation, and none yet completes the entire causal chain for an immunological switch in a solid-tumor carcinoma. The analysis identifies compensation and redundancy as the central biological obstacle: CCR2 blockade can recruit CXCR2-positive neutrophils, CSF1R inhibition can spare resistant SPP1-high macrophages, and CD40 or PI3Kγ activation can induce interferon-linked PD-L1 feedback. We therefore prioritize lineage-resolved paired tissue, preservation of cDC1 and cDC2 function, absolute cell quantification, orthogonal functional and spatial readouts, and randomized component-controlled trials. Disease context is decisive: tenosynovial giant-cell tumor establishes CSF1R dependence without proving immune conversion; macrophage-rich triple-negative breast cancer is a rational PI3Kγ test-bed; pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma permits sequence-aware CD40 and stromal studies; and microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer is a stringent failure benchmark. CAR-macrophages, in vivo mRNA/lipid-nanoparticle reprogramming, myeloid engagers, and artificial-intelligence-assisted spatial scoring are mapped to the same evidence requirements. MICAT is intended as a reproducible tool for pharmacological go/no-go decisions rather than a claim that target modulation alone constitutes therapeutic immune conversion.

title: Coxiella burnetii effector CelF reprograms host proteostasis via competitive disruption of the UBQLN1-PSMD4 axis to stabilize autophagic SNARE SNAP29 and modulate lysosomal metabolic maturation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy-lysosome pathway constitute the core proteolytic metabolic networks that maintain cellular protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and organelle metabolic identity. Intracellular pathogens frequently reprogram host metabolic pathways to establish replicative niches, yet how they manipulate proteostatic metabolism to remodel organelle maturation remains incompletely understood.
METHODS: CelF secretion was confirmed by TEM translocation assay. CRISPR-dCas9 was used to generate CelF knockdown and complementation strains, with celF transcription verified by RT-qPCR. Cell infection and SCID mouse models were used to assess intracellular survival, Coxiella-containing vacuole (CCV) maturation, and virulence of Coxiella burnetii. The effect of CelF on late autophagy was examined by dual-fluorescence LC3 and Western blotting. Then, UBQLN1 was identified as a CelF-interacting host protein by co-IP and pull-down, followed by truncation mapping. Finally, co-IP, UBQLN1 knockdown, Western blotting and MST assays were used to analyze the effect of CelF on SNARE assembly, SNAP29 degradation and ubiquitination, and competitive binding of CelF and PSMD4 to UBQLN1.
RESULTS: CelF depletion severely impaired the metabolic maturation of CCV, suppressed bacterial proliferation in macrophages, and attenuated virulence in vivo. Mechanistically, CelF acted as a molecular decoy that directly bound the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain of the proteasomal shuttle factor UBQLN1, competitively displacing the proteasome subunit PSMD4. This competitive interference blocked UBQLN1-mediated proteasomal delivery of SNAP29 without altering its ubiquitination status, thereby enhancing SNAP29 protein stability and promoting assembly of the STX17-SNAP29-VAMP8 fusogenic complex. The augmented SNARE activity drove autophagosome-lysosome fusion, sustained autophagic flux, and facilitated lysosomal metabolic remodeling to support CCV biogenesis.
DISCUSSION: Unlike canonical pathogen-encoded UPS modulators that function as E3 ligases or deubiquitinases, CelF operates purely through competitive protein-protein interaction, representing a previously unrecognized paradigm for microbial manipulation of host proteostatic metabolism. Our findings reveal that intracellular pathogens can actively orchestrate organelle metabolic identity by rewiring host proteostasis, and identify the UBQLN1-PSMD4-SNAP29 axis as a novel regulatory checkpoint for SNARE proteostasis and lysosomal metabolic maturation.

title: Advanced soilless cultivation of medicinal plants: integrating dynamic LED lighting, elicitation, and smart technologies for sustainable biomass and phytochemical production.
abstract: Countries with limited water and land resources confront a significant problem due to the growing demand for medicinal plants. These plants are used worldwide to extract and isolate therapeutically important bioactive molecules, known as secondary metabolites. Many medicinal plant species are currently facing significant conservation challenges due to excessive, unregulated harvesting, driven by rapidly growing demand for plant-derived therapies. Soilless farming techniques like hydroponics, aeroponics, and vertical farming offer a sustainable alternative for generating high-quality planting material on a large scale in a considerably shorter period and with less space. Soilless farming revolutionises agriculture and food production, making it particularly well-suited for urban agriculture by reducing maintenance requirements and maximizing crop yields. Soilless farming of numerous medicinal herbs, fruit crops, and vegetables has become increasingly popular in recent years, particularly for its ability to produce large amounts of biomass, high yields, and a wide range of pharmacologically active metabolites. These high-tech systems have significant promise for increased crop yields, cleaner produce, season-independent cultivation, and reduced environmental impact, particularly in water use and disease, compared to traditional soil-based systems. This review article rigorously evaluates recent advancements in soilless agriculture, including LED spectral regulation, nano-elicitation, microbial biostimulants and precursor-feeding strategies, reusable substrates, computational technologies, and CRISPR/Cas-based editing, with respect to their efficacy in generating high-quality plant biomass, improving automation, and optimizing shoot architecture. Implementing soilless farming to produce and synthesize bioactive molecules is expected to be crucial in enhancing sustainability and human well-being.

title: De novo assembly and comparative analysis of the first complete mitochondrial genome of the genus Anisomeles (Anisomeles indica).
abstract: Anisomeles indica (L.) Kuntze is an important traditional medicinal plant with diverse pharmacological activities, while no mitochondrial genome (mitogenome) has yet been reported for this species or any member of the genus, limiting our understanding of organelle genome evolution and molecular characteristics within Lamiaceae. In this study, we report the first complete mitogenome of the genus Anisomeles, which was de novo assembled and annotated for A. indica using PacBio high-fidelity (HiFi) sequencing data. The mitogenome of A. indica was assembled as a single master circular molecule with a length of 296,457 bp and a GC content of 45.42%. A total of 51 genes were identified, including 32 protein-coding genes (PCGs), three rRNA genes and 16 tRNA genes. Repeat analysis revealed relatively low repeat abundance, with 60 simple sequence repeats, 136 dispersed repeats, and 15 tandem repeats identified. Furthermore, 30 mitochondrial plastid DNA sequences were detected (24,696 bp), suggesting a substantial contribution of plastid-derived sequences to the mitogenome. RNA editing analysis predicted 444 editing sites across all mitochondrial PCGs except atp1. Phylogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial and plastid genome datasets supported a closer relationship of A. indica with Pogostemon than with Phlomoides. This study provides the first mitogenomic resource for Anisomeles and establishes a foundation for future studies of mitogenome evolution, comparative genomics, and phylogenetic relationships within Lamiaceae.

title: Genomic and clinical factors associated with drug-resistant tuberculosis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Drug-resistant tuberculosis is a significant global health issue caused by mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the infectious agent of the disease. WHO's End TB Strategy mandates drug susceptibility testing for rifampicin in all confirmed tuberculosis cases and fluoroquinolone testing for rifampicin-resistant cases.
OBJECTIVE: The review aims to analyse Mycobacterium tuberculosis genome mutations; Clinical factors linked to drug resistance. Major thematic findings: The mutant otsB1 trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase shows rifampicin resistance in hypoxic conditions. Pyruvate dehydrogenase E2 is vital for RNI resistance, host cell death, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth. Individuals with drug-susceptible tuberculosis showed higher plasma levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase. NO and iNOS expression can be influenced by factors other than mycobacterial infection. Activated macrophages convert L-arginine to NO via TNF-α and IFN-γ. Serum L-arginine levels were measured in individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and healthy controls. PPE51, PE15, and PE20 improve drug resistance by transporting metal ions and absorbing nutrients. In diagnosis, the CRISPR-guided mutagenic DNA polymerase identifies changes in drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacterium smegmatis, recognized for its rapid growth, and the slow-growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis were evaluated using CRISPR-guided DNA polymerase. Also, machine learning and whole-genome sequencing predicted isoniazid, Rifampicin, and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis with 90% precision. The BDQ DILI network can offer valuable support on monitor the adverse events of the Anti-tuberculosis therapy.
CONCLUSION: Whole genome sequencing, tNGS, and deletion-targeted multiplex PCR effectively detect mutations. Studying PE/PPE genes offers a key chance to drug-resistant tuberculosis research and improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes.

title: Biophysics-informed computational framework for predicting antisense oligonucleotide knockdown efficacy under small-data constraints.
abstract: A central strategy in treating neurodegenerative disorders, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), is lowering levels of disease-driving proteins. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) offer a direct RNA-targeted approach to reduce protein expression, but experimental discovery and optimization are constrained by small, heterogeneous datasets and target-specific variability. Computational models that predict ASO knockdown efficacy directly from sequence and context could improve candidate selection, yet generalization across gene families and experimental settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a biophysics-based computational framework for predicting RNase H-active ASO knockdown efficacy under small-data constraints. We curate and integrate heterogeneous literature-derived ASO efficacy measurements into a unified dataset and evaluate model transfer using independently generated experimental ASOs targeting ALS-relevant genes DAZAP1 and FAM69C. Knockdown efficacy is defined at the transcript level (%KD), providing a mechanistic measure of RNase H-mediated activity. To our knowledge, this is the first framework that combines ASO feature engineering with one-shot family calibration for prediction under realistic small-data conditions. We integrate sequence representations with physics-based features capturing RNA-DNA hybridization thermodynamics, targeting RNA accessibility. Compared to sequence-only baselines, this mechanistic feature augmentation reduces external wet-lab prediction error, improving generalization to independent experimental data. Despite these gains, uncalibrated predictions exhibit systematic target-family-specific scale bias. We address this challenge by using a minimal one-shot family calibration strategy that applies an additive offset derived from a single experimentally measured reference ASO per new target family. We further assess the model's behavior using a leave-one-family-out simulation on literature-derived ASO families, repeatedly applying one-shot calibration to quantify its expected benefit and variability under controlled small-n conditions. One-shot calibration markedly improves absolute prediction accuracy while preserving within-family ranking, without retraining or increasing model complexity. Out-of-distribution evaluation shows stable performance for DAZAP1 and increased uncertainty for FAM69C, consistent with the expected effects of very small sample sizes. Permutation-based interpretability analyses show that predictive signal is dominated by global sequence architecture, with thermodynamic and accessibility features providing correlated, secondary contributions. Together, these results establish a computational workflow in which literature-trained models can be transferred to new target genes using minimal experimental input, supporting systematic ASO prioritization in small-data models.

title: SUGP1 Deficiency Leads to Splicing Dysregulation and Reduced piRNA Abundance in Insects.
abstract: SUGP1 (SURP and G-patch domain containing 1) participates in splice-site recognition through its interaction with SF3B1, and loss of this factor leads to aberrant splicing. While its role in pre-mRNA splicing is well-documented, its impact on small RNA pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SUGP1 editing in Bombyx mori BmE cell populations and RNAi to systemically knock down SUGP1 in Drosophila melanogaster. SUGP1 loss caused widespread splicing abnormalities in both species and reduced transposon-derived piRNA abundance as shown by small RNA-seq. Notably, the expression and splicing patterns of known piRNA pathway genes remained largely unchanged. Integrating silkworm transcriptomic data with the Flag-SUGP1 Co-IP/MS interactome revealed no direct association with the components of the piRNA biogenesis pathway, but identified a physical interaction with the Y-box protein (YBX), suggesting a potential link connecting splicing surveillance to RNA metabolism and proteostasis. Collectively, these correlative findings suggest that SUGP1 depletion perturbs global RNA processing, and piRNA reduction may represent a secondary outcome associated with cellular stress or dysregulated RNA metabolism within these two tested insect systems. These results suggest a potential indirect link between SUGP1-dependent splicing regulation and piRNA abundance in the tested insect models.

title: Advancing the Translational Pipeline: From In Vivo and In Vitro 2D Models to Next-Generation Cell Culture Models for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Modelling and Drug Discovery.
abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives: This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods: A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. Moreover, recent bioengineering advancements enable the inclusion of functional neurovascular units, the integration of resident immune cells (microglia), and the use of 3D bioprinting to accelerate the functional maturation of age-related phenotypes. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, OMICS, and machine learning improve tools for studying ALS and identifying therapeutic targets. Conclusions: Novel cell culture models may bridge the gap between preclinical animal models and human clinical trials and reduce the duration and costs of translation. Future work is likely to integrate bioprinting with organ-on-chip microfluidics, CRISPR-based genetic editing, and multi-omics readouts to build increasingly faithful, patient-specific ALS models for both basic research and precision therapeutics.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle Delivery of CAR276 mRNA Enables Antigen-Specific Cytotoxicity in T Cells Against Glioblastoma Cells.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains the most aggressive and treatment-refractory primary brain tumor, with current therapeutic modalities providing minimal survival improvement. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapies succeeded in hematologic malignancies but are constrained in solid tumors by tumor heterogeneity, immunosuppressive microenvironment, and delivery challenges. CD276 (B7-H3), a pan-cancer antigen overexpressed in gliomas and correlated with poor patient outcomes, represents a compelling immunotherapeutic target. Methods: Here, we developed a non-viral lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for transient CAR mRNA delivery to T cells and evaluated its application for generating CD276 (B7-H3)-targeted CAR-T cells against GBM. An in-house-assembled T-mixer incorporating polyether ether ketone (PEEK) tubing was integrated with a dual-syringe-pump system for controlled LNP production. Results: LNPs formulated with clinically relevant ionizable lipids, SM-102 and DLin-MC3-DMA, demonstrated high encapsulation efficiency and effective mRNA delivery. Cell-type-dependent expression kinetics were further characterized following LNP-mediated reporter mRNA delivery in K562, NK, NK92, and T cells, revealing differences in transgene expression across cell populations. LNP-mediated delivery of CD276 CAR mRNA enabled generation of CAR-expressing T cells that exhibited antigen-specific cytotoxicity against CD276-positive LN229 GBM cells in vitro. Conclusions: Collectively, this study demonstrates the feasibility of an adaptable LNP-based platform for non-viral CAR mRNA engineering of T cells and CD276-targeted cytotoxicity against GBM cells in vitro. The combination of transient CAR expression and LNP-mediated mRNA delivery provides a foundation for further optimization and evaluation in preclinical in vivo models.

title: Integrated Microfluidic CRISPR-Based Diagnostic Device for Rapid Testing of HPVs.
abstract: Screening for high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is a pivotal strategy for the prevention of invasive cervical cancer, particularly in resource-constrained settings. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-based compact automated real-time detection system, termed Ccard, for rapid testing of HPV16, HPV18, and the internal reference gene GAPDH through a streamlined workflow. A simple room-temperature treatment efficiently releases nucleic acids directly from swab samples, bypassing the need for extraction. The mixture was driven through the channels and loaded into the reaction chambers on the microfluidic chip by a vacuum pump. The lyophilized reagents in the reaction zone of the microfluidic chip were redissolved. The system subsequently performs a single-step RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a reaction, with real-time detection enabled by an Internet of Things device. The assay achieved detection within 30 min, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 5 copies/µL for both HPV16 and HPV18. Validation with clinical samples demonstrated high sensitivity (96.8% for HPV16 and 100% for HPV18) and 100% specificity. These results highlight the reliability, precision, and strong potential of the Ccard system for rapid testing of HR-HPVs.

title: Targeting Peripheral T-Cell Lymphomas with Chimeric Antigen Receptor Therapy: Mechanistic Challenges, Clinical Landscape and Future Engineering Perspectives.
abstract: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) comprise a biologically diverse and clinically aggressive family of mature T/NK-cell neoplasms, for which outcomes remain poor in the majority of patients treated with conventional anthracycline-based frontline regimens. Contemporary classifications (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC) increasingly incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular information, underscoring that "PTCL-NOS" is not a single disease but rather a diagnostic umbrella that includes biologically distinct entities and molecular subgroups. Among these are the TBX21- and GATA3-driven PTCL-NOS subsets, the latter associated with inferior survival and a distinctive cytokine/microenvironmental program. These advances, many of which were shaped by long-standing contributions from the Bologna group, support a rational shift from empiric chemotherapy toward mechanism-based and immune-based interventions. CAR-engineered cellular therapies have revolutionized the care of B-cell malignancies, yet translation to PTCL has been delayed by lineage-specific barriers: (i) fratricide during manufacturing when targeting shared T-cell antigens (e.g., CD5, CD7), (ii) the risk of profound and prolonged T-cell aplasia (a markedly less "replaceable" toxicity than B-cell aplasia), and (iii) product contamination by malignant T-cells in autologous platforms. Recent progress in genome editing (CRISPR/Cas9 and base editing), intracellular antigen "blocking" strategies, and alternative effectors (allogeneic "universal" CAR-T, CAR-NK, and iPSC-derived platforms) has begun to address these obstacles at the manufacturing level, while their downstream clinical consequences (e.g., prolonged cytopenias, infectious risk and delayed immune reconstitution) remain incompletely resolved. Early-phase clinical trials now demonstrate clinically meaningful responses for select targets, particularly CD7, CD5, TRBC1 and CD30, for the pan-T targets. However, the strongest efficacy data remain largely derived from T-cell lymphoblastic malignancies (T-ALL/T-LBL), whereas evidence in mature PTCL remains limited and at an earlier stage, with target-specific differences in safety, immune reconstitution and relapse patterns. This review synthesizes the biological rationale for antigen selection in PTCL, the emerging clinical evidence for leading CAR targets, and the engineering strategies most likely to improve the therapeutic index. It also proposes an integrated hematology perspective on how CAR-based therapies might be positioned relative to transplant and evolving targeted agents in relapsed/refractory PTCL.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease.
abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

title: Engineering of the High-Precision Cas12m Dual Base Editor-Loaded Virus-like Particles for A-to-G and C-to-T Conversions.
abstract: Background/Objectives: CRISPR/Cas-dependent base editing enables the precise correction of genomic sequences by direct modification of DNA bases without creating potentially mutagenic DNA double-strand breaks. Base editing is considered a therapeutic approach for rare monogenic disorders or viral infections. However, many variants of base editors suffer from limited specificity because they induce bystander edits within a broad editing window. However, nucleotide substitution is sufficient to correct a mutation or to achieve a therapeutic effect. Methods: PCR, cloning by restriction digest, and ligation were used to create genetic constructs. The editing efficiency was evaluated using NGS. Virus-like particles were produced in HEK293T cells using transient expression. VLPs were visualized by electron microscopy. Results: Using dual base editors that induce C-to-T and A-to-G substitutions, we show that high editing precision can be achieved by engineering the linker between the MmCas12m domain and the deaminase domain of the editor. By testing different linker sequences, we have created high-precision dual base editors with narrowed editing windows that can edit a single nucleotide at a target position with high accuracy. Conclusions: We found that shortening the linker to an acceptable length provides a single-nucleotide substitution in vitro with minimal bystander activity (less than 0.8%), while the high-precision MmCas12m dual base editor retains up to 90% of the editing efficiency of the original base editor. These high-precision base editors will be useful in cases where high precision is required, and editing of adjacent nucleotides is undesirable.

title: Long-Read Evidence for Repeat-Associated Structural Heterogeneity in the Mitochondrial Genome of Rhododendron spinuliferum.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Plant mitochondrial genomes are structurally dynamic, and assembled paths may not reflect all molecular configurations. We characterized the mitochondrial genome of Rhododendron spinuliferum and evaluated repeat-associated structural heterogeneity and transcript support for mitochondrial RNA processing. Methods: Public PacBio HiFi reads were assembled and curated; Illumina reads from a second individual provided cross-individual sequence support. Candidate local connections were assessed by strict single-read two-junction phasing. Gene content, repeats, plastid-derived sequences, comparative genomics, phylogeny, predicted C-to-U RNA-editing sites, and mature exon junctions were also examined. Results: Three representative assembly paths totaled 786,593 bp and contained 32 protein-coding loci, three rRNA genes, and 19 tRNA types. A total of 226 HiFi reads supported four local configurations associated with two repeat pairs, and all four persisted across 24 filtering combinations. Nine mitochondrial plastid DNA transfer blocks covered 6.77 kb. Public RNA-seq data provided read-level support for 211 of 475 predicted editing sites and all 12 examined mature exon junctions of nad1, nad2, and nad5. Across six congeners, 99.7% of resolved homologous positions corresponding to RNA-supported sites retained genomic C. Conclusions: These results support repeat-associated local structural heterogeneity in the R. spinuliferum mitogenome and provide a curated DNA- and RNA-supported resource for comparative Rhododendron mitochondrial genomics.

title: Inherited Anemia: A Contemporary Clinical and Lab Review.
abstract: Inherited anemias represent a diverse group of genetic disorders characterized by impaired red blood cell production, increased destruction, or abnormal hemoglobin synthesis. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the contemporary clinical landscape, diagnostic workflows, and therapeutic advancements for both major and rare inherited anemias. Major hemoglobinopathies, including thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD), continue to impose a significant global health burden, while rare conditions such as hereditary hemolytic anemias (HHAs), congenital dyserythropoietic anemias (CDAs), and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) present unique diagnostic challenges. Recent years have seen a paradigm shift in laboratory investigations, primarily driven by the integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) and third-generation sequencing (TGS) into clinical practice. These technologies have revolutionized the identification of causative variants, particularly in complex or multiallelic cases that elude traditional biochemical assays. Furthermore, specialized flow cytometry, such as eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding, remains critical for the diagnosis of red cell membrane defects. Therapeutic management is also undergoing a transformation. Beyond traditional supportive care and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), groundbreaking gene-editing therapies, most notably CRISPR/Cas9-mediated BCL11A enhancer editing, offer the potential for curative outcomes in beta-hemoglobinopathies. Novel pharmacological agents, such as luspatercept for thalassemia and mitapivat for pyruvate kinase deficiency, are providing targeted options to improve erythropoiesis and reduce transfusion burden. Despite these advances, challenges remain in ensuring equitable access to these high-cost interventions and addressing the diagnostic gaps in resource-limited settings.

title: Recent Advances in Lipid Nanoparticles for Cancer Vaccines: From Antigen Delivery to Personalized Immunotherapy.
abstract: In recent years, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have shown great promise as highly flexible delivery systems for cancer vaccines, which enable effective cargo delivery and allow for controlling their distribution, cell-targeting ability and immunogenicity. Innovations in ionizable lipid chemistry, biodegradable formulations, RNA engineering and LNP design resulted in improvements in RNA encapsulation, endosomal escape, delivery outside the liver, and targeting of lymphoid organs and antigen-presenting cells. All these achievements led to an expansion of strategies for developing cancer vaccines from using only mRNA to personal neoantigen vaccines, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), peptide/protein vaccines, and multi-purpose platforms that combine antigen delivery and modulation of the immune system. LNPs are also studied as tools for altering the tumor microenvironment (TME) and boosting anti-tumor immunity through local delivery of cytokines and innate immune modulators. Preliminary clinical results with personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines show strong potential for this approach. However, inflammatory toxicity, suitability for repeated dosing, off-target delivery, difficulties with large-scale production, formulation stability, personalized production schedule and regulatory issues are still significant challenges. New biodegradable and PEG-free formulations, innovations in manufacturing and lyophilization technology, and AI-based approaches in lipid screening could help overcome some of these problems.

title: The Role of SOD1 and Oxidative Stress in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Overview.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-κB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. However, the clinical benefit remains modest. RNA interference has reached human trials, while CRISPR/Cas9 remains in the preclinical stage. Both approaches have shown promising results in experimental models. Further research into ALS pathogenesis is needed to develop treatments that integrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gene-editing strategies.

title: HDAC Inhibitors Potentiate Doxorubicin Cytotoxicity in HepG2 Cells and Alter DNA-Repair- and p53-Associated Transcriptional Programs.
abstract: Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACis) can enhance responses to DNA-damaging chemotherapy, but how they alter doxorubicin (DOX)-induced transcriptional programs remains incompletely understood. We investigated the effects of valproic acid (VPA) and vorinostat (SAHA) on DOX cytotoxicity and associated molecular responses in HepG2 cells. HDAC inhibition, cell viability, apoptosis, and DOX IC50 values were assessed using histone H3 acetylation, cell counting, Alamar Blue assays, and cleaved caspase-3 immunofluorescence. Transcriptomic responses were analyzed by RNA sequencing, differential expression analysis, and Hallmark gene set enrichment analysis, with selected findings evaluated by RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and comparison with published CRISPR/Cas9 DOX-response data. Both HDAC inhibitors increased histone H3 acetylation and enhanced DOX cytotoxicity, markedly reducing DOX IC50 values. VPA co-treatment also increased DOX-induced cleaved caspase-3 signaling. RNA-seq showed broad transcriptional remodeling, including depletion of the DNA-repair gene set following VPA treatment and attenuation of canonical p53-responsive genes during HDACi-DOX co-treatment. Several HDACi-repressed DNA-repair genes overlapped with genes whose loss sensitized cells to DOX in a published CRISPR screen. HDAC inhibition therefore enhances DOX cytotoxicity and is accompanied by alterations in DNA-repair-associated and p53-responsive transcriptional programs.

title: Circulating Tumour Cell GALNT13 Expression Is Associated with Prognosis and Treatment Response in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Reliable circulating biomarkers for prognosis and treatment monitoring in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain limited. Liquid biopsy offers a minimally invasive approach to identify clinically informative tumour-derived markers. Given the emerging role of GalNAc-transferases in cancer biology, we evaluated GALNT13 expression in peripheral blood as a potential biomarker for prognosis and disease monitoring in lung cancer patients. Sensitive molecular assays (nested and digital RT-PCR) were developed to detect GALNT13 mRNA in circulating tumour cells (CTCs). These methods were applied to peripheral blood samples from non-small cell lung cancer patients to assess prognostic value and enable longitudinal monitoring. A cohort of 143 NSCLC patients was analysed, of whom 60% were GALNT13-positive in peripheral blood at baseline. During a five-year follow-up, GALNT13 positivity was significantly associated with reduced overall survival. In several patients, increases in GALNT13 levels preceded radiologic evidence of disease progression. GALNT13 expression in CTCs emerges as a promising biomarker for prognosis and treatment monitoring in NSCLC. Prospective studies in larger cohorts are warranted to validate its clinical utility.

title: CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL Signaling Drives TGF-β2-Mediated Immune Evasion and Pancreatic Cancer Progression.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by extensive neural remodeling and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, both of which contribute to disease progression and therapeutic resistance. However, whether nociceptor-derived signals directly reprogram PDAC cells to promote immune evasion remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized tumor-intrinsic neuroimmune mechanism driven by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) signaling through the receptor complex RAMP1/CALCRL on PDAC cells. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Ramp1 or Calcrl did not alter PDAC cell proliferation in vitro but markedly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in immunocompetent mice. These antitumor effects were lost in immunodeficient hosts, indicating that the pro-tumorigenic function of CGRP signaling depends on an intact host immune system. Consistently, tumor cell-specific loss of Ramp1 or Calcrl remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell effector activity. Mechanistically, CGRP stimulation promoted TGF-β2 expression and secretion by PDAC cells in a RAMP1-dependent manner. Tumor-derived TGF-β2 subsequently acted in a paracrine fashion to suppress CD8+ T-cell activation and cytotoxic function, whereas genetic disruption of RAMP1 or pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling relieved this immunosuppression. Together, these findings define a CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL-TGF-β2 signaling axis through which nociceptive input is converted into tumor-driven adaptive immune evasion in PDAC. This pathway reveals a previously underappreciated mechanism linking neural signaling to PDAC progression and identifies CGRP receptor signaling as a potential therapeutic vulnerability for restoring antitumor immunity and improving the responsiveness of PDAC to immunotherapy.

title: Mitochondrial Metabolic Reprogramming and Immune Evasion in Colorectal Cancer: Research Advances and Mechanistic Perspectives.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most prevalent malignancies of the gastrointestinal tract worldwide. Notably, most patients with microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors show primary resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), creating an unmet clinical need. The mechanisms underlying immune evasion and strategies to overcome therapeutic resistance have therefore become important topics in CRC immunology research. Recent studies indicate that mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC. Tumor cells display metabolic plasticity through dynamic shifts between glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which can intensify the depletion of critical nutrients, particularly glucose and glutamine, within the tumor microenvironment (TME). These metabolic changes can also promote the accumulation of immunosuppressive metabolites, including lactate, thereby impairing the function of effector cells such as CD8+ T cells and dendritic cells (DCs) and supporting the expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Lactate may further reshape the immune landscape through hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 1 (HCAR1) signaling and histone lactylation. In parallel, mitochondrial quality control can regulate tumor immunogenicity by influencing mtDNA availability and cGAS-STING signaling. Therapeutic approaches targeting glycolysis, glutamine metabolism, fatty acid oxidation, lactate transport, and mitochondrial dynamics have shown immune-sensitizing activity in preclinical models. Nanodelivery systems and gene-editing technologies may improve the spatial and cellular specificity of these interventions. This review summarizes how mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC and evaluates mitochondria-directed strategies for improving treatment responsiveness, particularly in MSS CRC.

title: Terpenoids: A Comprehensive Review on Biosynthesis, Applications and Enhancement Strategies for Translational Research.
abstract: There is growing interest in natural bioactive compounds as potentially safer and more sustainable sources of therapeutic agents. Terpenoids, one of the most structurally diverse and biologically active classes of natural products, are derived from repeating isoprene units and possess a broad range of pharmacological and industrial applications. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in terpenoid biosynthesis, structural classification, and therapeutic applications. It also discusses emerging approaches for enhancing large-scale production, improving functional efficacy, and overcoming pharmacokinetic limitations. Attention is given to terpenoids currently undergoing clinical evaluation, along with their progress toward commercial development. Despite substantial preclinical evidence supporting their therapeutic potential, the clinical translation of many terpenoids remains limited. Key challenges include poor aqueous solubility, low permeability, slow dissolution, and high lipophilicity, which can collectively restrict systemic bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, only a relatively small proportion of biologically active terpenoids have progressed to advanced stages of clinical development, highlighting a considerable gap between experimental findings and clinical application. This review integrates current knowledge of terpenoid biosynthesis, biological activities, production strategies, and translational development while highlighting sustainable and scientifically driven approaches that may facilitate their future therapeutic and commercial utilization.

title: Neurobiological Pathways Underlying Opioid Addiction and Overdose: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Targets, and Insights from Zebrafish Model.
abstract: The worldwide opioid epidemic continues to claim thousands of lives each year and remains one of the most urgent global public health challenges, driven by the high abuse potential and overdose risk of potent, fully synthetic μ-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists such as fentanyl. While fentanyl is highly effective in pain management, it also carries severe risks including respiratory depression, addiction, and fatal overdose. Understanding the neurobiological pathways underlying these risks is essential for developing safer analgesics and effective interventions. The MOR, a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that modulates neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission in important brain circuits like the ventral tegmental area (VTA), nucleus accumbens (NAc), and prefrontal cortex (PFC), is the primary receptor through which opioids exert their therapeutic effects. Dopaminergic dysregulation, transcriptional remodeling, and altered synaptic plasticity are neuroadaptations brought on by long-term opioid exposure that contribute to dependence and relapse. Life-threatening opioid toxicity is primarily driven by MOR-mediated suppression of respiratory networks, with risk shaped by dose, pharmacokinetics, receptor efficacy, and circuit sensitivity. Zebrafish (Danio rerio) provide a powerful complementary system for dissecting opioid-related neurocircuitry and screening for potential therapeutics. Zebrafish share conserved opioid-signaling components with mammals, and larval transparency facilitates in vivo imaging of neuronal activity at cellular resolution. Behavioral paradigms capture reward-related and drug-seeking phenotypes, while CRISPR-based approaches offer a means to investigate receptor-specific functions in validated models. In addition, zebrafish larvae provide an efficient platform for high-throughput screening of compounds that modulate opioid signaling and respiratory-related phenotypes. Together, insights from human, rodent, and zebrafish studies provide a more integrated understanding of opioid overdose and addiction neurobiology. This review incorporates current knowledge on the molecular and circuit-level mechanisms driving these processes and discusses how zebrafish models accelerate the discovery of safer analgesics and novel treatments for opioid use disorder and overdose.

title: Surveillance, Detection and Therapeutic Innovation in Antimicrobial Resistance in the Age of Polycrisis: From Genomic and Digital Innovation to One Health Integration.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is increasingly strained by interconnected global crises, i.e., pandemics, climate change, armed conflicts, population mobility, and health inequalities, that disrupt healthcare delivery, diagnostic capacity, and laboratory infrastructure. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and digital surveillance offer the potential to shift from reactive reporting to predictive intelligence that anticipates resistance threats, although current implementations remain sector-specific, retrospective, and project-funded. Environmental surveillance, particularly wastewater monitoring coupled with genomic epidemiology, provides early warnings at population and ecosystem levels. The future integration of AI across human, animal, and environmental sectors could enable unified One Health intelligence; no such integrated platform is currently operational. This review focuses primarily on bacterial AMR. It examines how global drivers strain surveillance, how genomic, metagenomic, digital, and AI-enabled technologies reshape AMR detection and prediction, and the emerging non-antibiotic therapeutic landscape, including bacteriophage therapy, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, microbiota-directed interventions, nanomedicine, host-directed therapies, photodynamic therapy, and vaccines. It then explores how these innovations can be integrated within a One Health framework to support coordinated global preparedness. Addressing the AMR crisis will require not only technological innovation but also equitable implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and resilient systems.

title: JAG1-siRNA-Lipid Nanoparticles Suppress Infantile Hemangioma Angiogenesis.
abstract: Background: Infantile hemangioma (IH) is the most common benign vascular tumor of infancy, and propranolol, the current first-line treatment, requires prolonged twice-daily dosing and has adverse systemic effects. Methods: Using the public GSE127487 transcriptomic dataset together with weighted gene coexpression network analysis and protein-protein interaction network analysis, we identified JAG1, a principal endothelial Notch ligand, as the most connected node in the disease protein-protein interaction network, with elevated expression across all clinical stages of IH. To test its use as a drug target, we engineered a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) composed of SM-102/DSPC/cholesterol/DMG-PEG2000 that carried JAG1-specific siRNA. Results: At an N/P ratio of 8, the formulation efficiently encapsulated the siRNA, protected it from serum nucleases, and remained colloidally stable. LNP-mediated JAG1 knockdown reduced Matrigel network formation by hemangioma stem cells in vitro. In a hemangioma xenograft model, the intratumoral delivery of JAG1 siRNA reduced tumor volume by approximately 75%, tumor weight by approximately 80%, and microvessel density by more than half, without overt toxicity to the measures collected (body weight and clinical observation). Conclusions: In this preclinical model, JAG1 emerges as a credible therapeutic target, and LNP-delivered JAG1 siRNA is a promising gene-silencing strategy against IH angiogenesis.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Genome-Wide CRISPR-Cas Screens to Identify Host Factors Involved in HIV-1 Infection.
abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication depends on a complex interplay between viral proteins and host cellular factors, which represent promising therapeutic targets. However, systematic integration of results from genome-wide CRISPR screens for HIV host factors remains limited. Here, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens to identify host dependency, restriction, and latency-promoting factors in HIV-1 infection. Following PRISMA guidelines, we identified 11 eligible studies from which we extracted 26 gene lists. These were classified into three phenotypic categories, including dependency (5 lists), restriction (10 lists), and latency-promoting (7 lists), and integrated using meta-analysis by information content (MAIC). GO over-representation analysis and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis were performed on MAIC-ranked gene lists to characterize pathway architectures. MAIC successfully recovered well-established host factors, including the entry receptors CD4, CCR5, and CXCR4; the integration cofactor PSIP1 (LEDGF/p75); and the restriction factors TRIM5, TRIM22, PML, G3BP1, and EIF2AK2. RNF114 emerged as the top-ranked restriction factor, supported by four independent publication-level categories. Additional high-confidence hits included TRIM56, BIRC3, DTX3L, and components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system across the dependency and latency datasets, further supporting the robustness of the MAIC framework. Beyond these canonical factors, we identified multiple undercharacterized genes and pathways, including coagulation and IL-17 signaling in dependency factors, SUMOylation and DNA damage response in restriction factors, and the Integrator complex and proteasome-granule co-enrichment in latency-promoting factors. Leading-edge analysis confirmed that most of these non-canonical enrichments are driven by coherent gene modules rather than a small set of pleiotropic hubs. These findings reveal distinct pathway architectures across the three infection states and highlight previously unrecognized host processes that may serve as targets for antiviral therapy. Our analysis provides a comprehensive resource for guiding future mechanistic studies of host-HIV interactions and developing strategies to enhance immunity, block viral replication, and reverse latency.

title: Construction and Immunological Evaluation of a Bicomponent Zika mRNA Vaccine.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: There is evidence for the protective effects of antibodies targeting non-structural protein 1 (NS1) of Zika virus (ZIKV); however, effective vaccines against ZIKV remain lacking.
METHODS: In this study, lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated mRNA vaccines were designed based on the envelope domain III (EDIII) and NS1 sequences of the ZIKV FSS13025 strain, while protective efficacy was evaluated in a murine model using a ZIKV isolate obtained from Zhejiang Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Zhejiang CDC).
RESULTS: The vaccines were evaluated for key quality attributes-including particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and encapsulation efficiency-as well as immunogenicity and protective efficacy. Both monovalent vaccine components exhibited uniform particle sizes (PDI < 0.2) and high encapsulation efficiencies (≥80%) and induced high levels of antigen-specific antibodies in mice in a dose-dependent manner. The EDIII mRNA vaccine elicited moderate ZIKV-neutralizing antibody titers as measured by PRNT50, whereas the NS1 vaccine did not induce detectable neutralizing antibodies. Both bicomponent (EDIII + NS1) mRNA vaccines induced a Th1-biased cellular immune response in mouse splenocytes, with significantly greater IFN-γ production compared with either monovalent vaccine. In viral challenge experiments using 1 × 105 PFU ZIKV (Zhejiang CDC isolate, intraperitoneal), the bicomponent vaccine provided complete protection, with 100% survival across all dose groups. In contrast, the EDIII and NS1 monovalent vaccines showed partial protection: mortality was observed in the 20 μg dose groups and exceeded 50% in the 10 μg dose groups.
CONCLUSIONS: These results demonstrate that the bicomponent EDIII + NS1 mRNA vaccine combination confers superior protective efficacy compared with either component alone, consistent with a synergistic effect between humoral and cellular immune responses. This study provides a novel strategy for next-generation Zika vaccine development.

title: Construction of Recombinant PRV Expressing PRRSV Antigens and Evaluation of Their Protective Efficacy in Pigs Against Homologous Challenge.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains a major threat to the global swine industry, while the emergence of variant pseudorabies virus (PRV) strains has further complicated disease control in China. This study aimed to develop a PRV-based viral vector platform for PRRSV antigen delivery and evaluate its safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy. Methods: A five-gene-deleted variant PRV strain, PRV-JM-DF, was used as the vector backbone. Candidate genomic insertion sites and endogenous late promoters were systematically screened, followed by construction of recombinant PRVs expressing PRRSV GP2, GP3, GP4, GP5, and M individually or as tandem antigen constructs. Recombinant viruses were characterized for antigen expression, replication, and genetic stability. Safety and immunogenicity were initially evaluated in female BALB/c mice, and the leading candidates were further assessed for safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy in 18 Landrace pigs of either sex following challenge with highly pathogenic PRRSV HuN4. Results: The TK locus supported efficient foreign-gene expression, and pUL39 exhibited the highest activity among the tested endogenous late promoters. The recombinant viruses retained replication competence and genetic stability. Among the candidates, rPRV-C-4T induced robust PRRSV- and PRV-specific neutralizing antibody responses and showed no obvious adverse effects during the experimental observation period in pigs. Following HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge, all rPRV-C-4T-immunized pigs survived and exhibited reduced viremia, viral shedding and tissue viral loads, together with markedly alleviated pathological lesions. Conclusions: rPRV-C-4T provided protection against homologous HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge while maintaining PRV-directed immune responses, supporting its potential as a PRV-vectored multivalent vaccine candidate.

title: Retinitis Pigmentosa: A Review of Its Pathogenesis and Emerging Molecular and Cellular Therapies.
abstract: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is the most common inherited retinal dystrophy and remains largely untreatable. This review summarizes RP pathogenesis and critically appraises emerging therapeutic strategies, including gene augmentation, gene editing, RNA-based therapies, gene-agnostic and neuroprotective approaches, stem-cell therapy and their delivery platforms. We compare these strategies according to mutation mechanism, disease stage, durability, delivery route, and current level of clinical evidence. Although several approaches have shown improved structural and functional outcomes in preclinical and early-phase studies, RPE65-directed gene augmentation (voretigen neparvovec) remains the only approved therapy, and even it does not halt degeneration. For most modalities, long-term efficacy, safety, durability and clinical validation are not yet established, and translation is further constrained by delivery, immunogenicity, manufacturing, and cost. Rather than a realized paradigm shift, current evidence points to a rapidly advancing but still largely investigational field with successful clinical translation remaining elusive.

title: Development of mitochondrial base editing technology and its application in animals.
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations constitute major genetic determinants of mitochondrial disorders and contribute to the progressive dysfunction of energy-demanding tissues. However, precise manipulation of the mitochondrial genome remains a formidable challenge for decades due to the unique structural and biological features of mitochondria. Recent breakthroughs in mitochondrial base-editing technologies address longstanding barriers in mitochondrial genome engineering by enabling programmable nucleotide conversion without introducing DNA double-strand breaks. Mitochondrial base editing evolves rapidly from a proof-of-concept strategy in cultured cells into a versatile platform for generating animal models, dissecting mitochondrial gene function and exploring therapeutic interventions for mitochondrial diseases. Recent advances enable the creation of animals carrying defined pathogenic mtDNA variants and provide initial evidence supporting the feasibility of in vivo mitochondrial genome correction and disease amelioration. Here, we review the evolution of mitochondrial base-editing technologies and summarize the major editing platforms, with particular emphasis on recent advances in editor engineering, expansion of targeting capabilities, generation of animal disease models and emerging therapeutic applications. We further discuss the remaining challenges, including editing precision, target-site accessibility, delivery efficiency, and comprehensive safety evaluation. Finally, we highlight future opportunities for developing next-generation mitochondrial genome-editing systems and advancing their translation toward clinical applications.

title: Pyroptosis in cancer nanotherapy: Molecular mechanisms and advanced nanosystems (Review).
abstract: Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by activation of inflammasome complexes and caspase signaling cascades, ultimately leading to the cleavage and activation of pore‑forming executioners such as gasdermin D (GSDMD), ‑E and ‑B. Accumulating evidence indicates that pyroptosis induction in cancer cells exerts potent antitumor effects. As a result, recent therapeutic strategies such as cancer nanotherapy have increasingly focused on harnessing pyroptotic cell death to improve cancer treatment outcomes. This review aimed to explore recent advances in nanotechnology‑based approaches designed to induce pyroptosis in cancer cells, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance antitumor immunity and overcome treatment resistance. It explored four distinct nanoplatforms: i) Chemo‑photodynamic systems that trigger GSDME‑mediated death by generating reactive oxygen species; ii) magneto‑plasmonic nanoparticles that use GSDME activation to modulate the tumor microenvironment, turning 'cold' tumors 'hot'; iii) bioorthogonal chemical delivery tools leveraging click chemistry for site‑specific gasdermin release; and iv) nano‑CRISPR activation scaffolds designed to boost GSDME expression and work alongside cisplatin. Beyond these platforms, the present review highlights how immune cell‑derived granzymes and interferon‑γ drive vital downstream pyroptotic pathways via GSDME and GSDMB activation. Lastly, the review weighs clinical risks, such as chronic systemic inflammation and tumor‑promoting environments, providing a realistic perspective on how to safely progress these preclinical nanotherapies into selective, effective clinical immunotherapies.

title: Gene therapy for epilepsy: From SCN1A to broadened therapeutic horizons (Review).
abstract: Genetic epilepsy, for which the molecular mechanisms are relatively well defined in numerous monogenic forms, represents an attractive model for the transition from symptomatic seizure control to mechanism‑driven correction. However, gene therapy strategies differ in their mechanisms of action, adaptability to specific mutations and translational maturity, making rational selection of interventions based on variant‑specific functional consequences an important clinical challenge. The present review examined five nucleic acid‑based therapeutic strategies, namely gene supplementation, enhancement of endogenous gene expression, gene silencing, DNA editing and RNA editing, for major causative genes, using mutation‑specific functional consequences [loss‑of‑function (LOF) vs. gain‑of‑function] as the primary framework for therapeutic decision‑making. The mechanisms and suitability of each approach are analysed, and their performance in terms of cell‑type specificity, delivery vectors and safety is evaluated by integrating evidence from animal models, induced pluripotent stem cell‑derived neurons and organoids and clinical trials. The present review also summarised key translational barriers, including vector cargo constraints, blood‑brain barrier penetration, off‑target and immune‑associated risks, therapeutic dosing windows and the timing of developmental intervention. Antisense oligonucleotides and regulatory adeno‑associated viral approaches, supported by mature delivery platforms and manageable safety profiles, have progressed furthest towards clinical validation. Endogenous gene activation strategies, such as CRISPR activation, offer a gene replacement‑free approach for LOF disorders but remain preclinical. DNA and RNA editing, while potentially capable of durable disease modification, require further evidence on delivery efficiency and long‑term homeostatic safety. Gene therapy for genetic epilepsy is undergoing a key transition from proof‑of‑concept studies to individualised clinical application. Future progress will depend on integrating personalised intervention design, multi‑target therapeutic combinations, artificial intelligence‑assisted sequence optimisation and standardised translational models, with the potential to drive a paradigm shift from seizure suppression to mechanistic correction.

title: Astrocytic Cystine/Glutamate Antiporters Promote Diabetic Encephalopathy via the Induction of Glutamate Excitotoxicity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cystine/glutamate antiporter (xCT) imports extracellular cystine in exchange for intracellular glutamate. Although it plays an essential role in diabetes-associated processes such as impaired wound healing, its contribution to diabetic encephalopathy (DE) remains unclear.
METHODS: Wild-type and xCT-deficient (xCT-/-) mice were subjected to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) induction using a highfat diet combined with streptozotocin. xCT expression and activity in the brain were evaluated through quantitative polymerase chain reaction, Western blotting, immunofluorescence, chloride-dependent [14C]-L-cystine uptake, and measurements of extracellular glutamate. An adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 approach was employed to generate region-specific, cell type-restricted xCT knockout animals. Neuronal injury and cognitive function were evaluated via in vivo propidium iodide (PI) and neuronal nuclei antigen (NeuN) double staining, the Y-maze spontaneous alternation test, the Morris water maze test, and the object location test.
RESULTS: xCT deficiency protected mice from T2DM-induced DE. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia upregulated xCT expression via activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), thereby enhancing xCT function in hippocampal astrocytes. This maladaptive increase promoted excessive extracellular glutamate, neuronal loss, and cognitive impairment. Both astrocyte-specific deletion of xCT and pharmacological inhibition of xCT ameliorated these deficits.
CONCLUSION: These findings identify astrocytic xCT as a key driver of diabetes-induced glutamate excitotoxicity and DE progression, underscoring its potential as a therapeutic target.

title: Decoding proteomic complexity of transcript variants and homologous isoforms for precision therapeutics.
abstract: The traditional "one gene, one protein" paradigm is insufficient to capture the vast phenotypic and physiological complexity of eukaryotes. This review aims to comprehensively elucidate the molecular mechanisms of transcriptomic diversification, namely, alternative splicing, alternative usage of promoter, and alternative polyadenylation, and their profound impacts on cellular homeostasis and human disease. By synthesizing recent breakthroughs in targeted long-read RNA sequencing, single-cell isoform-specific multiomics, and AI-driven 3D structural modeling, we systematically examine how transcript variants are generated and functionally annotated. Our analysis highlights that multiple transcript variants originating from a single genetic locus are not merely redundant copies; rather, subtle sequence alterations dynamically rewire protein-protein interaction networks and dictate precise subcellular localization. The exquisite spatiotemporal regulation of these variants controls critical cell fate decisions and organ development. Consequently, the pathological dysregulation of these processes, frequently termed spliceopathies, acts as a primary driver in severe pathologies, including cancer multidrug resistance, metabolic reprogramming, and neurodegenerative disorders. In conclusion, understanding the eukaryotic proteome requires a fundamental shift from conventional gene-level to isoform-level perspectives. Decoding the complex regulatory syntax of transcript variants paves the way for next-generation precision medicine, highlighting the therapeutic potential of RNA-targeted interventions, such as antisense oligonucleotides and CRISPR-based RNA editing, to correct pathogenic isoforms.

title: Knockdown of the long non-coding RNA DNAAF3-AS1 activates the p53 pathway and remodels the H3K36me3 landscape
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs are increasingly recognised as chromatin regulators, yet most remain functionally uncharacterised. DNAAF3-AS1, transcribed antisense to the ciliary dynein assembly factor gene DNAAF3, is almost exclusively associated with H3K36me3 in the HiMoRNA database. H3K36me3 ChIP-seq in human dermal fibroblasts following DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown with two independent antisense oligonucleotides revealed a marked reduction of gene-body H3K36me3, with residual signal shifted towards promoters. In FANTOM6 CAGE, DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown activated the p53 pathway and triggered differential promoter usage in genes enriched for p53 and apoptotic regulators. Consistently, genes that gained gene-body H3K36me3 upon knockdown were enriched for apoptosis-related pathways. In line with high expression of DNAAF3-AS1 in testis, analysis based on the adult human testis single-cell atlas suggests that DNAAF3-AS1 may contribute to promoter-level H3K36me3 regulation during late spermatogenesis. Together, these results identify DNAAF3-AS1 as a chromatin-associated lncRNA that links H3K36me3 maintenance to p53 signalling.

title: Naked antisense oligonucleotides access the cytosol during early endocytic trafficking
abstract: Phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) enter cells, but their site of productive escape remains uncertain. We combined live-cell imaging and ratiometric pH measurements to follow a Malat1-targeting ASO internalized without a delivery vehicle. In U2OS cells, less than 4% of internalized ASO reached the nucleus under conditions that reduced Malat1 RNA by >90%. Most ASO accumulated in late endosomes, endolysosomes and lysosomes as foci and broadly distributed luminal signal. These compartments underwent neutralization without detectable membrane rupture or galectin-3 recruitment. ASO foci showed constrained motion, consistent with association with endolysosomal constituents. L-leucyl-L-leucine methyl ester-induced membrane damage or Calcium dependent lysosome exocytosis released dextran while retaining luminal ASO. Loss of the stress-granule scaffolding proteins G3BP1/2 modestly enhanced ASO activity without detectable endolysosomal damage. Tantalosin, a small molecule that perturbs endosomal recycling, redistributed the ESCRT-III protein IST1 to endosomes. It enhanced early escape of SYTOX Green and ASOs, detected by nuclear accumulation, and increased Malat1 knockdown, with cell-type-dependent responses. Tantalosin did not detectably increase nuclear ASO accumulation after sequestration in late compartments. These findings place productive ASO escape early in endocytic trafficking, most likely in early or recycling endosomes, before sequestration in largely nonproductive late compartments.

title: Double-Stranded RNA Profiling with Mass Photometry
abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is a potent immunogenic impurity and its detection is a critical quality attribute in characterizing mRNA therapeutics. Standard analytical methods (e.g., sandwich ELISA) are only able to resolve the bulk presence of dsRNA and cannot characterize the different sub-species that may be present within a mRNA sample.. In this study, we use mass photometry (MP) as a single-molecule analytical platform for the simultaneous detection and characterization of dsRNA impurities in mRNA samples. We demonstrate how ionic strength can interfere with the stability of the mAb/dsRNA complex and measure the binding affinity (1 nM) under a set of parameters for reproducible characterization of the complex. We then leverage the J2 antibody to identify antibody/dsRNA complexes that then resolve dsRNA-positive species within an mRNA sample based on discrete molecular weight profiles. Furthermore, we introduce a novel MP assay that harnesses the repulsive surface chemistry of uncoated glass to exclude the bulk mRNA analyte to enable the use of higher loading concentrations to sensitively profile trace dsRNA impurities as antibody-bound species. This work establishes MP as a valuable next generation mRNA analytical tool for analyzing dsRNA byproducts within mRNA samples.

title: Fundamentals on the Kinetic and Thermodynamic Analysis of Oligonucleotide DNA Hybridization by Surface Plasmon Resonance: A Guide for HIF1α Antisense Design.
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) are nucleotide polymers that hybridize to sense strands and have been successful in treating a variety of diseases. A wide range of strategies have been investigated to optimize and develop ASO for clinical studies. A key objective for this study was to provide an overview of the range of detailed data that can be obtained and provide an updated method review on how to design surface plasmon resonance (SPR) kinetic experiments for DNA oligonucleotide hybridization studies that can also be applied to other ASO including peptide nucleic acids (PNA). We describe many lessons learned from published literature and provide a state-of-the-art strategy and methods for generating not only kinetic but also thermodynamic characterizations of oligonucleotide hybridization. In this study we have performed an SPR kinetic and thermodynamic analysis for the hybridization of HIF1 antisense DNA strands to its immobilized Intron2-Exon3 splice site sense DNA strand to provide insight, in general, on the optimal length and insight into optimal design of DNA ASOs. We provide a process on how to design experiments to: 1.) obtain oligonucleotide-length dependent kinetics, 2.) analyze reactions to obtain association and dissociation rate kinetics (ka, kd), assess if hybridization follows a 2-state model and to obtain kinetic dissociation constants (Kd), 3.) perform temperature-dependent hybridization kinetics to obtain thermodynamic values ({Delta}H{degrees}, {Delta}S{degrees} and {Delta}G{degrees}) that can give insight into the molecular interactions driving hybridization, 4.) compare experimental thermodynamic values to values derived from nearest-neighbor prediction models to identify atypical reactions and importantly 5.) enable calculations to predict oligomer hybridization affinity at the physiological 37 {degrees}C temperature to assess if the design of the oligomer will have the required cellular activity for a therapeutic effect. The strategy and results presented throughout the paper are compared to previous SPR reports and suggestions made to optimize kinetic studies.

title: Dual-Antigen CCHFV Vaccine Induces Neutralizing Immunity and Protection Against Lethal Challenge
abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a WHO-priority pathogen with high mortality and wide global distribution. A major challenge in CCHFV vaccine development is identifying antigens that induce functional cellular and humoral immunity. We previously showed that the CCHF nucleoprotein (NP) elicits protective responses in mice and non-human primates but does not induce neutralizing antibodies. We therefore systematically screened six chimeric DNA vaccines expressing different CCHF glycoproteins combined with NP. A construct comprising the ectodomain of the glycoprotein Gc and NP elicited robust antibody and T-cell responses to both antigens. The Gc-NP gene was subsequently developed as a lipid nanoparticle-formulated mRNA vaccine using a scalable manufacturing pipeline. Gc-NP mRNA-LNP induced robust antigen-specific humoral and cellular responses comparable to those elicited by the corresponding DNA vaccine, despite the substantially lower dose. Both vaccine approaches generated Gc-directed neutralizing antibody responses against CCHFV pseudovirus and protected mice against homologous Hoti and heterologous IbAr10200 strain challenge. These findings demonstrate that systematic antigen screening combined with genetic vaccine platforms can identify a potent multi-antigen CCHF vaccine candidate.

title: A transient third metal ion shapes the catalytic cycle of a group I intron ribozyme.
abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of bio-chemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg 2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between G exo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5 ' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the G exo in the first step, and analogously the G ω in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the p K a at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.
